It is not far-fetched that it is fabricated (mawdu'), for all these expressions are rejected and far from the speech of one given *jawami' al-kalim* (concise, comprehensive speech). al-Tha'labi related it from the hadith of 'Aishah, and al-Khatib related it from the hadith of Anas, and al-Khatib related something similar from the hadith of 'Ali, more briefly than this.

al-Bazzar related from Ibn 'Abbas who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said concerning Surah Ya-Sin: "I wish that it were in the heart of every person of my Ummah." Its chain is thus: He said: Salamah ibn Shabib narrated to us; Ibrahim ibn al-Hakam ibn Aban narrated to us, from his father, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, and he mentioned it.

al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh related, and al-Suyuti said with a weak chain, from Anas who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever persists in reciting Ya-Sin every night and then dies, dies as a martyr (shahid)."

al-Darimi related from Ibn 'Abbas who said: Whoever recites Ya-Sin in the morning, is given ease for his day until evening, and whoever recites it at the beginning of his night, is given ease for his night until morning.

**In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful**

**His saying: ﴿Ya-Sin﴾ [1]**

The majority (al-Jumhur) recited it with the nun sukun (silent). Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Hamzah, Hafs, Qalun, and Warsh recited with idgham (assimilation) of the nun into the waw that follows it. 'Isa ibn 'Umar recited it with a fatha on the nun, and Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Abi Ishaq, and Nasr ibn 'Asim recited it with a kasra. The fatha is for *bina'* (indeclinability) or because it is the object of an implied verb whose estimate is: *utlu Ya-Sin* (recite Ya-Sin). The kasra is also for *bina'*, like *jayr*. It was said: the fatha and kasra are to avoid the meeting of two sakins (unvowelled letters).

As for the reason for the majority's recitation with sukun on the nun, it is because it is recited in the manner of a list (ta'did), so it has no share of *i'rab* (grammatical inflection).

Harun al-A'war, Muhammad ibn al-Sumayfa', and al-Kalbi recited it with a damma on the nun, for *bina'*, like *mundhu*, *haythu*, and *qattu*. It was also said: it is the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "this is Ya-Sin." It is not declined (*mamnu' min al-sarf*) due to being a proper noun (*'alamiyyah*) and feminine gender (*ta'nith*).

There is disagreement about the meaning of this word. It was said: its meaning is "O man" or "O person."

Ibn al-Anbari said: Pausing on *Ya-Sin* is good (hasan) for the one who says it is the opening of the surah. For the one who says its meaning is "O man," one does not pause on it.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr and others said: It is one of the names of Muhammad (ﷺ), and the evidence is ﴿Indeed you are among the messengers﴾. From it is the saying of al-Sa'd al-Himyari:

*O soul, do not exhaust yourself in sincere advice,*
*striving for love, except for the family of Ya-Sin.*

From it is His saying: ﴿Peace upon the family of Ilyasin﴾ [al-Saffat: 130], meaning: upon the family of Muhammad. What is meant by "Ilyasin" will come in al-Saffat.

al-Wahidi said: Ibn 'Abbas and the commentators said: It means "O person," meaning Muhammad (ﷺ).

Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: Its meaning is "O master of mankind."

Malik said: It is one of the names of Allah, the Exalted. Ashhab related this from him.

Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami related from Ja'far al-Sadiq that its meaning is "O master."

Ka'b said: It is an oath which Allah swore by. al-Zajjaj preferred that its meaning is "O Muhammad."

They differed on whether it is Arabic or non-Arabic. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and 'Ikrimah said: it is Abyssinian (Habashi).

al-Kalbi said: It is Syriac (Suryani), which the Arabs spoke, so it became part of their language. al-Sha'bi said: It is in the language of Tayy. al-Hasan said: It is in the language of Kalb. What has preceded in Ta-Ha and at the beginning of Surah al-Baqarah suffices here without lengthening.

**And the Wise Qur'an [2]**

Genitive (*bi al-jarr*), on the basis that it is sworn by directly (*muqsam bihi ibtida'an*).

It was also said: it is conjoined (ma'tuf) to Ya-Sin, on the estimate that it is in the genitive by an implied oath particle.

al-Naqqash said: Allah did not swear by the messengership of any of His prophets in His Book except for Muhammad (ﷺ), exalting him and glorifying him. *Al-Hakim* means the perfectly established (*al-muhkam*), which does not contradict or conflict with itself; or *al-Hakim* means its Speaker (qa'iluhu).

The response of the oath is: ﴿Indeed you are among the messengers﴾. This is a rebuttal of those among the disbelievers who denied his messengership by their saying: ﴿You are not a messenger﴾ [al-Ra'd: 43].

His saying: ﴿This is a straight path﴾ is another predicate of *inna* (indeed), meaning: indeed you are upon a straight path. The straight path is the upright way that leads to the desired goal.

al-Zajjaj said: It is according to the way of the prophets who preceded you. It may also be in the accusative position as a circumstantial (*hal*).

**﴿The revelation of the All-Mighty, the Most Merciful﴾ [5]**

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, and Abu Bakr recited *tanzilu* with a damma, on the basis that it is the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "it is the revelation." It may also be the predicate of His saying *Ya-Sin* if it is made a name of the surah. The rest recited it with a fatha, on the basis of it being a verbal noun (*masdariyyah*), i.e., "Allah revealed that revelation, the revelation of the All-Mighty, the Most Merciful."

The meaning is: "Indeed you, O Muhammad, are [of] the revelation of the All-Mighty, the Most Merciful." The first (the damma) is preferable.

It was said: it is in the accusative as a praise (*al-mad*) according to the reading of those who recited it with a fatha. He, glorified is He, expressed the revealed thing by a verbal noun as an intensification, until it is as if it were the very revelation itself.

Abu Haywah, al-Tirmidhi, Abu Ja'far Yazid ibn al-Qa'qa', and Shaybah recited *tanzili* with a kasra, as an attribute (na't) of the Qur'an or a substitute (badal) for it.

The *lam* in ﴿so that you may warn a people whose fathers were not warned﴾ may be connected to *tanzil*, or to an implied verb indicated by "from among the messengers," i.e., "We sent you so that you may warn." The *ma* in *ma undhira aba'uhum* is negating: i.e., their fathers were not warned. It may also be relative (*mawsulah*) or descriptive (*mawsufah*), i.e., "to warn a people, that which their fathers were warned," or "to warn them of a punishment with which their fathers were warned." It may also be verbal (*masdariyyah*), i.e., "the warning of their fathers." On the view that it is negating, the meaning is: "no messenger from among themselves came to their fathers." It may also be meant that their nearest fathers were not warned, due to the long duration of the interval (fatrah). His saying: ﴿so they are heedless﴾ is connected to the negation of warning according to the first aspect, i.e., their fathers were not warned, so because of that they are heedless. According to the later aspects, it is connected to His saying "so that you may warn," i.e., they are heedless of what We warned their fathers with. Most of the people of tafsir went to the view that the meaning is negation, and this is the apparent sense of the arrangement, because the clause ﴿so they are heedless﴾ follows what precedes it.

The *lam* in His saying: ﴿Certainly the word has come into effect upon most of them﴾ is the *lam* that prefaces an oath, i.e., "By Allah, certainly the word has come into effect upon most of them." The meaning of *haqqa* is: it was established and became obligatory. *Al-qawl* (the word), i.e., the punishment, is upon most of them, i.e., most of the people of Makkah, or most of the disbelievers in general, or most of the disbelievers of the Arabs, namely those who died upon disbelief and persisted in it throughout their lives. The statement ﴿so they do not believe﴾ therefore follows from what precedes it in this sense, i.e., because Allah, glorified is He, knew of them their persistence in the disbelief they were in and that they would die upon it. It was also said: the word mentioned here is His saying, glorified is He: ﴿So the truth is, and the truth I say: I will surely fill Hell with you and with those who follow you﴾ [Sad: 84–85].

The sentence ﴿Indeed We have placed upon their necks shackles﴾ is an affirmation of what precedes it; it depicts their condition with the condition of those whose necks were chained. So the shackles reach up to the chins, and therefore they cannot turn, nor can they bend their necks. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿so they are with heads raised﴾, i.e., raising their heads while lowering their gaze.

al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: *al-muqmah* is one who lowers his gaze after raising his head. The meaning of *al-iqmah* is raising the head and lowering the gaze. It is said: "the camel *aqmaha* his head and *qamaha*," when he raised his head and did not drink water.

al-Azhari said: Allah meant that when their hands were chained at their necks, the shackles raised them up to their chins, and their heads were raised upward (*su'da'*). So they are with heads raised due to the shackles lifting them.

Qatadah said: The meaning of *muqmahun* is "shackled." The first is preferable, and from it is the saying of the poet:

*And we, around its edges, are sitting,*
*lowering our gaze like camels with raised heads (qimah).*

(p-1219) Al-Zajjaj said: It is said that the two months of Kanun (December and January) are called "the two months of qimah," because when camels come to water they raise their heads because of the intense cold. He cited the verse of Abu Zayd al-Hudhali:

*A youth like the son of al-Aghharr, when we spend the winter, and provisions become scarce in the two months of qimah.*

Abu Ubaydah said: "qamaha al-ba'ir" means the camel raised its head from the trough without drinking.

Abu Ubaydah also said: It is a parable (mathal) that God struck for them, regarding their refusal to accept guidance, like the refusal of one who is shackled. This is as it is said: "So-and-so is a donkey," meaning he does not see guidance. As the poet said:

*For them, against right guidance, are shackles and fetters.*

Al-Farra' said: This is a figurative expression, meaning: We have restrained them from spending in the way of God. It is like His saying: ﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck﴾ [al-Isra: 29]. Al-Dahhak also said this.

It is said: The verse refers to what is done to people in the Fire, namely the placing of shackles on their necks, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿When the shackles are on their necks﴾ [Ghafir: 71]. Ibn Abbas recited: "Inna ja'alna fi aymanihim aghlalan" (Indeed We have put shackles on their right hands). Al-Zajjaj said: that is, on their hands.

Al-Nahhas said: This reading is an explanation (tafsir), and one may not recite in a way that contradicts the Mushaf (the written codex of the Qur'an).

He said: According to the reading of the majority, there is an ellipsis in the sentence. The estimated meaning is: We have put shackles on their necks and on their hands, so they reach up to the chins. The word *hiya* (it/they, feminine) is a reference to the hands, not to the necks. The Arabs omit such things. A parallel is God's saying: ﴿garments that protect you from the heat﴾ [al-Nahl: 81], where the implied meaning is: "and garments that protect you from the cold," because whatever protects from heat also protects from cold. Since the shackle is on the neck, it must also be on the hand, especially since God said *fa-hiya ila al-adhqan* (so they reach up to the chins), so it is known that the hands are meant. *Fa-hum muqmahun* means they are raising their heads, unable to lower them, because one whose hands are chained up to his chin has his head raised.

It is related from Ibn Abbas that he recited "Inna ja'alna fi aydihim aghlalan" (Indeed We have put shackles on their hands), and from Ibn Mas'ud that he recited "Inna ja'alna fi aymanihim aghlalan," as was previously narrated from the reading of Ibn Abbas.

﴿And We have placed a barrier before them and a barrier behind them﴾: that is, We have prevented them from faith by barriers, so they cannot come out of disbelief into faith, like one who is enclosed in barriers in front of him and behind him. *Sadd* with a *damma* or a *fatha* on the *sin* are two dialectal forms. Of this meaning in the verse is the poet's saying:

*And from the calamities, may you have no father, that the earth was closed upon me with barriers.*

*I do not find my way therein to the place of a ridge between Iraq and the land of Murad.*

﴿So We covered them﴾: that is, We covered their sight, so because of that they ﴿do not see﴾, meaning they are not able to see anything.

Al-Farra' said: "fa-albasna absarahum ghishawatan" means We clothed their sight with a covering, that is, blindness, so they do not see the path of guidance. Qatadah likewise said that the meaning is that they do not see guidance.

Al-Suddi said: They do not see Muhammad (ﷺ) when they plotted to kill him.

Al-Dahhak said: ﴿And We have placed a barrier before them﴾ means this world, and ﴿a barrier behind them﴾ means the Hereafter, ﴿so We covered them, so they do not see﴾ means they are blind to the resurrection and blind to accepting the laws in this world.

It is said: What is before them is the Hereafter and what is behind them is this world. The majority read with the unpointed *ghayn* (*ghashayna*, "We covered"), meaning We covered their sight; this is according to an ellipsis of a noun.

Ibn Abbas, Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, al-Hasan, Yahya ibn Ya'mar, Abu Raja', and Ikrimah read it with the *ghayn* unpointed (*ghashayna*) from *al-ashaa*, which is weakness of sight. From it is God's saying: ﴿And whoever turns away from the remembrance of the Most Merciful﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 36].

﴿It is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe﴾: that is, your warning them and not warning them is the same.

Al-Zajjaj said: That is, whoever God has misguided to this degree, warning does not benefit him. Warning only benefits the one mentioned in His saying: ﴿You can only warn one who follows the Reminder and fears the Most Merciful in the unseen﴾, that is, one who follows the Qur'an and fears God in this world. The clause *la yu'minun* (they do not believe) is a new sentence explaining what precedes it, namely the equality; or it is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal), or it is a substitute (badal). *Bi-al-ghayb* (in the unseen) is in an accusative position as a circumstantial phrase, either from the subject or the object.

﴿So give him good news of forgiveness and a noble reward﴾: that is, give good news to this one who followed the Reminder and feared the Most Merciful in the unseen, of a great forgiveness and a noble reward, that is, a good one, which is Paradise.

Then He, glorified is He, informed of His giving life to the dead, saying: ﴿Indeed, it is We who bring the dead to life﴾, that is, We resurrect them after death.

Al-Hasan and al-Dahhak said: That is, We give them life by faith after ignorance. The first is preferable.

Then He threatened them with the recording of their deeds, saying: ﴿And We record what they have sent forward﴾, that is, what they have put forward of righteous and evil deeds, ﴿and their traces﴾, that is, what they have left behind of good deeds whose benefit does not end after death, such as one who establishes a good tradition, or the like; or evil deeds that remain after the death of their doer, such as one who establishes an evil tradition.

Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said: A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿A soul will know what it has sent forward and what it has left behind﴾ [al-Infitar: 5], and His saying: ﴿On that Day, man will be informed of what he sent forward and left behind﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 13]. It is also said that the verse means the traces of those who walk to the mosques, and this is what a group of the Companions and the Successors said.

Al-Nahhas said: This is the most preferable of what has been said about the verse, because it was revealed concerning that.

It is answered that the consideration is the generality of the verse, not the specific cause of its revelation. Its generality requires the recording of all traces of good and evil. Among the good is teaching the knowledgeable and authoring their works, endowments for good causes, the building of mosques and bridges.

Among the evil is the innovation of injustices, and the introduction of what harms people, which the people of tyranny imitate and act upon, such as unjust taxes or other things. This is why He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And everything We have enumerated in a clear Imam﴾, that is, everything of the deeds of the servants and other things, whatever it is, is in a clear Imam, that is, a book that is followed, clarifying everything.

Mujahid, Qatadah, and Ibn Zayd said: It means the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz). Another group said: It means the pages of deeds.

The majority read *wa-naktubu* (we record) in the active voice. Zirr and Masruq read it in the passive voice.

The majority read *kulla shay'in ahsaynahu* with *kulla* in the accusative, by the construction of *ishtighal* (the verb governs its object through a pronoun). Abu al-Sammal read it with *raf'* (nominative), as a subject (ibtida').

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas regarding His saying *Ya-Sin*, that they both said: "O Muhammad."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated through several chains from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying *Ya-Sin*, that he said: "O human being."

Abd ibn Humayd narrated from al-Hasan, al-Dahhak, and Ikrimah something similar.

Ibn Mardawayh and Abu Nu'aym in *al-Dala'il* narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to recite in the mosque and would recite aloud, until some people from Quraysh were harmed by it, so they stood up to seize him, and suddenly their hands were gathered up to their necks, and suddenly they were blind and could not see. So they came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'We beseech you by God and by kinship, O Muhammad.' He said: There was no clan of Quraysh except that the Prophet (ﷺ) had kinship with them. So the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed until that left them, and then this was revealed: ﴿Ya-Sin. By the wise Qur'an﴾ up to His saying: ﴿Or you did not warn them, they will not believe﴾. He said: None of that group believed."

There are other narrations about the cause of the revelation of this, and this narration is the best of them and the closest to soundness.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him: "The shackles are what is between the chest and the chin. ﴿So they are raising their heads﴾, as a riding animal raises its head because of the bridle."

Ibn Mardawayh also narrated from him regarding His saying: ﴿And We have placed a barrier before them﴾ up to the end of the verse: "They used to pass by the Prophet (ﷺ) and not see him."

Ibn Mardawayh also narrated from him: "Quraysh gathered at the door of the Prophet (ﷺ), waiting for his exit in order to harm him. This grieved him, so Gabriel came to him with Surah Ya-Sin and ordered him to go out to them. He took a handful of dirt and went out reciting it, throwing the dirt on their heads. They did not see him until he passed. Then one of them touched his head and found the dirt. Another came and said: 'What is keeping you here?' They said: 'We are waiting for Muhammad.' He said: 'I saw him entering the mosque.' He said: 'Get up, for he has bewitched you.'"

Abd al-Razzaq, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it as good), al-Bazzar, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who graded it as sound), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: "The Banu Salamah were in one part of Medina, and they wanted to move closer to the mosque. So God revealed: ﴿Indeed, it is We who bring the dead to life, and We record what they have sent forward and their traces﴾. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) summoned them and said: 'Indeed, He records your traces.' Then he recited the verse to them, and they stayed."

Al-Firyabi, Ahmad in *al-Zuhd*, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Majah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated something similar from Ibn Abbas.

In Sahih Muslim and elsewhere, from the hadith of Jabir, who said: "The Banu Salamah wanted to sell their houses and move close to the mosque. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to them: 'O Banu Salamah, your houses record your traces.'"

**Commentary on Surah Ya-Sin**

It is Makkiyyah (Meccan, revealed in Makkah). Al-Qurtubi said: "There is consensus (ijma') on this, except that a group said that the verse ﴿And We record what they have sent before and their traces﴾ [Ya-Sin: 12] was revealed concerning the Banu Salamah of the Ansar, when they wanted to leave their homes and move to live near the Mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The explanation of that will come later."

Ibn al-Duraysi, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il* related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Surah Ya-Sin was revealed in Makkah." Ibn Mardawayh related the same from 'Aishah.

al-Darimi, al-Tirmidhi, Muhammad ibn Nasr, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* related from Anas that he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, everything has a heart, and the heart of the Qur'an is Ya-Sin. Whoever recites Ya-Sin, Allah records for him the reward of reciting the Qur'an ten times." al-Tirmidhi said after relating it: "This is a gharib (rare) hadith, which we only know from the hadith of Humayd ibn 'Abd al-Rahman. Its chain includes Harun Abu Muhammad, who is an unknown (majhul) shaykh. There is also a report on this topic from Abu Bakr, but it is not sound because its chain is weak."

al-Bazzar related from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, everything has a heart, and the heart of the Qur'an is Ya-Sin." Then he said after relating it: "We do not know of anyone who narrated it except Zayd, from Humayd," meaning Zayd ibn al-Hubab, from Humayd al-Makki, mawla (client) of the family of 'Alqamah.

al-Darimi, Abu Ya'la, al-Tabarani in *al-Awsat*, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* related from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Ya-Sin on a night seeking the Face of Allah, He forgives him for that night." Ibn Kathir said: "Its chain is good (jayyid)."

Ibn Hibban and al-Diya' related from Jundab ibn 'Abd Allah who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites Ya-Sin on a night seeking the Face of Allah, He forgives him."

Its chain in the *Sahih* of Ibn Hibban is thus: "Muhammad ibn Ishaq ibn Ibrahim, client of Thaqif, narrated to us; al-Walid ibn Shuja' ibn al-Walid al-Kubi narrated to us; my father narrated to us; Ziyad ibn Khaythamah narrated to us; Muhammad ibn Juhadah narrated to us, from al-Hasan, from Jundab ibn 'Abd Allah who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood and mentioned it..."

Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, Muhammad ibn Nasr, Ibn Hibban, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* related from Ma'qil ibn Yasar that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Ya-Sin is the heart of the Qur'an. No servant recites it seeking Allah and the Last Abode except that He forgives him what he has previously done of sin. So recite it over your dead." Ahmad was mentioned two chains for this: one of them includes an unknown narrator, and the other, he said, is from Abu 'Uthman, and it is not from al-Nahdi from his father, from Ma'qil.

Sa'id ibn Mansur and al-Bayhaqi related from Hassan ibn 'Atiyyah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites Ya-Sin, it is as if he recited the Qur'an ten times."

Ibn al-Duraysi, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Khatib, and al-Bayhaqi related from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Surah Ya-Sin is called in the Torah al-Mu'ammimah (the All-Encompassing). It encompasses its reciter with the good of this world and the Hereafter, it strives on his behalf against the afflictions of this world and the Hereafter, it repels from him the terrors of the Hereafter, and it is called al-Dafi'ah (the Repeller) and al-Qadiyah (the Fulfiller). It repels from its companion every evil and fulfils for him every need. Whoever recites it, it is equal to twenty pilgrimages; whoever hears it, it is equal for him to a thousand dinars spent in the way of Allah; and whoever writes it and then drinks it, it enters his belly with a thousand cures, a thousand lights, a thousand certainties, a thousand blessings, a thousand mercies, and it removes from him every rancour and disease."

al-Bayhaqi said: "'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr al-Judh'ani is alone in narrating it, from Sulayman ibn Rafi' al-Janadi, and he is munkar (rejected)."

I say: This is the hadith whose weakness of chain al-Tirmidhi previously pointed out. It is not far-fetched that it is fabricated (mawdu'), for all these expressions are rejected and far from the speech of one given *jawami' al-kalim* (concise, comprehensive speech). al-Tha'labi related it from the hadith of 'Aishah, and al-Khatib related it from the hadith of Anas, and al-Khatib related something similar from the hadith of 'Ali, more briefly than this.

al-Bazzar related from Ibn 'Abbas who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said concerning Surah Ya-Sin: "I wish that it were in the heart of every person of my Ummah." Its chain is thus: He said: Salamah ibn Shabib narrated to us; Ibrahim ibn al-Hakam ibn Aban narrated to us, from his father, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, and he mentioned it.

al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh related, and al-Suyuti said with a weak chain, from Anas who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever persists in reciting Ya-Sin every night and then dies, dies as a martyr (shahid)."

al-Darimi related from Ibn 'Abbas who said: Whoever recites Ya-Sin in the morning, is given ease for his day until evening, and whoever recites it at the beginning of his night, is given ease for his night until morning.

**In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful**

**His saying: ﴿Ya-Sin﴾ [1]**

The majority (al-Jumhur) recited it with the nun sukun (silent). Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Hamzah, Hafs, Qalun, and Warsh recited with idgham (assimilation) of the nun into the waw that follows it. 'Isa ibn 'Umar recited it with a fatha on the nun, and Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Abi Ishaq, and Nasr ibn 'Asim recited it with a kasra. The fatha is for *bina'* (indeclinability) or because it is the object of an implied verb whose estimate is: *utlu Ya-Sin* (recite Ya-Sin). The kasra is also for *bina'*, like *jayr*. It was said: the fatha and kasra are to avoid the meeting of two sakins (unvowelled letters).

As for the reason for the majority's recitation with sukun on the nun, it is because it is recited in the manner of a list (ta'did), so it has no share of *i'rab* (grammatical inflection).

Harun al-A'war, Muhammad ibn al-Sumayfa', and al-Kalbi recited it with a damma on the nun, for *bina'*, like *mundhu*, *haythu*, and *qattu*. It was also said: it is the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "this is Ya-Sin." It is not declined (*mamnu' min al-sarf*) due to being a proper noun (*'alamiyyah*) and feminine gender (*ta'nith*).

There is disagreement about the meaning of this word. It was said: its meaning is "O man" or "O person."

Ibn al-Anbari said: Pausing on *Ya-Sin* is good (hasan) for the one who says it is the opening of the surah. For the one who says its meaning is "O man," one does not pause on it.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr and others said: It is one of the names of Muhammad (ﷺ), and the evidence is ﴿Indeed you are among the messengers﴾. From it is the saying of al-Sa'd al-Himyari:

*O soul, do not exhaust yourself in sincere advice,*
*striving for love, except for the family of Ya-Sin.*

From it is His saying: ﴿Peace upon the family of Ilyasin﴾ [al-Saffat: 130], meaning: upon the family of Muhammad. What is meant by "Ilyasin" will come in al-Saffat.

al-Wahidi said: Ibn 'Abbas and the commentators said: It means "O person," meaning Muhammad (ﷺ).

Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: Its meaning is "O master of mankind."

Malik said: It is one of the names of Allah, the Exalted. Ashhab related this from him.

Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami related from Ja'far al-Sadiq that its meaning is "O master."

Ka'b said: It is an oath which Allah swore by. al-Zajjaj preferred that its meaning is "O Muhammad."

They differed on whether it is Arabic or non-Arabic. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and 'Ikrimah said: it is Abyssinian (Habashi).

al-Kalbi said: It is Syriac (Suryani), which the Arabs spoke, so it became part of their language. al-Sha'bi said: It is in the language of Tayy. al-Hasan said: It is in the language of Kalb. What has preceded in Ta-Ha and at the beginning of Surah al-Baqarah suffices here without lengthening.

**And the Wise Qur'an [2]**

Genitive (*bi al-jarr*), on the basis that it is sworn by directly (*muqsam bihi ibtida'an*).

It was also said: it is conjoined (ma'tuf) to Ya-Sin, on the estimate that it is in the genitive by an implied oath particle.

al-Naqqash said: Allah did not swear by the messengership of any of His prophets in His Book except for Muhammad (ﷺ), exalting him and glorifying him. *Al-Hakim* means the perfectly established (*al-muhkam*), which does not contradict or conflict with itself; or *al-Hakim* means its Speaker (qa'iluhu).

The response of the oath is: ﴿Indeed you are among the messengers﴾. This is a rebuttal of those among the disbelievers who denied his messengership by their saying: ﴿You are not a messenger﴾ [al-Ra'd: 43].

His saying: ﴿This is a straight path﴾ is another predicate of *inna* (indeed), meaning: indeed you are upon a straight path. The straight path is the upright way that leads to the desired goal.

al-Zajjaj said: It is according to the way of the prophets who preceded you. It may also be in the accusative position as a circumstantial (*hal*).

**﴿The revelation of the All-Mighty, the Most Merciful﴾ [5]**

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, and Abu Bakr recited *tanzilu* with a damma, on the basis that it is the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "it is the revelation." It may also be the predicate of His saying *Ya-Sin* if it is made a name of the surah. The rest recited it with a fatha, on the basis of it being a verbal noun (*masdariyyah*), i.e., "Allah revealed that revelation, the revelation of the All-Mighty, the Most Merciful."

The meaning is: "Indeed you, O Muhammad, are [of] the revelation of the All-Mighty, the Most Merciful." The first (the damma) is preferable.

It was said: it is in the accusative as a praise (*al-mad*) according to the reading of those who recited it with a fatha. He, glorified is He, expressed the revealed thing by a verbal noun as an intensification, until it is as if it were the very revelation itself.

Abu Haywah, al-Tirmidhi, Abu Ja'far Yazid ibn al-Qa'qa', and Shaybah recited *tanzili* with a kasra, as an attribute (na't) of the Qur'an or a substitute (badal) for it.

The *lam* in ﴿so that you may warn a people whose fathers were not warned﴾ may be connected to *tanzil*, or to an implied verb indicated by "from among the messengers," i.e., "We sent you so that you may warn." The *ma* in *ma undhira aba'uhum* is negating: i.e., their fathers were not warned. It may also be relative (*mawsulah*) or descriptive (*mawsufah*), i.e., "to warn a people, that which their fathers were warned," or "to warn them of a punishment with which their fathers were warned." It may also be verbal (*masdariyyah*), i.e., "the warning of their fathers." On the view that it is negating, the meaning is: "no messenger from among themselves came to their fathers." It may also be meant that their nearest fathers were not warned, due to the long duration of the interval (fatrah). His saying: ﴿so they are heedless﴾ is connected to the negation of warning according to the first aspect, i.e., their fathers were not warned, so because of that they are heedless. According to the later aspects, it is connected to His saying "so that you may warn," i.e., they are heedless of what We warned their fathers with. Most of the people of tafsir went to the view that the meaning is negation, and this is the apparent sense of the arrangement, because the clause ﴿so they are heedless﴾ follows what precedes it.

The *lam* in His saying: ﴿Certainly the word has come into effect upon most of them﴾ is the *lam* that prefaces an oath, i.e., "By Allah, certainly the word has come into effect upon most of them." The meaning of *haqqa* is: it was established and became obligatory. *Al-qawl* (the word), i.e., the punishment, is upon most of them, i.e., most of the people of Makkah, or most of the disbelievers in general, or most of the disbelievers of the Arabs, namely those who died upon disbelief and persisted in it throughout their lives. The statement ﴿so they do not believe﴾ therefore follows from what precedes it in this sense, i.e., because Allah, glorified is He, knew of them their persistence in the disbelief they were in and that they would die upon it. It was also said: the word mentioned here is His saying, glorified is He: ﴿So the truth is, and the truth I say: I will surely fill Hell with you and with those who follow you﴾ [Sad: 84–85].

The sentence ﴿Indeed We have placed upon their necks shackles﴾ is an affirmation of what precedes it; it depicts their condition with the condition of those whose necks were chained. So the shackles reach up to the chins, and therefore they cannot turn, nor can they bend their necks. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿so they are with heads raised﴾, i.e., raising their heads while lowering their gaze.

al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: *al-muqmah* is one who lowers his gaze after raising his head. The meaning of *al-iqmah* is raising the head and lowering the gaze. It is said: "the camel *aqmaha* his head and *qamaha*," when he raised his head and did not drink water.

al-Azhari said: Allah meant that when their hands were chained at their necks, the shackles raised them up to their chins, and their heads were raised upward (*su'da'*). So they are with heads raised due to the shackles lifting them.

Qatadah said: The meaning of *muqmahun* is "shackled." The first is preferable, and from it is the saying of the poet:

*And we, around its edges, are sitting,*
*lowering our gaze like camels with raised heads (qimah).*

(p-1219) Al-Zajjaj said: It is said that the two months of Kanun (December and January) are called "the two months of qimah," because when camels come to water they raise their heads because of the intense cold. He cited the verse of Abu Zayd al-Hudhali:

*A youth like the son of al-Aghharr, when we spend the winter, and provisions become scarce in the two months of qimah.*

Abu Ubaydah said: "qamaha al-ba'ir" means the camel raised its head from the trough without drinking.

Abu Ubaydah also said: It is a parable (mathal) that God struck for them, regarding their refusal to accept guidance, like the refusal of one who is shackled. This is as it is said: "So-and-so is a donkey," meaning he does not see guidance. As the poet said:

*For them, against right guidance, are shackles and fetters.*

Al-Farra' said: This is a figurative expression, meaning: We have restrained them from spending in the way of God. It is like His saying: ﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck﴾ [al-Isra: 29]. Al-Dahhak also said this.

It is said: The verse refers to what is done to people in the Fire, namely the placing of shackles on their necks, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿When the shackles are on their necks﴾ [Ghafir: 71]. Ibn Abbas recited: "Inna ja'alna fi aymanihim aghlalan" (Indeed We have put shackles on their right hands). Al-Zajjaj said: that is, on their hands.

Al-Nahhas said: This reading is an explanation (tafsir), and one may not recite in a way that contradicts the Mushaf (the written codex of the Qur'an).

He said: According to the reading of the majority, there is an ellipsis in the sentence. The estimated meaning is: We have put shackles on their necks and on their hands, so they reach up to the chins. The word *hiya* (it/they, feminine) is a reference to the hands, not to the necks. The Arabs omit such things. A parallel is God's saying: ﴿garments that protect you from the heat﴾ [al-Nahl: 81], where the implied meaning is: "and garments that protect you from the cold," because whatever protects from heat also protects from cold. Since the shackle is on the neck, it must also be on the hand, especially since God said *fa-hiya ila al-adhqan* (so they reach up to the chins), so it is known that the hands are meant. *Fa-hum muqmahun* means they are raising their heads, unable to lower them, because one whose hands are chained up to his chin has his head raised.

It is related from Ibn Abbas that he recited "Inna ja'alna fi aydihim aghlalan" (Indeed We have put shackles on their hands), and from Ibn Mas'ud that he recited "Inna ja'alna fi aymanihim aghlalan," as was previously narrated from the reading of Ibn Abbas.

﴿And We have placed a barrier before them and a barrier behind them﴾: that is, We have prevented them from faith by barriers, so they cannot come out of disbelief into faith, like one who is enclosed in barriers in front of him and behind him. *Sadd* with a *damma* or a *fatha* on the *sin* are two dialectal forms. Of this meaning in the verse is the poet's saying:

*And from the calamities, may you have no father, that the earth was closed upon me with barriers.*

*I do not find my way therein to the place of a ridge between Iraq and the land of Murad.*

﴿So We covered them﴾: that is, We covered their sight, so because of that they ﴿do not see﴾, meaning they are not able to see anything.

Al-Farra' said: "fa-albasna absarahum ghishawatan" means We clothed their sight with a covering, that is, blindness, so they do not see the path of guidance. Qatadah likewise said that the meaning is that they do not see guidance.

Al-Suddi said: They do not see Muhammad (ﷺ) when they plotted to kill him.

Al-Dahhak said: ﴿And We have placed a barrier before them﴾ means this world, and ﴿a barrier behind them﴾ means the Hereafter, ﴿so We covered them, so they do not see﴾ means they are blind to the resurrection and blind to accepting the laws in this world.

It is said: What is before them is the Hereafter and what is behind them is this world. The majority read with the unpointed *ghayn* (*ghashayna*, "We covered"), meaning We covered their sight; this is according to an ellipsis of a noun.

Ibn Abbas, Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, al-Hasan, Yahya ibn Ya'mar, Abu Raja', and Ikrimah read it with the *ghayn* unpointed (*ghashayna*) from *al-ashaa*, which is weakness of sight. From it is God's saying: ﴿And whoever turns away from the remembrance of the Most Merciful﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 36].

﴿It is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe﴾: that is, your warning them and not warning them is the same.

Al-Zajjaj said: That is, whoever God has misguided to this degree, warning does not benefit him. Warning only benefits the one mentioned in His saying: ﴿You can only warn one who follows the Reminder and fears the Most Merciful in the unseen﴾, that is, one who follows the Qur'an and fears God in this world. The clause *la yu'minun* (they do not believe) is a new sentence explaining what precedes it, namely the equality; or it is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal), or it is a substitute (badal). *Bi-al-ghayb* (in the unseen) is in an accusative position as a circumstantial phrase, either from the subject or the object.

﴿So give him good news of forgiveness and a noble reward﴾: that is, give good news to this one who followed the Reminder and feared the Most Merciful in the unseen, of a great forgiveness and a noble reward, that is, a good one, which is Paradise.

Then He, glorified is He, informed of His giving life to the dead, saying: ﴿Indeed, it is We who bring the dead to life﴾, that is, We resurrect them after death.

Al-Hasan and al-Dahhak said: That is, We give them life by faith after ignorance. The first is preferable.

Then He threatened them with the recording of their deeds, saying: ﴿And We record what they have sent forward﴾, that is, what they have put forward of righteous and evil deeds, ﴿and their traces﴾, that is, what they have left behind of good deeds whose benefit does not end after death, such as one who establishes a good tradition, or the like; or evil deeds that remain after the death of their doer, such as one who establishes an evil tradition.

Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said: A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿A soul will know what it has sent forward and what it has left behind﴾ [al-Infitar: 5], and His saying: ﴿On that Day, man will be informed of what he sent forward and left behind﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 13]. It is also said that the verse means the traces of those who walk to the mosques, and this is what a group of the Companions and the Successors said.

Al-Nahhas said: This is the most preferable of what has been said about the verse, because it was revealed concerning that.

It is answered that the consideration is the generality of the verse, not the specific cause of its revelation. Its generality requires the recording of all traces of good and evil. Among the good is teaching the knowledgeable and authoring their works, endowments for good causes, the building of mosques and bridges.

Among the evil is the innovation of injustices, and the introduction of what harms people, which the people of tyranny imitate and act upon, such as unjust taxes or other things. This is why He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And everything We have enumerated in a clear Imam﴾, that is, everything of the deeds of the servants and other things, whatever it is, is in a clear Imam, that is, a book that is followed, clarifying everything.

Mujahid, Qatadah, and Ibn Zayd said: It means the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz). Another group said: It means the pages of deeds.

The majority read *wa-naktubu* (we record) in the active voice. Zirr and Masruq read it in the passive voice.

The majority read *kulla shay'in ahsaynahu* with *kulla* in the accusative, by the construction of *ishtighal* (the verb governs its object through a pronoun). Abu al-Sammal read it with *raf'* (nominative), as a subject (ibtida').

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas regarding His saying *Ya-Sin*, that they both said: "O Muhammad."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated through several chains from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying *Ya-Sin*, that he said: "O human being."

Abd ibn Humayd narrated from al-Hasan, al-Dahhak, and Ikrimah something similar.

Ibn Mardawayh and Abu Nu'aym in *al-Dala'il* narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to recite in the mosque and would recite aloud, until some people from Quraysh were harmed by it, so they stood up to seize him, and suddenly their hands were gathered up to their necks, and suddenly they were blind and could not see. So they came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'We beseech you by God and by kinship, O Muhammad.' He said: There was no clan of Quraysh except that the Prophet (ﷺ) had kinship with them. So the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed until that left them, and then this was revealed: ﴿Ya-Sin. By the wise Qur'an﴾ up to His saying: ﴿Or you did not warn them, they will not believe﴾. He said: None of that group believed."

There are other narrations about the cause of the revelation of this, and this narration is the best of them and the closest to soundness.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him: "The shackles are what is between the chest and the chin. ﴿So they are raising their heads﴾, as a riding animal raises its head because of the bridle."

Ibn Mardawayh also narrated from him regarding His saying: ﴿And We have placed a barrier before them﴾ up to the end of the verse: "They used to pass by the Prophet (ﷺ) and not see him."

Ibn Mardawayh also narrated from him: "Quraysh gathered at the door of the Prophet (ﷺ), waiting for his exit in order to harm him. This grieved him, so Gabriel came to him with Surah Ya-Sin and ordered him to go out to them. He took a handful of dirt and went out reciting it, throwing the dirt on their heads. They did not see him until he passed. Then one of them touched his head and found the dirt. Another came and said: 'What is keeping you here?' They said: 'We are waiting for Muhammad.' He said: 'I saw him entering the mosque.' He said: 'Get up, for he has bewitched you.'"

Abd al-Razzaq, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it as good), al-Bazzar, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who graded it as sound), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: "The Banu Salamah were in one part of Medina, and they wanted to move closer to the mosque. So God revealed: ﴿Indeed, it is We who bring the dead to life, and We record what they have sent forward and their traces﴾. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) summoned them and said: 'Indeed, He records your traces.' Then he recited the verse to them, and they stayed."

Al-Firyabi, Ahmad in *al-Zuhd*, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Majah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated something similar from Ibn Abbas.

In Sahih Muslim and elsewhere, from the hadith of Jabir, who said: "The Banu Salamah wanted to sell their houses and move close to the mosque. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to them: 'O Banu Salamah, your houses record your traces.'"

**Commentary on Surah Ya-Sin**

It is Makkiyyah (Meccan, revealed in Makkah). Al-Qurtubi said: "There is consensus (ijma') on this, except that a group said that the verse ﴿And We record what they have sent before and their traces﴾ [Ya-Sin: 12] was revealed concerning the Banu Salamah of the Ansar, when they wanted to leave their homes and move to live near the Mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The explanation of that will come later."

Ibn al-Duraysi, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il* related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Surah Ya-Sin was revealed in Makkah." Ibn Mardawayh related the same from 'Aishah.

al-Darimi, al-Tirmidhi, Muhammad ibn Nasr, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* related from Anas that he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, everything has a heart, and the heart of the Qur'an is Ya-Sin. Whoever recites Ya-Sin, Allah records for him the reward of reciting the Qur'an ten times." al-Tirmidhi said after relating it: "This is a gharib (rare) hadith, which we only know from the hadith of Humayd ibn 'Abd al-Rahman. Its chain includes Harun Abu Muhammad, who is an unknown (majhul) shaykh. There is also a report on this topic from Abu Bakr, but it is not sound because its chain is weak."

al-Bazzar related from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, everything has a heart, and the heart of the Qur'an is Ya-Sin." Then he said after relating it: "We do not know of anyone who narrated it except Zayd, from Humayd," meaning Zayd ibn al-Hubab, from Humayd al-Makki, mawla (client) of the family of 'Alqamah.

al-Darimi, Abu Ya'la, al-Tabarani in *al-Awsat*, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* related from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Ya-Sin on a night seeking the Face of Allah, He forgives him for that night." Ibn Kathir said: "Its chain is good (jayyid)."

Ibn Hibban and al-Diya' related from Jundab ibn 'Abd Allah who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites Ya-Sin on a night seeking the Face of Allah, He forgives him."

Its chain in the *Sahih* of Ibn Hibban is thus: "Muhammad ibn Ishaq ibn Ibrahim, client of Thaqif, narrated to us; al-Walid ibn Shuja' ibn al-Walid al-Kubi narrated to us; my father narrated to us; Ziyad ibn Khaythamah narrated to us; Muhammad ibn Juhadah narrated to us, from al-Hasan, from Jundab ibn 'Abd Allah who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood and mentioned it..."

Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, Muhammad ibn Nasr, Ibn Hibban, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* related from Ma'qil ibn Yasar that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Ya-Sin is the heart of the Qur'an. No servant recites it seeking Allah and the Last Abode except that He forgives him what he has previously done of sin. So recite it over your dead." Ahmad was mentioned two chains for this: one of them includes an unknown narrator, and the other, he said, is from Abu 'Uthman, and it is not from al-Nahdi from his father, from Ma'qil.

Sa'id ibn Mansur and al-Bayhaqi related from Hassan ibn 'Atiyyah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites Ya-Sin, it is as if he recited the Qur'an ten times."

Ibn al-Duraysi, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Khatib, and al-Bayhaqi related from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Surah Ya-Sin is called in the Torah al-Mu'ammimah (the All-Encompassing). It encompasses its reciter with the good of this world and the Hereafter, it strives on his behalf against the afflictions of this world and the Hereafter, it repels from him the terrors of the Hereafter, and it is called al-Dafi'ah (the Repeller) and al-Qadiyah (the Fulfiller). It repels from its companion every evil and fulfils for him every need. Whoever recites it, it is equal to twenty pilgrimages; whoever hears it, it is equal for him to a thousand dinars spent in the way of Allah; and whoever writes it and then drinks it, it enters his belly with a thousand cures, a thousand lights, a thousand certainties, a thousand blessings, a thousand mercies, and it removes from him every rancour and disease."

al-Bayhaqi said: "'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr al-Judh'ani is alone in narrating it, from Sulayman ibn Rafi' al-Janadi, and he is munkar (rejected)."

I say: This is the hadith whose weakness of chain al-Tirmidhi previously pointed out. It is not far-fetched that it is fabricated (mawdu'), for all these expressions are rejected and far from the speech of one given *jawami' al-kalim* (concise, comprehensive speech). al-Tha'labi related it from the hadith of 'Aishah, and al-Khatib related it from the hadith of Anas, and al-Khatib related something similar from the hadith of 'Ali, more briefly than this.

al-Bazzar related from Ibn 'Abbas who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said concerning Surah Ya-Sin: "I wish that it were in the heart of every person of my Ummah." Its chain is thus: He said: Salamah ibn Shabib narrated to us; Ibrahim ibn al-Hakam ibn Aban narrated to us, from his father, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, and he mentioned it.

al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh related, and al-Suyuti said with a weak chain, from Anas who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever persists in reciting Ya-Sin every night and then dies, dies as a martyr (shahid)."

al-Darimi related from Ibn 'Abbas who said: Whoever recites Ya-Sin in the morning, is given ease for his day until evening, and whoever recites it at the beginning of his night, is given ease for his night until morning.

**In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful**

**His saying: ﴿Ya-Sin﴾ [1]**

The majority (al-Jumhur) recited it with the nun sukun (silent). Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Hamzah, Hafs, Qalun, and Warsh recited with idgham (assimilation) of the nun into the waw that follows it. 'Isa ibn 'Umar recited it with a fatha on the nun, and Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Abi Ishaq, and Nasr ibn 'Asim recited it with a kasra. The fatha is for *bina'* (indeclinability) or because it is the object of an implied verb whose estimate is: *utlu Ya-Sin* (recite Ya-Sin). The kasra is also for *bina'*, like *jayr*. It was said: the fatha and kasra are to avoid the meeting of two sakins (unvowelled letters).

As for the reason for the majority's recitation with sukun on the nun, it is because it is recited in the manner of a list (ta'did), so it has no share of *i'rab* (grammatical inflection).

Harun al-A'war, Muhammad ibn al-Sumayfa', and al-Kalbi recited it with a damma on the nun, for *bina'*, like *mundhu*, *haythu*, and *qattu*. It was also said: it is the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "this is Ya-Sin." It is not declined (*mamnu' min al-sarf*) due to being a proper noun (*'alamiyyah*) and feminine gender (*ta'nith*).

There is disagreement about the meaning of this word. It was said: its meaning is "O man" or "O person."

Ibn al-Anbari said: Pausing on *Ya-Sin* is good (hasan) for the one who says it is the opening of the surah. For the one who says its meaning is "O man," one does not pause on it.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr and others said: It is one of the names of Muhammad (ﷺ), and the evidence is ﴿Indeed you are among the messengers﴾. From it is the saying of al-Sa'd al-Himyari:

*O soul, do not exhaust yourself in sincere advice,*
*striving for love, except for the family of Ya-Sin.*

From it is His saying: ﴿Peace upon the family of Ilyasin﴾ [al-Saffat: 130], meaning: upon the family of Muhammad. What is meant by "Ilyasin" will come in al-Saffat.

al-Wahidi said: Ibn 'Abbas and the commentators said: It means "O person," meaning Muhammad (ﷺ).

Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: Its meaning is "O master of mankind."

Malik said: It is one of the names of Allah, the Exalted. Ashhab related this from him.

Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami related from Ja'far al-Sadiq that its meaning is "O master."

Ka'b said: It is an oath which Allah swore by. al-Zajjaj preferred that its meaning is "O Muhammad."

They differed on whether it is Arabic or non-Arabic. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and 'Ikrimah said: it is Abyssinian (Habashi).

al-Kalbi said: It is Syriac (Suryani), which the Arabs spoke, so it became part of their language. al-Sha'bi said: It is in the language of Tayy. al-Hasan said: It is in the language of Kalb. What has preceded in Ta-Ha and at the beginning of Surah al-Baqarah suffices here without lengthening.

**And the Wise Qur'an [2]**

Genitive (*bi al-jarr*), on the basis that it is sworn by directly (*muqsam bihi ibtida'an*).

It was also said: it is conjoined (ma'tuf) to Ya-Sin, on the estimate that it is in the genitive by an implied oath particle.

al-Naqqash said: Allah did not swear by the messengership of any of His prophets in His Book except for Muhammad (ﷺ), exalting him and glorifying him. *Al-Hakim* means the perfectly established (*al-muhkam*), which does not contradict or conflict with itself; or *al-Hakim* means its Speaker (qa'iluhu).

The response of the oath is: ﴿Indeed you are among the messengers﴾. This is a rebuttal of those among the disbelievers who denied his messengership by their saying: ﴿You are not a messenger﴾ [al-Ra'd: 43].

His saying: ﴿This is a straight path﴾ is another predicate of *inna* (indeed), meaning: indeed you are upon a straight path. The straight path is the upright way that leads to the desired goal.

al-Zajjaj said: It is according to the way of the prophets who preceded you. It may also be in the accusative position as a circumstantial (*hal*).

**﴿The revelation of the All-Mighty, the Most Merciful﴾ [5]**

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, and Abu Bakr recited *tanzilu* with a damma, on the basis that it is the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "it is the revelation." It may also be the predicate of His saying *Ya-Sin* if it is made a name of the surah. The rest recited it with a fatha, on the basis of it being a verbal noun (*masdariyyah*), i.e., "Allah revealed that revelation, the revelation of the All-Mighty, the Most Merciful."

The meaning is: "Indeed you, O Muhammad, are [of] the revelation of the All-Mighty, the Most Merciful." The first (the damma) is preferable.

It was said: it is in the accusative as a praise (*al-mad*) according to the reading of those who recited it with a fatha. He, glorified is He, expressed the revealed thing by a verbal noun as an intensification, until it is as if it were the very revelation itself.

Abu Haywah, al-Tirmidhi, Abu Ja'far Yazid ibn al-Qa'qa', and Shaybah recited *tanzili* with a kasra, as an attribute (na't) of the Qur'an or a substitute (badal) for it.

The *lam* in ﴿so that you may warn a people whose fathers were not warned﴾ may be connected to *tanzil*, or to an implied verb indicated by "from among the messengers," i.e., "We sent you so that you may warn." The *ma* in *ma undhira aba'uhum* is negating: i.e., their fathers were not warned. It may also be relative (*mawsulah*) or descriptive (*mawsufah*), i.e., "to warn a people, that which their fathers were warned," or "to warn them of a punishment with which their fathers were warned." It may also be verbal (*masdariyyah*), i.e., "the warning of their fathers." On the view that it is negating, the meaning is: "no messenger from among themselves came to their fathers." It may also be meant that their nearest fathers were not warned, due to the long duration of the interval (fatrah). His saying: ﴿so they are heedless﴾ is connected to the negation of warning according to the first aspect, i.e., their fathers were not warned, so because of that they are heedless. According to the later aspects, it is connected to His saying "so that you may warn," i.e., they are heedless of what We warned their fathers with. Most of the people of tafsir went to the view that the meaning is negation, and this is the apparent sense of the arrangement, because the clause ﴿so they are heedless﴾ follows what precedes it.

The *lam* in His saying: ﴿Certainly the word has come into effect upon most of them﴾ is the *lam* that prefaces an oath, i.e., "By Allah, certainly the word has come into effect upon most of them." The meaning of *haqqa* is: it was established and became obligatory. *Al-qawl* (the word), i.e., the punishment, is upon most of them, i.e., most of the people of Makkah, or most of the disbelievers in general, or most of the disbelievers of the Arabs, namely those who died upon disbelief and persisted in it throughout their lives. The statement ﴿so they do not believe﴾ therefore follows from what precedes it in this sense, i.e., because Allah, glorified is He, knew of them their persistence in the disbelief they were in and that they would die upon it. It was also said: the word mentioned here is His saying, glorified is He: ﴿So the truth is, and the truth I say: I will surely fill Hell with you and with those who follow you﴾ [Sad: 84–85].

The sentence ﴿Indeed We have placed upon their necks shackles﴾ is an affirmation of what precedes it; it depicts their condition with the condition of those whose necks were chained. So the shackles reach up to the chins, and therefore they cannot turn, nor can they bend their necks. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿so they are with heads raised﴾, i.e., raising their heads while lowering their gaze.

al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: *al-muqmah* is one who lowers his gaze after raising his head. The meaning of *al-iqmah* is raising the head and lowering the gaze. It is said: "the camel *aqmaha* his head and *qamaha*," when he raised his head and did not drink water.

al-Azhari said: Allah meant that when their hands were chained at their necks, the shackles raised them up to their chins, and their heads were raised upward (*su'da'*). So they are with heads raised due to the shackles lifting them.

Qatadah said: The meaning of *muqmahun* is "shackled." The first is preferable, and from it is the saying of the poet:

*And we, around its edges, are sitting,*
*lowering our gaze like camels with raised heads (qimah).*

(p-1219) Al-Zajjaj said: It is said that the two months of Kanun (December and January) are called "the two months of qimah," because when camels come to water they raise their heads because of the intense cold. He cited the verse of Abu Zayd al-Hudhali:

*A youth like the son of al-Aghharr, when we spend the winter, and provisions become scarce in the two months of qimah.*

Abu Ubaydah said: "qamaha al-ba'ir" means the camel raised its head from the trough without drinking.

Abu Ubaydah also said: It is a parable (mathal) that God struck for them, regarding their refusal to accept guidance, like the refusal of one who is shackled. This is as it is said: "So-and-so is a donkey," meaning he does not see guidance. As the poet said:

*For them, against right guidance, are shackles and fetters.*

Al-Farra' said: This is a figurative expression, meaning: We have restrained them from spending in the way of God. It is like His saying: ﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck﴾ [al-Isra: 29]. Al-Dahhak also said this.

It is said: The verse refers to what is done to people in the Fire, namely the placing of shackles on their necks, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿When the shackles are on their necks﴾ [Ghafir: 71]. Ibn Abbas recited: "Inna ja'alna fi aymanihim aghlalan" (Indeed We have put shackles on their right hands). Al-Zajjaj said: that is, on their hands.

Al-Nahhas said: This reading is an explanation (tafsir), and one may not recite in a way that contradicts the Mushaf (the written codex of the Qur'an).

He said: According to the reading of the majority, there is an ellipsis in the sentence. The estimated meaning is: We have put shackles on their necks and on their hands, so they reach up to the chins. The word *hiya* (it/they, feminine) is a reference to the hands, not to the necks. The Arabs omit such things. A parallel is God's saying: ﴿garments that protect you from the heat﴾ [al-Nahl: 81], where the implied meaning is: "and garments that protect you from the cold," because whatever protects from heat also protects from cold. Since the shackle is on the neck, it must also be on the hand, especially since God said *fa-hiya ila al-adhqan* (so they reach up to the chins), so it is known that the hands are meant. *Fa-hum muqmahun* means they are raising their heads, unable to lower them, because one whose hands are chained up to his chin has his head raised.

It is related from Ibn Abbas that he recited "Inna ja'alna fi aydihim aghlalan" (Indeed We have put shackles on their hands), and from Ibn Mas'ud that he recited "Inna ja'alna fi aymanihim aghlalan," as was previously narrated from the reading of Ibn Abbas.

﴿And We have placed a barrier before them and a barrier behind them﴾: that is, We have prevented them from faith by barriers, so they cannot come out of disbelief into faith, like one who is enclosed in barriers in front of him and behind him. *Sadd* with a *damma* or a *fatha* on the *sin* are two dialectal forms. Of this meaning in the verse is the poet's saying:

*And from the calamities, may you have no father, that the earth was closed upon me with barriers.*

*I do not find my way therein to the place of a ridge between Iraq and the land of Murad.*

﴿So We covered them﴾: that is, We covered their sight, so because of that they ﴿do not see﴾, meaning they are not able to see anything.

Al-Farra' said: "fa-albasna absarahum ghishawatan" means We clothed their sight with a covering, that is, blindness, so they do not see the path of guidance. Qatadah likewise said that the meaning is that they do not see guidance.

Al-Suddi said: They do not see Muhammad (ﷺ) when they plotted to kill him.

Al-Dahhak said: ﴿And We have placed a barrier before them﴾ means this world, and ﴿a barrier behind them﴾ means the Hereafter, ﴿so We covered them, so they do not see﴾ means they are blind to the resurrection and blind to accepting the laws in this world.

It is said: What is before them is the Hereafter and what is behind them is this world. The majority read with the unpointed *ghayn* (*ghashayna*, "We covered"), meaning We covered their sight; this is according to an ellipsis of a noun.

Ibn Abbas, Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, al-Hasan, Yahya ibn Ya'mar, Abu Raja', and Ikrimah read it with the *ghayn* unpointed (*ghashayna*) from *al-ashaa*, which is weakness of sight. From it is God's saying: ﴿And whoever turns away from the remembrance of the Most Merciful﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 36].

﴿It is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe﴾: that is, your warning them and not warning them is the same.

Al-Zajjaj said: That is, whoever God has misguided to this degree, warning does not benefit him. Warning only benefits the one mentioned in His saying: ﴿You can only warn one who follows the Reminder and fears the Most Merciful in the unseen﴾, that is, one who follows the Qur'an and fears God in this world. The clause *la yu'minun* (they do not believe) is a new sentence explaining what precedes it, namely the equality; or it is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal), or it is a substitute (badal). *Bi-al-ghayb* (in the unseen) is in an accusative position as a circumstantial phrase, either from the subject or the object.

﴿So give him good news of forgiveness and a noble reward﴾: that is, give good news to this one who followed the Reminder and feared the Most Merciful in the unseen, of a great forgiveness and a noble reward, that is, a good one, which is Paradise.

Then He, glorified is He, informed of His giving life to the dead, saying: ﴿Indeed, it is We who bring the dead to life﴾, that is, We resurrect them after death.

Al-Hasan and al-Dahhak said: That is, We give them life by faith after ignorance. The first is preferable.

Then He threatened them with the recording of their deeds, saying: ﴿And We record what they have sent forward﴾, that is, what they have put forward of righteous and evil deeds, ﴿and their traces﴾, that is, what they have left behind of good deeds whose benefit does not end after death, such as one who establishes a good tradition, or the like; or evil deeds that remain after the death of their doer, such as one who establishes an evil tradition.

Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said: A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿A soul will know what it has sent forward and what it has left behind﴾ [al-Infitar: 5], and His saying: ﴿On that Day, man will be informed of what he sent forward and left behind﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 13]. It is also said that the verse means the traces of those who walk to the mosques, and this is what a group of the Companions and the Successors said.

Al-Nahhas said: This is the most preferable of what has been said about the verse, because it was revealed concerning that.

It is answered that the consideration is the generality of the verse, not the specific cause of its revelation. Its generality requires the recording of all traces of good and evil. Among the good is teaching the knowledgeable and authoring their works, endowments for good causes, the building of mosques and bridges.

Among the evil is the innovation of injustices, and the introduction of what harms people, which the people of tyranny imitate and act upon, such as unjust taxes or other things. This is why He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And everything We have enumerated in a clear Imam﴾, that is, everything of the deeds of the servants and other things, whatever it is, is in a clear Imam, that is, a book that is followed, clarifying everything.

Mujahid, Qatadah, and Ibn Zayd said: It means the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz). Another group said: It means the pages of deeds.

The majority read *wa-naktubu* (we record) in the active voice. Zirr and Masruq read it in the passive voice.

The majority read *kulla shay'in ahsaynahu* with *kulla* in the accusative, by the construction of *ishtighal* (the verb governs its object through a pronoun). Abu al-Sammal read it with *raf'* (nominative), as a subject (ibtida').

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas regarding His saying *Ya-Sin*, that they both said: "O Muhammad."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated through several chains from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying *Ya-Sin*, that he said: "O human being."

Abd ibn Humayd narrated from al-Hasan, al-Dahhak, and Ikrimah something similar.

Ibn Mardawayh and Abu Nu'aym in *al-Dala'il* narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to recite in the mosque and would recite aloud, until some people from Quraysh were harmed by it, so they stood up to seize him, and suddenly their hands were gathered up to their necks, and suddenly they were blind and could not see. So they came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'We beseech you by God and by kinship, O Muhammad.' He said: There was no clan of Quraysh except that the Prophet (ﷺ) had kinship with them. So the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed until that left them, and then this was revealed: ﴿Ya-Sin. By the wise Qur'an﴾ up to His saying: ﴿Or you did not warn them, they will not believe﴾. He said: None of that group believed."

There are other narrations about the cause of the revelation of this, and this narration is the best of them and the closest to soundness.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him: "The shackles are what is between the chest and the chin. ﴿So they are raising their heads﴾, as a riding animal raises its head because of the bridle."

Ibn Mardawayh also narrated from him regarding His saying: ﴿And We have placed a barrier before them﴾ up to the end of the verse: "They used to pass by the Prophet (ﷺ) and not see him."

Ibn Mardawayh also narrated from him: "Quraysh gathered at the door of the Prophet (ﷺ), waiting for his exit in order to harm him. This grieved him, so Gabriel came to him with Surah Ya-Sin and ordered him to go out to them. He took a handful of dirt and went out reciting it, throwing the dirt on their heads. They did not see him until he passed. Then one of them touched his head and found the dirt. Another came and said: 'What is keeping you here?' They said: 'We are waiting for Muhammad.' He said: 'I saw him entering the mosque.' He said: 'Get up, for he has bewitched you.'"

Abd al-Razzaq, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it as good), al-Bazzar, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who graded it as sound), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: "The Banu Salamah were in one part of Medina, and they wanted to move closer to the mosque. So God revealed: ﴿Indeed, it is We who bring the dead to life, and We record what they have sent forward and their traces﴾. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) summoned them and said: 'Indeed, He records your traces.' Then he recited the verse to them, and they stayed."

Al-Firyabi, Ahmad in *al-Zuhd*, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Majah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated something similar from Ibn Abbas.

In Sahih Muslim and elsewhere, from the hadith of Jabir, who said: "The Banu Salamah wanted to sell their houses and move close to the mosque. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to them: 'O Banu Salamah, your houses record your traces.'"

**Commentary on Surah Ya-Sin**

It is Makkiyyah (Meccan, revealed in Makkah). Al-Qurtubi said: "There is consensus (ijma') on this, except that a group said that the verse ﴿And We record what they have sent before and their traces﴾ [Ya-Sin: 12] was revealed concerning the Banu Salamah of the Ansar, when they wanted to leave their homes and move to live near the Mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The explanation of that will come later."

Ibn al-Duraysi, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il* related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Surah Ya-Sin was revealed in Makkah." Ibn Mardawayh related the same from 'Aishah.

al-Darimi, al-Tirmidhi, Muhammad ibn Nasr, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* related from Anas that he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, everything has a heart, and the heart of the Qur'an is Ya-Sin. Whoever recites Ya-Sin, Allah records for him the reward of reciting the Qur'an ten times." al-Tirmidhi said after relating it: "This is a gharib (rare) hadith, which we only know from the hadith of Humayd ibn 'Abd al-Rahman. Its chain includes Harun Abu Muhammad, who is an unknown (majhul) shaykh. There is also a report on this topic from Abu Bakr, but it is not sound because its chain is weak."

al-Bazzar related from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, everything has a heart, and the heart of the Qur'an is Ya-Sin." Then he said after relating it: "We do not know of anyone who narrated it except Zayd, from Humayd," meaning Zayd ibn al-Hubab, from Humayd al-Makki, mawla (client) of the family of 'Alqamah.

al-Darimi, Abu Ya'la, al-Tabarani in *al-Awsat*, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* related from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Ya-Sin on a night seeking the Face of Allah, He forgives him for that night." Ibn Kathir said: "Its chain is good (jayyid)."

Ibn Hibban and al-Diya' related from Jundab ibn 'Abd Allah who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites Ya-Sin on a night seeking the Face of Allah, He forgives him."

Its chain in the *Sahih* of Ibn Hibban is thus: "Muhammad ibn Ishaq ibn Ibrahim, client of Thaqif, narrated to us; al-Walid ibn Shuja' ibn al-Walid al-Kubi narrated to us; my father narrated to us; Ziyad ibn Khaythamah narrated to us; Muhammad ibn Juhadah narrated to us, from al-Hasan, from Jundab ibn 'Abd Allah who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood and mentioned it..."

Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, Muhammad ibn Nasr, Ibn Hibban, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* related from Ma'qil ibn Yasar that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Ya-Sin is the heart of the Qur'an. No servant recites it seeking Allah and the Last Abode except that He forgives him what he has previously done of sin. So recite it over your dead." Ahmad was mentioned two chains for this: one of them includes an unknown narrator, and the other, he said, is from Abu 'Uthman, and it is not from al-Nahdi from his father, from Ma'qil.

Sa'id ibn Mansur and al-Bayhaqi related from Hassan ibn 'Atiyyah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites Ya-Sin, it is as if he recited the Qur'an ten times."

Ibn al-Duraysi, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Khatib, and al-Bayhaqi related from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Surah Ya-Sin is called in the Torah al-Mu'ammimah (the All-Encompassing). It encompasses its reciter with the good of this world and the Hereafter, it strives on his behalf against the afflictions of this world and the Hereafter, it repels from him the terrors of the Hereafter, and it is called al-Dafi'ah (the Repeller) and al-Qadiyah (the Fulfiller). It repels from its companion every evil and fulfils for him every need. Whoever recites it, it is equal to twenty pilgrimages; whoever hears it, it is equal for him to a thousand dinars spent in the way of Allah; and whoever writes it and then drinks it, it enters his belly with a thousand cures, a thousand lights, a thousand certainties, a thousand blessings, a thousand mercies, and it removes from him every rancour and disease."

al-Bayhaqi said: "'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr al-Judh'ani is alone in narrating it, from Sulayman ibn Rafi' al-Janadi, and he is munkar (rejected)."

I say: This is the hadith whose weakness of chain al-Tirmidhi previously pointed out. It is not far-fetched that it is fabricated (mawdu'), for all these expressions are rejected and far from the speech of one given *jawami' al-kalim* (concise, comprehensive speech). al-Tha'labi related it from the hadith of 'Aishah, and al-Khatib related it from the hadith of Anas, and al-Khatib related something similar from the hadith of 'Ali, more briefly than this.

al-Bazzar related from Ibn 'Abbas who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said concerning Surah Ya-Sin: "I wish that it were in the heart of every person of my Ummah." Its chain is thus: He said: Salamah ibn Shabib narrated to us; Ibrahim ibn al-Hakam ibn Aban narrated to us, from his father, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, and he mentioned it.

al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh related, and al-Suyuti said with a weak chain, from Anas who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever persists in reciting Ya-Sin every night and then dies, dies as a martyr (shahid)."

al-Darimi related from Ibn 'Abbas who said: Whoever recites Ya-Sin in the morning, is given ease for his day until evening, and whoever recites it at the beginning of his night, is given ease for his night until morning.

**In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful**

**His saying: ﴿Ya-Sin﴾ [1]**

The majority (al-Jumhur) recited it with the nun sukun (silent). Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Hamzah, Hafs, Qalun, and Warsh recited with idgham (assimilation) of the nun into the waw that follows it. 'Isa ibn 'Umar recited it with a fatha on the nun, and Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Abi Ishaq, and Nasr ibn 'Asim recited it with a kasra. The fatha is for *bina'* (indeclinability) or because it is the object of an implied verb whose estimate is: *utlu Ya-Sin* (recite Ya-Sin). The kasra is also for *bina'*, like *jayr*. It was said: the fatha and kasra are to avoid the meeting of two sakins (unvowelled letters).

As for the reason for the majority's recitation with sukun on the nun, it is because it is recited in the manner of a list (ta'did), so it has no share of *i'rab* (grammatical inflection).

Harun al-A'war, Muhammad ibn al-Sumayfa', and al-Kalbi recited it with a damma on the nun, for *bina'*, like *mundhu*, *haythu*, and *qattu*. It was also said: it is the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "this is Ya-Sin." It is not declined (*mamnu' min al-sarf*) due to being a proper noun (*'alamiyyah*) and feminine gender (*ta'nith*).

There is disagreement about the meaning of this word. It was said: its meaning is "O man" or "O person."

Ibn al-Anbari said: Pausing on *Ya-Sin* is good (hasan) for the one who says it is the opening of the surah. For the one who says its meaning is "O man," one does not pause on it.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr and others said: It is one of the names of Muhammad (ﷺ), and the evidence is ﴿Indeed you are among the messengers﴾. From it is the saying of al-Sa'd al-Himyari:

*O soul, do not exhaust yourself in sincere advice,*
*striving for love, except for the family of Ya-Sin.*

From it is His saying: ﴿Peace upon the family of Ilyasin﴾ [al-Saffat: 130], meaning: upon the family of Muhammad. What is meant by "Ilyasin" will come in al-Saffat.

al-Wahidi said: Ibn 'Abbas and the commentators said: It means "O person," meaning Muhammad (ﷺ).

Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: Its meaning is "O master of mankind."

Malik said: It is one of the names of Allah, the Exalted. Ashhab related this from him.

Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami related from Ja'far al-Sadiq that its meaning is "O master."

Ka'b said: It is an oath which Allah swore by. al-Zajjaj preferred that its meaning is "O Muhammad."

They differed on whether it is Arabic or non-Arabic. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and 'Ikrimah said: it is Abyssinian (Habashi).

al-Kalbi said: It is Syriac (Suryani), which the Arabs spoke, so it became part of their language. al-Sha'bi said: It is in the language of Tayy. al-Hasan said: It is in the language of Kalb. What has preceded in Ta-Ha and at the beginning of Surah al-Baqarah suffices here without lengthening.

**And the Wise Qur'an [2]**

Genitive (*bi al-jarr*), on the basis that it is sworn by directly (*muqsam bihi ibtida'an*).

It was also said: it is conjoined (ma'tuf) to Ya-Sin, on the estimate that it is in the genitive by an implied oath particle.
