On the first reading, when He, the Exalted, said ﴿Indeed, you are among the messengers﴾ [Ya-Sin: 3] and ﴿so that you may warn a people﴾ [Ya-Sin: 6], the meaning is: say to them, "I am not an innovation among the messengers. Before me, a short while ago, messengers came to the companions of the town, warned them as I have warned you, mentioned the Oneness of God, warned of the Resurrection, and gave good tidings of the bliss of the abode of permanence."

On the second reading, when He had said that warning does not benefit one whom God has led astray, and that He has decreed for him that he will not believe, the Prophet (ﷺ) was told: present to yourself and to your people a parable, i.e., liken for them, in your own mind, a parable of the companions of the town, where three messengers came to them and they did not believe. The messengers bore harm patiently, while you came to them alone, and your people are more numerous than the people of the three. For they (the messengers) came to the people of the town, whereas I have sent you to mankind entirely.

The meaning is: present to them a parable like the parable of the companions of the town, i.e., relate to them a wondrous story, the story of the companions of the town. The word "parable" has been omitted, and "the companions of the town" has been put in its place in terms of i'rab (grammatical case).

It has been said: there is no need for an implied word. Rather, the meaning is: make the companions of the town a parable for them, so that "a parable" and "the companions of the town" are two objects of "present" (iḍrib). Or "the companions of the town" is a substitute (badal) for "a parable." We have already discussed which of these two objects is the first: is it "a parable" or "the companions of the town"?

It has also been said: the striking of a parable (ḍarb al-mathal) is used at times to compare a strange situation with another similar to it, as in His saying: ﴿God presents as a parable for those who disbelieve the wife of Noah and the wife of Lot﴾ [al-Tahrim: 10]. And it is used at other times to mention a strange situation and explain it to people without intending to match it with a counterpart, as in His saying: ﴿and We presented to you the parables﴾ [Ibrahim: 45], i.e., We made clear to you wondrous and strange conditions, which in their strangeness are like parables. So His saying here, "and present to them a parable," admits of taking both senses into account.

His saying ﴿when the messengers came to it﴾ is a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for "the companions of the town." The messengers were the disciples of Jesus, whom he sent to the people of Antioch to call them to God.

God, the Exalted, attributed the sending to Himself in His saying ﴿when We sent to them two﴾, because Jesus sent them by the command of God, the Exalted. It is also permissible that God sent them after Jesus was raised to heaven. They denied them regarding their message. It has been said: they struck them and imprisoned them.

It is said: the names of the two were Yuhanna and Sham'un. It is said: the names of the three were Sadiq, Masduq and Shalum, as stated by Ibn Jarir and others.

It is said: they were Sam'an, Yahya and Bulus. ﴿So We reinforced them with a third﴾. The majority read it with the shadda (doubled z), and Abu Bakr, from ʿAsim, read it with the z unshaddahed.

Al-Jawhari said: "fa-ʿazzaznā" may be pronounced with or without doubling, i.e., "we strengthened and fortified," so the two readings have the same meaning on this view.

It has been said: the unshaddahed form means "we overpowered and subdued," and from it is His saying ﴿and he overpowered me in the speech﴾ [Sad: 23]. The shaddahed form means "we strengthened and multiplied."

It is said: this third one was Shamʿun. It is said: it was someone else. They said, "Indeed we are sent to you," i.e., the three said it together, and they brought this statement (p-1221) emphatically, because the denial directed at the two had already preceded.

Denying the two is also denying the third, because they were all sent with one thing, namely calling to God, Mighty and Majestic. This sentence is a resumptive (mustaʾnafa) answer to an implied question, as if it were said: what did these messengers say after being reinforced with a third?

Likewise, the sentence ﴿They said, "You are only human beings like us"﴾ is a resumptive answer to an implied question: as if it were said: what did the people of Antioch say to them? So it was said: they said, "You are only human beings like us," i.e., you share with us in humanity, so you have no distinction over us in which you are singled out.

Then they openly denied the sending down of the heavenly scriptures, saying: ﴿and the Most Merciful has sent down nothing; you are only lying﴾, meaning: concerning what you claim, and what others among those before you, of the messengers and their followers, claim. So the messengers answered them by affirming their mission with a statement emphasized strongly, because the people of Antioch repeated the denial.

That is their saying: ﴿Our Lord knows that we are indeed sent to you﴾. They emphasized the answer with the oath that is understood from their saying "Our Lord knows," and with "inna," and with the lam.

﴿And we are not responsible except for clear conveyance﴾, i.e., what is incumbent upon us from our Lord is only to convey His message in a manner that is manifest and clear, and nothing beyond that is upon us. This sentence is resumptive, like the one before it.

Likewise the sentence ﴿They said, "Indeed we see an omen in you"﴾ is a resumptive answer to an implied question, i.e., "we consider you ill-omened." They found no answer to give to the messengers except this answer, which is founded on ignorance, indicating great stupidity, and the absence of any argument with which you could repel the messengers.

Muqatil said: rain was withheld from them for three years.

It has been said: they had been warning them for ten years. Then they returned to tyranny and arrogance, when their chests were constricted and the excuses wore them out, so they said: ﴿If you do not desist, we will surely stone you﴾, i.e., if you do not abandon this claim and turn away from this statement, we will stone you with stones, and there will surely touch you from us a painful punishment, i.e., severe and terrible.

Al-Farra' said: most of what is in the Qur'an concerning stoning means killing. Qatadah said: it is in its literal sense of stoning with stones.

It has been said: the meaning of "painful punishment" is killing. It has been said: it is reviling. It has been said: it is painful torment without being restricted to a particular kind. This last is the apparent meaning.

Then the messengers answered them, repelling what they claimed of ill omen from them, so they said: ﴿Your omen is with you﴾, i.e., your ill omen is with you, from your own selves, attached to your necks, and it is not from our ill omen.

Al-Farra' said: "Your omen is with you" means your provision and your deeds. Qatadah said the same.

The majority read "ṭāʾirukum" as an active participle, meaning what has flown to you of good and evil. al-Hasan read "aṭayrukum," i.e., your ill-omening. ﴿Is it because you were reminded?﴾ The majority, among the seven and others, read it with an interrogative hamzah followed by the conditional "in" (idhā/in), with disagreement among them regarding easing and full pronunciation of the hamzah, and inserting an alif between the two hamzahs or not.

Abu Jaʿfar, Zirr ibn Hubaysh, Ibn al-Sumayfaʿ and Talhah read it with two fat-hah-marked hamzahs.

al-Aʿmash, ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar and al-Hasan read "ayna" with a fat-hah on the hamzah and a sukun on the yā', in the form of an adverb of place.

Sibawayh and Yunus disagreed on this: when an interrogative and a conditional come together, which of them is answered? Sibawayh held that the interrogative is answered, while Yunus held that the conditional is answered. On both views, the answer here is omitted, i.e., "Is it because you were reminded? Then your omen is with you," the preceding context indicating it.

al-Majishun read "an dhukkirtum" with an open hamzah, meaning "because you were reminded."

Then they turned away from what the interrogative and the conditional imply, namely that reminding is a cause of ill omen, and they said: ﴿Rather, you are a people who transgress﴾, i.e., the matter is not as you say; rather, you are a people whose habit is excess in disobedience.

Qatadah said: "transgressing" in your ill-omening. Yahya ibn Salam said: transgressing in your disbelief.

Ibn Bahr said: "al-saraf" here means corruption, and "al-israf" in its origin is exceeding the limit in opposing the truth.

﴿And there came from the farthest part of the city a man running﴾. He was Habib ibn Musa the carpenter, and he was a carpenter. It is said he was a cobbler, and it is said a launderer.

Mujahid and Muqatil said: he was Habib ibn Isra'il, a carpenter, and he used to carve idols.

Qatadah said: he used to worship God in a cave, and when he heard the news of the messengers he came running. The sentence ﴿He said, "O my people, follow the messengers"﴾ is a resumptive answer to an implied question: as if it were said: what did he say to them when he came? So it was said: "O my people, follow these messengers who were sent to you, for they have come with the truth."

Then he emphasized that and repeated it, saying: ﴿Follow those who do not ask you for a reward﴾, i.e., they do not ask you for a reward for what they have brought you of guidance, ﴿and they are guided﴾, meaning the messengers.

Then he presented the speech in the form of advice to himself, while he intended to counsel his people, saying: ﴿And why should I not worship He who originated me?﴾, i.e., what hinders me from my side from worshipping He who created me?

Then he returned to addressing them, to show that he did not mean himself but meant them by his speech, and said: ﴿and to Him you will be returned﴾. He did not say "to Him I will return," and in this there is exaggeration in warning.

Then he returned to the first line of argument, for the purpose of emphasis and further clarification, and said: ﴿Shall I take besides Him gods?﴾ He directed the denial towards himself, though they were the ones intended by it, i.e., I do not take gods besides God and worship them, and abandon the worship of the One who deserves worship, who is He who originated me.

Then he explained the state of these idols which they worship besides God, the Exalted, as a denial against them and an explanation of the misguidance of their minds and the deficiency of their perception, and said: ﴿If the Most Merciful wills harm for me, their intercession will avail me nothing at all﴾, i.e., nothing of benefit, whatever it may be, and they cannot rescue me from that harm which the Most Merciful wills for me. This sentence is either an attribute of "gods," or a resumptive sentence explaining their state in not benefiting or averting. His saying "will avail me nothing" is the answer to the condition. Talhah ibn Musarrif read "in yuridni" with a fat-hah on the yā'.

He said: ﴿Indeed, then I would be in clear error﴾, i.e., indeed, if I took gods besides Him, I would be in manifest and clear error. This is an allusion to them, as has preceded. "Error" means loss.

Then he declared his faith in a declaration after which no doubt remains, saying: ﴿Indeed I have believed in your Lord, so listen to me﴾. He addressed these words to the messengers.

The exegetes said: the people wanted to kill him, so he turned to the messengers and said: "Indeed I have believed in your Lord, O messengers, so listen to me," i.e., listen to my faith, and bear witness for me to it.

It has been said: he addressed these words to his people when they wanted to kill him, out of steadfastness in religion and rigor for the truth. When he said this and declared his faith, they rose against him and killed him. It is said (p-1222) that they trampled him with their feet. It is said that they burned him. It is said that they dug a pit for him and threw him into it. It is said that they did not kill him, but God raised him to heaven, so he is in Paradise, and Hasan said this. It is said that they sawed him with a saw.

It was said: "Enter Paradise," i.e., it was said to him this as an honour, that he would enter it after his killing, as is God's custom with His martyred servants.

According to the view of one who said he was raised to heaven and was not killed, the meaning is: when they wanted to kill him, God saved him from being killed. It was said to him: "Enter Paradise," and when he entered it and beheld it: ﴿It was said, "Enter Paradise." He said, "Would that my people knew what my Lord has forgiven me and made me among the honoured"﴾. The sentence is a resumptive answer to an implied question, i.e., what did he say after it was said to him, "Enter Paradise," and he entered it? So it was said: he said, "Would that my people knew," etc.

The "mā" in "bi-mā ghafara lī" is the verbal-source (maṣdariyya) "mā", i.e., "by the forgiveness of my Lord." It has been said it is the relative (mawṣūla), i.e., "by that which my Lord forgave me," the returning pronoun being omitted, i.e., "my Lord forgave it to me." This has been deemed weak, because there is no sense in his wishing that his people knew about his forgiven sins; what is meant is only his wish that his people would know of his Lord's forgiveness of him.

al-Farra' said: it is an interrogative meaning amazement, as if he said: "for what reason did my Lord forgive me?"

al-Kisa'i said: if this were correct, he would have said "bi-mā" without an alif.

This is answered by saying that it has been attested in the language of the Arabs to be used with the alif, even though it is less common than omitting it. Among that is the verse of the poet:

"On what grounds does a base fellow revile me, like a pig rolling in ash?"

In the meaning of his wishing (tamanni), there are two opinions. The first is that he wished they would know his condition, so that they would know the goodness of his end and the praiseworthy outcome of his affair, as a humiliation to them.

It has also been said that he wished they would know this so that they would believe as he believed and come to a state like his.

Al-Firyabi recorded from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿And set forth for them a parable: the companions of the town﴾, that he said: "It is Antioch." Ibn Abi Hatim recorded the same from Buraydah.

Ibn Sa'd and Ibn Asakir recorded, through the route of al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Between Musa ibn Imran and Isa ibn Maryam there were one thousand and nine hundred years, and there was no fatrah (a gap in which no prophet was sent) between them. A thousand prophets from the Children of Israel were sent between them, besides those who were sent from other than them. Between the birth of Isa and the Prophet (ﷺ) there were five hundred and sixty-nine years. In the first part of that period three prophets were sent, and this is His saying: ﴿When We sent to them two, and they denied them, so We strengthened [them] with a third﴾. The one who was strengthened by them was Shim'un, and he was one of the Hawariyyun (the disciples). The fatrah during which Allah sent no messenger was four hundred and thirty-four years."

Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from him also, regarding His saying ﴿Your omen is with you﴾, that he said: "Your ill omen is with you."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from him also, regarding His saying ﴿And there came from the farthest part of the city a man﴾, that he said: "He is Habib the carpenter."

Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from him through another route that he said: "The name of the companion of Ya Sin was Habib, and leprosy had spread in him quickly."

Al-Hakim recorded from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "When the companion of Ya Sin said, ﴿O my people, follow the messengers﴾, they throttled him so that he would die. Then he turned to the prophets and said, ﴿Indeed I have believed in your Lord, so hear me﴾," meaning: "So bear witness for me."

The word "parable" has been omitted, and "the companions of the town" has been put in its place in terms of i'rab (grammatical case).

It is said: the names of the two were Yuhanna and Sham'un. It is said: the names of the three were Sadiq, Masduq and Shalum, as stated by Ibn Jarir and others.

It has been said: the unshaddahed form means "we overpowered and subdued," and from it is His saying ﴿and he overpowered me in the speech﴾ [Sad: 23]. The shaddahed form means "we strengthened and multiplied."

It is said: this third one was Shamʿun. It is said: it was someone else. They said, "Indeed we are sent to you," i.e., the three said it together, and they brought this statement (p-1221) emphatically, because the denial directed at the two had already preceded.

So it was said: they said, "You are only human beings like us," i.e., you share with us in humanity, so you have no distinction over us in which you are singled out.

So the messengers answered them by affirming their mission with a statement emphasized strongly, because the people of Antioch repeated the denial.

That is their saying: ﴿Our Lord knows that we are indeed sent to you﴾. They emphasized the answer with the oath that is understood from their saying "Our Lord knows," and with "inna," and with the lam.

Muqatil said: rain was withheld from them for three years.

Abu Jaʿfar, Zirr ibn Hubaysh, Ibn al-Sumayfaʿ and Talhah read it with two fat-hah-marked hamzahs.

al-Aʿmash, ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar and al-Hasan read "ayna" with a fat-hah on the hamzah and a sukun on the yā', in the form of an adverb of place.

Sibawayh held that the interrogative is answered, while Yunus held that the conditional is answered. On both views, the answer here is omitted, i.e., "Is it because you were reminded? Ibn Bahr said: "al-saraf" here means corruption, and "al-israf" in its origin is exceeding the limit in opposing the truth.

﴿And there came from the farthest part of the city a man running﴾. He was Habib ibn Musa the carpenter, and he was a carpenter. It is said he was a cobbler, and it is said a launderer.

Mujahid and Muqatil said: he was Habib ibn Isra'il, a carpenter, and he used to carve idols.

Qatadah said: he used to worship God in a cave, and when he heard the news of the messengers he came running. The sentence ﴿He said, "O my people, follow the messengers"﴾ is a resumptive answer to an implied question: as if it were said: what did he say to them when he came? So it was said: "O my people, follow these messengers who were sent to you, for they have come with the truth."

Then he emphasized that and repeated it, saying: ﴿Follow those who do not ask you for a reward﴾, i.e., they do not ask you for a reward for what they have brought you of guidance, ﴿and they are guided﴾, meaning the messengers.

Then he presented the speech in the form of advice to himself, while he intended to counsel his people, saying: ﴿And why should I not worship He who originated me?﴾, i.e., what hinders me from my side from worshipping He who created me?

Then he returned to addressing them, to show that he did not mean himself but meant them by his speech, and said: ﴿and to Him you will be returned﴾. He did not say "to Him I will return," and in this there is exaggeration in warning.

Then he returned to the first line of argument, for the purpose of emphasis and further clarification, and said: ﴿Shall I take besides Him gods?﴾ He directed the denial towards himself, though they were the ones intended by it, i.e., I do not take gods besides God and worship them, and abandon the worship of the One who deserves worship, who is He who originated me.

Talhah ibn Musarrif read "in yuridni" with a fat-hah on the yā'.

He said: ﴿Indeed, then I would be in clear error﴾, i.e., indeed, if I took gods besides Him, I would be in manifest and clear error. This is an allusion to them, as has preceded. "Error" means loss.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 36, verses 13–27 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿And present to them a parable: the companions of the town﴾. The discussion of its like has already passed in Surat al-Baqarah and Surat al-Naml. The meaning is: present a parable on their behalf, or present for yourself the companions of the town as a parable, i.e., liken them in your own mind to the companions of the town. On the first reading, when He, the Exalted, said ﴿Indeed, you are among the messengers﴾ [Ya-Sin: 3] and ﴿so that you may warn a people﴾ [Ya-Sin: 6], the meaning is: say to them, "I am not an innovation among the messengers. Before me, a short while ago, messengers came to the companions of the town, warned them as I have warned you, mentioned the Oneness of God, warned of the Resurrection, and gave good tidings of the bliss of the abode of permanence."

On the second reading, when He had said that warning does not benefit one whom God has led astray, and that He has decreed for him that he will not believe, the Prophet (ﷺ) was told: present to yourself and to your people a parable, i.e., liken for them, in your own mind, a parable of the companions of the town, where three messengers came to them and they did not believe. The messengers bore harm patiently, while you came to them alone, and your people are more numerous than the people of the three. For they (the messengers) came to the people of the town, whereas I have sent you to mankind entirely.

The meaning is: present to them a parable like the parable of the companions of the town, i.e., relate to them a wondrous story, the story of the companions of the town. The word "parable" has been omitted, and "the companions of the town" has been put in its place in terms of i'rab (grammatical case).

It has been said: there is no need for an implied word. Rather, the meaning is: make the companions of the town a parable for them, so that "a parable" and "the companions of the town" are two objects of "present" (iḍrib). Or "the companions of the town" is a substitute (badal) for "a parable." We have already discussed which of these two objects is the first: is it "a parable" or "the companions of the town"?

It has also been said: the striking of a parable (ḍarb al-mathal) is used at times to compare a strange situation with another similar to it, as in His saying: ﴿God presents as a parable for those who disbelieve the wife of Noah and the wife of Lot﴾ [al-Tahrim: 10]. And it is used at other times to mention a strange situation and explain it to people without intending to match it with a counterpart, as in His saying: ﴿and We presented to you the parables﴾ [Ibrahim: 45], i.e., We made clear to you wondrous and strange conditions, which in their strangeness are like parables. So His saying here, "and present to them a parable," admits of taking both senses into account.

Al-Qurtubi said: this town is Antioch according to the statement of all the exegetes. His saying ﴿when the messengers came to it﴾ is a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for "the companions of the town." The messengers were the disciples of Jesus, whom he sent to the people of Antioch to call them to God.

God, the Exalted, attributed the sending to Himself in His saying ﴿when We sent to them two﴾, because Jesus sent them by the command of God, the Exalted. It is also permissible that God sent them after Jesus was raised to heaven. They denied them regarding their message. It has been said: they struck them and imprisoned them.

It is said: the names of the two were Yuhanna and Sham'un. It is said: the names of the three were Sadiq, Masduq and Shalum, as stated by Ibn Jarir and others.

It is said: they were Sam'an, Yahya and Bulus. ﴿So We reinforced them with a third﴾. The majority read it with the shadda (doubled z), and Abu Bakr, from ʿAsim, read it with the z unshaddahed.

Al-Jawhari said: "fa-ʿazzaznā" may be pronounced with or without doubling, i.e., "we strengthened and fortified," so the two readings have the same meaning on this view.

It has been said: the unshaddahed form means "we overpowered and subdued," and from it is His saying ﴿and he overpowered me in the speech﴾ [Sad: 23]. The shaddahed form means "we strengthened and multiplied."

It is said: this third one was Shamʿun. It is said: it was someone else. They said, "Indeed we are sent to you," i.e., the three said it together, and they brought this statement (p-1221) emphatically, because the denial directed at the two had already preceded.

Denying the two is also denying the third, because they were all sent with one thing, namely calling to God, Mighty and Majestic. This sentence is a resumptive (mustaʾnafa) answer to an implied question, as if it were said: what did these messengers say after being reinforced with a third?

Likewise, the sentence ﴿They said, "You are only human beings like us"﴾ is a resumptive answer to an implied question: as if it were said: what did the people of Antioch say to them? So it was said: they said, "You are only human beings like us," i.e., you share with us in humanity, so you have no distinction over us in which you are singled out.

Then they openly denied the sending down of the heavenly scriptures, saying: ﴿and the Most Merciful has sent down nothing; you are only lying﴾, meaning: concerning what you claim, and what others among those before you, of the messengers and their followers, claim. So the messengers answered them by affirming their mission with a statement emphasized strongly, because the people of Antioch repeated the denial.

That is their saying: ﴿Our Lord knows that we are indeed sent to you﴾. They emphasized the answer with the oath that is understood from their saying "Our Lord knows," and with "inna," and with the lam.

﴿And we are not responsible except for clear conveyance﴾, i.e., what is incumbent upon us from our Lord is only to convey His message in a manner that is manifest and clear, and nothing beyond that is upon us. This sentence is resumptive, like the one before it.

Likewise the sentence ﴿They said, "Indeed we see an omen in you"﴾ is a resumptive answer to an implied question, i.e., "we consider you ill-omened." They found no answer to give to the messengers except this answer, which is founded on ignorance, indicating great stupidity, and the absence of any argument with which you could repel the messengers.

Muqatil said: rain was withheld from them for three years.

It has been said: they had been warning them for ten years. Then they returned to tyranny and arrogance, when their chests were constricted and the excuses wore them out, so they said: ﴿If you do not desist, we will surely stone you﴾, i.e., if you do not abandon this claim and turn away from this statement, we will stone you with stones, and there will surely touch you from us a painful punishment, i.e., severe and terrible.

Al-Farra' said: most of what is in the Qur'an concerning stoning means killing. Qatadah said: it is in its literal sense of stoning with stones.

It has been said: the meaning of "painful punishment" is killing. It has been said: it is reviling. It has been said: it is painful torment without being restricted to a particular kind. This last is the apparent meaning.

Then the messengers answered them, repelling what they claimed of ill omen from them, so they said: ﴿Your omen is with you﴾, i.e., your ill omen is with you, from your own selves, attached to your necks, and it is not from our ill omen.

Al-Farra' said: "Your omen is with you" means your provision and your deeds. Qatadah said the same.

The majority read "ṭāʾirukum" as an active participle, meaning what has flown to you of good and evil. al-Hasan read "aṭayrukum," i.e., your ill-omening. ﴿Is it because you were reminded?﴾ The majority, among the seven and others, read it with an interrogative hamzah followed by the conditional "in" (idhā/in), with disagreement among them regarding easing and full pronunciation of the hamzah, and inserting an alif between the two hamzahs or not.

Abu Jaʿfar, Zirr ibn Hubaysh, Ibn al-Sumayfaʿ and Talhah read it with two fat-hah-marked hamzahs.

al-Aʿmash, ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar and al-Hasan read "ayna" with a fat-hah on the hamzah and a sukun on the yā', in the form of an adverb of place.

Sibawayh and Yunus disagreed on this: when an interrogative and a conditional come together, which of them is answered? Sibawayh held that the interrogative is answered, while Yunus held that the conditional is answered. On both views, the answer here is omitted, i.e., "Is it because you were reminded? Then your omen is with you," the preceding context indicating it.

al-Majishun read "an dhukkirtum" with an open hamzah, meaning "because you were reminded."

Then they turned away from what the interrogative and the conditional imply, namely that reminding is a cause of ill omen, and they said: ﴿Rather, you are a people who transgress﴾, i.e., the matter is not as you say; rather, you are a people whose habit is excess in disobedience.

Qatadah said: "transgressing" in your ill-omening. Yahya ibn Salam said: transgressing in your disbelief.

Ibn Bahr said: "al-saraf" here means corruption, and "al-israf" in its origin is exceeding the limit in opposing the truth.

﴿And there came from the farthest part of the city a man running﴾. He was Habib ibn Musa the carpenter, and he was a carpenter. It is said he was a cobbler, and it is said a launderer.

Mujahid and Muqatil said: he was Habib ibn Isra'il, a carpenter, and he used to carve idols.

Qatadah said: he used to worship God in a cave, and when he heard the news of the messengers he came running. The sentence ﴿He said, "O my people, follow the messengers"﴾ is a resumptive answer to an implied question: as if it were said: what did he say to them when he came? So it was said: "O my people, follow these messengers who were sent to you, for they have come with the truth."

Then he emphasized that and repeated it, saying: ﴿Follow those who do not ask you for a reward﴾, i.e., they do not ask you for a reward for what they have brought you of guidance, ﴿and they are guided﴾, meaning the messengers.

Then he presented the speech in the form of advice to himself, while he intended to counsel his people, saying: ﴿And why should I not worship He who originated me?﴾, i.e., what hinders me from my side from worshipping He who created me?

Then he returned to addressing them, to show that he did not mean himself but meant them by his speech, and said: ﴿and to Him you will be returned﴾. He did not say "to Him I will return," and in this there is exaggeration in warning.

Then he returned to the first line of argument, for the purpose of emphasis and further clarification, and said: ﴿Shall I take besides Him gods?﴾ He directed the denial towards himself, though they were the ones intended by it, i.e., I do not take gods besides God and worship them, and abandon the worship of the One who deserves worship, who is He who originated me.

Then he explained the state of these idols which they worship besides God, the Exalted, as a denial against them and an explanation of the misguidance of their minds and the deficiency of their perception, and said: ﴿If the Most Merciful wills harm for me, their intercession will avail me nothing at all﴾, i.e., nothing of benefit, whatever it may be, and they cannot rescue me from that harm which the Most Merciful wills for me. This sentence is either an attribute of "gods," or a resumptive sentence explaining their state in not benefiting or averting. His saying "will avail me nothing" is the answer to the condition. Talhah ibn Musarrif read "in yuridni" with a fat-hah on the yā'.

He said: ﴿Indeed, then I would be in clear error﴾, i.e., indeed, if I took gods besides Him, I would be in manifest and clear error. This is an allusion to them, as has preceded. "Error" means loss.

Then he declared his faith in a declaration after which no doubt remains, saying: ﴿Indeed I have believed in your Lord, so listen to me﴾. He addressed these words to the messengers.

The exegetes said: the people wanted to kill him, so he turned to the messengers and said: "Indeed I have believed in your Lord, O messengers, so listen to me," i.e., listen to my faith, and bear witness for me to it.

It has been said: he addressed these words to his people when they wanted to kill him, out of steadfastness in religion and rigor for the truth. When he said this and declared his faith, they rose against him and killed him. It is said (p-1222) that they trampled him with their feet. It is said that they burned him. It is said that they dug a pit for him and threw him into it. It is said that they did not kill him, but God raised him to heaven, so he is in Paradise, and Hasan said this. It is said that they sawed him with a saw.

It was said: "Enter Paradise," i.e., it was said to him this as an honour, that he would enter it after his killing, as is God's custom with His martyred servants.

According to the view of one who said he was raised to heaven and was not killed, the meaning is: when they wanted to kill him, God saved him from being killed. It was said to him: "Enter Paradise," and when he entered it and beheld it: ﴿It was said, "Enter Paradise." He said, "Would that my people knew what my Lord has forgiven me and made me among the honoured"﴾. The sentence is a resumptive answer to an implied question, i.e., what did he say after it was said to him, "Enter Paradise," and he entered it? So it was said: he said, "Would that my people knew," etc.

The "mā" in "bi-mā ghafara lī" is the verbal-source (maṣdariyya) "mā", i.e., "by the forgiveness of my Lord." It has been said it is the relative (mawṣūla), i.e., "by that which my Lord forgave me," the returning pronoun being omitted, i.e., "my Lord forgave it to me." This has been deemed weak, because there is no sense in his wishing that his people knew about his forgiven sins; what is meant is only his wish that his people would know of his Lord's forgiveness of him.

al-Farra' said: it is an interrogative meaning amazement, as if he said: "for what reason did my Lord forgive me?"

al-Kisa'i said: if this were correct, he would have said "bi-mā" without an alif.

This is answered by saying that it has been attested in the language of the Arabs to be used with the alif, even though it is less common than omitting it. Among that is the verse of the poet:

"On what grounds does a base fellow revile me, like a pig rolling in ash?"

In the meaning of his wishing (tamanni), there are two opinions. The first is that he wished they would know his condition, so that they would know the goodness of his end and the praiseworthy outcome of his affair, as a humiliation to them.

It has also been said that he wished they would know this so that they would believe as he believed and come to a state like his.

Al-Firyabi recorded from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿And set forth for them a parable: the companions of the town﴾, that he said: "It is Antioch." Ibn Abi Hatim recorded the same from Buraydah.

Ibn Sa'd and Ibn Asakir recorded, through the route of al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Between Musa ibn Imran and Isa ibn Maryam there were one thousand and nine hundred years, and there was no fatrah (a gap in which no prophet was sent) between them. A thousand prophets from the Children of Israel were sent between them, besides those who were sent from other than them. Between the birth of Isa and the Prophet (ﷺ) there were five hundred and sixty-nine years. In the first part of that period three prophets were sent, and this is His saying: ﴿When We sent to them two, and they denied them, so We strengthened [them] with a third﴾. The one who was strengthened by them was Shim'un, and he was one of the Hawariyyun (the disciples). The fatrah during which Allah sent no messenger was four hundred and thirty-four years."

Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from him also, regarding His saying ﴿Your omen is with you﴾, that he said: "Your ill omen is with you."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from him also, regarding His saying ﴿And there came from the farthest part of the city a man﴾, that he said: "He is Habib the carpenter."

Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from him through another route that he said: "The name of the companion of Ya Sin was Habib, and leprosy had spread in him quickly."

Al-Hakim recorded from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "When the companion of Ya Sin said, ﴿O my people, follow the messengers﴾, they throttled him so that he would die. Then he turned to the prophets and said, ﴿Indeed I have believed in your Lord, so hear me﴾," meaning: "So bear witness for me."

On the first reading, when He, the Exalted, said ﴿Indeed, you are among the messengers﴾ [Ya-Sin: 3] and ﴿so that you may warn a people﴾ [Ya-Sin: 6], the meaning is: say to them, "I am not an innovation among the messengers. Before me, a short while ago, messengers came to the companions of the town, warned them as I have warned you, mentioned the Oneness of God, warned of the Resurrection, and gave good tidings of the bliss of the abode of permanence."

On the second reading, when He had said that warning does not benefit one whom God has led astray, and that He has decreed for him that he will not believe, the Prophet (ﷺ) was told: present to yourself and to your people a parable, i.e., liken for them, in your own mind, a parable of the companions of the town, where three messengers came to them and they did not believe. The messengers bore harm patiently, while you came to them alone, and your people are more numerous than the people of the three. For they (the messengers) came to the people of the town, whereas I have sent you to mankind entirely.

The meaning is: present to them a parable like the parable of the companions of the town, i.e., relate to them a wondrous story, the story of the companions of the town. The word "parable" has been omitted, and "the companions of the town" has been put in its place in terms of i'rab (grammatical case).

It has been said: there is no need for an implied word. Rather, the meaning is: make the companions of the town a parable for them, so that "a parable" and "the companions of the town" are two objects of "present" (iḍrib). Or "the companions of the town" is a substitute (badal) for "a parable." We have already discussed which of these two objects is the first: is it "a parable" or "the companions of the town"?

It has also been said: the striking of a parable (ḍarb al-mathal) is used at times to compare a strange situation with another similar to it, as in His saying: ﴿God presents as a parable for those who disbelieve the wife of Noah and the wife of Lot﴾ [al-Tahrim: 10]. And it is used at other times to mention a strange situation and explain it to people without intending to match it with a counterpart, as in His saying: ﴿and We presented to you the parables﴾ [Ibrahim: 45], i.e., We made clear to you wondrous and strange conditions, which in their strangeness are like parables. Al-Qurtubi said: this town is Antioch according to the statement of all the exegetes. His saying ﴿when the messengers came to it﴾ is a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for "the companions of the town." The messengers were the disciples of Jesus, whom he sent to the people of Antioch to call them to God.

God, the Exalted, attributed the sending to Himself in His saying ﴿when We sent to them two﴾, because Jesus sent them by the command of God, the Exalted. It is also permissible that God sent them after Jesus was raised to heaven. They denied them regarding their message. It has been said: they struck them and imprisoned them.

It is said: the names of the two were Yuhanna and Sham'un. It is said: the names of the three were Sadiq, Masduq and Shalum, as stated by Ibn Jarir and others.

It is said: they were Sam'an, Yahya and Bulus. ﴿So We reinforced them with a third﴾. The majority read it with the shadda (doubled z), and Abu Bakr, from ʿAsim, read it with the z unshaddahed.

Al-Jawhari said: "fa-ʿazzaznā" may be pronounced with or without doubling, i.e., "we strengthened and fortified," so the two readings have the same meaning on this view.

It has been said: the unshaddahed form means "we overpowered and subdued," and from it is His saying ﴿and he overpowered me in the speech﴾ [Sad: 23]. The shaddahed form means "we strengthened and multiplied."

It is said: this third one was Shamʿun. It is said: it was someone else. They said, "Indeed we are sent to you," i.e., the three said it together, and they brought this statement (p-1221) emphatically, because the denial directed at the two had already preceded.

Likewise, the sentence ﴿They said, "You are only human beings like us"﴾ is a resumptive answer to an implied question: as if it were said: what did the people of Antioch say to them? So it was said: they said, "You are only human beings like us," i.e., you share with us in humanity, so you have no distinction over us in which you are singled out.

Then they openly denied the sending down of the heavenly scriptures, saying: ﴿and the Most Merciful has sent down nothing; you are only lying﴾, meaning: concerning what you claim, and what others among those before you, of the messengers and their followers, claim. So the messengers answered them by affirming their mission with a statement emphasized strongly, because the people of Antioch repeated the denial.

That is their saying: ﴿Our Lord knows that we are indeed sent to you﴾. They emphasized the answer with the oath that is understood from their saying "Our Lord knows," and with "inna," and with the lam.

﴿And we are not responsible except for clear conveyance﴾, i.e., what is incumbent upon us from our Lord is only to convey His message in a manner that is manifest and clear, and nothing beyond that is upon us. This sentence is resumptive, like the one before it.

Likewise the sentence ﴿They said, "Indeed we see an omen in you"﴾ is a resumptive answer to an implied question, i.e., "we consider you ill-omened." They found no answer to give to the messengers except this answer, which is founded on ignorance, indicating great stupidity, and the absence of any argument with which you could repel the messengers.

Muqatil said: rain was withheld from them for three years.

It has been said: they had been warning them for ten years. Then they returned to tyranny and arrogance, when their chests were constricted and the excuses wore them out, so they said: ﴿If you do not desist, we will surely stone you﴾, i.e., if you do not abandon this claim and turn away from this statement, we will stone you with stones, and there will surely touch you from us a painful punishment, i.e., severe and terrible.

Al-Farra' said: most of what is in the Qur'an concerning stoning means killing. Qatadah said: it is in its literal sense of stoning with stones.

It has been said: the meaning of "painful punishment" is killing. It has been said: it is reviling. It has been said: it is painful torment without being restricted to a particular kind. This last is the apparent meaning.

Al-Farra' said: "Your omen is with you" means your provision and your deeds. Qatadah said the same.

Abu Jaʿfar, Zirr ibn Hubaysh, Ibn al-Sumayfaʿ and Talhah read it with two fat-hah-marked hamzahs.

al-Aʿmash, ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar and al-Hasan read "ayna" with a fat-hah on the hamzah and a sukun on the yā', in the form of an adverb of place.

Sibawayh and Yunus disagreed on this: when an interrogative and a conditional come together, which of them is answered? Sibawayh held that the interrogative is answered, while Yunus held that the conditional is answered. On both views, the answer here is omitted, i.e., "Is it because you were reminded? Then your omen is with you," the preceding context indicating it.

al-Majishun read "an dhukkirtum" with an open hamzah, meaning "because you were reminded."

Then they turned away from what the interrogative and the conditional imply, namely that reminding is a cause of ill omen, and they said: ﴿Rather, you are a people who transgress﴾, i.e., the matter is not as you say; rather, you are a people whose habit is excess in disobedience.

Qatadah said: "transgressing" in your ill-omening. Yahya ibn Salam said: transgressing in your disbelief.

Ibn Bahr said: "al-saraf" here means corruption, and "al-israf" in its origin is exceeding the limit in opposing the truth.

﴿And there came from the farthest part of the city a man running﴾. He was Habib ibn Musa the carpenter, and he was a carpenter. It is said he was a cobbler, and it is said a launderer.

Mujahid and Muqatil said: he was Habib ibn Isra'il, a carpenter, and he used to carve idols.

Qatadah said: he used to worship God in a cave, and when he heard the news of the messengers he came running. The sentence ﴿He said, "O my people, follow the messengers"﴾ is a resumptive answer to an implied question: as if it were said: what did he say to them when he came? So it was said: "O my people, follow these messengers who were sent to you, for they have come with the truth."

Then he emphasized that and repeated it, saying: ﴿Follow those who do not ask you for a reward﴾, i.e., they do not ask you for a reward for what they have brought you of guidance, ﴿and they are guided﴾, meaning the messengers.

Then he presented the speech in the form of advice to himself, while he intended to counsel his people, saying: ﴿And why should I not worship He who originated me?﴾, i.e., what hinders me from my side from worshipping He who created me?

Then he returned to addressing them, to show that he did not mean himself but meant them by his speech, and said: ﴿and to Him you will be returned﴾. He did not say "to Him I will return," and in this there is exaggeration in warning.

Then he returned to the first line of argument, for the purpose of emphasis and further clarification, and said: ﴿Shall I take besides Him gods?﴾ He directed the denial towards himself, though they were the ones intended by it, i.e., I do not take gods besides God and worship them, and abandon the worship of the One who deserves worship, who is He who originated me.

Then he explained the state of these idols which they worship besides God, the Exalted, as a denial against them and an explanation of the misguidance of their minds and the deficiency of their perception, and said: ﴿If the Most Merciful wills harm for me, their intercession will avail me nothing at all﴾, i.e., nothing of benefit, whatever it may be, and they cannot rescue me from that harm which the Most Merciful wills for me. Talhah ibn Musarrif read "in yuridni" with a fat-hah on the yā'.

He said: ﴿Indeed, then I would be in clear error﴾, i.e., indeed, if I took gods besides Him, I would be in manifest and clear error. This is an allusion to them, as has preceded. "Error" means loss.

al-Aʿmash, ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar and al-Hasan read "ayna" with a fat-hah on the hamzah and a sukun on the yā', in the form of an adverb of place.

Sibawayh and Yunus disagreed on this: when an interrogative and a conditional come together, which of them is answered? Sibawayh held that the interrogative is answered, while Yunus held that the conditional is answered. On both views, the answer here is omitted, i.e., "Is it because you were reminded? Then your omen is with you," the preceding context indicating it.

al-Majishun read "an dhukkirtum" with an open hamzah, meaning "because you were reminded."

Then they turned away from what the interrogative and the conditional imply, namely that reminding is a cause of ill omen, and they said: ﴿Rather, you are a people who transgress﴾, i.e., the matter is not as you say; rather, you are a people whose habit is excess in disobedience.

Qatadah said: "transgressing" in your ill-omening. Yahya ibn Salam said: transgressing in your disbelief.

Ibn Bahr said: "al-saraf" here means corruption, and "al-israf" in its origin is exceeding the limit in opposing the truth.

﴿And there came from the farthest part of the city a man running﴾. He was Habib ibn Musa the carpenter, and he was a carpenter. It is said he was a cobbler, and it is said a launderer.

Mujahid and Muqatil said: he was Habib ibn Isra'il, a carpenter, and he used to carve idols.

Qatadah said: he used to worship God in a cave, and when he heard the news of the messengers he came running. The sentence ﴿He said, "O my people, follow the messengers"﴾ is a resumptive answer to an implied question: as if it were said: what did he say to them when he came? So it was said: "O my people, follow these messengers who were sent to you, for they have come with the truth."

Then he emphasized that and repeated it, saying: ﴿Follow those who do not ask you for a reward﴾, i.e., they do not ask you for a reward for what they have brought you of guidance, ﴿and they are guided﴾, meaning the messengers.

Then he presented the speech in the form of advice to himself, while he intended to counsel his people, saying: ﴿And why should I not worship He who originated me?﴾, i.e., what hinders me from my side from worshipping He who created me?

Then he returned to addressing them, to show that he did not mean himself but meant them by his speech, and said: ﴿and to Him you will be returned﴾. He did not say "to Him I will return," and in this there is exaggeration in warning.

Then he returned to the first line of argument, for the purpose of emphasis and further clarification, and said: ﴿Shall I take besides Him gods?﴾ He directed the denial towards himself, though they were the ones intended by it, i.e., I do not take gods besides God and worship them, and abandon the worship of the One who deserves worship, who is He who originated me.

Then he explained the state of these idols which they worship besides God, the Exalted, as a denial against them and an explanation of the misguidance of their minds and the deficiency of their perception, and said: ﴿If the Most Merciful wills harm for me, their intercession will avail me nothing at all﴾, i.e., nothing of benefit, whatever it may be, and they cannot rescue me from that harm which the Most Merciful wills for me. This sentence is either an attribute of "gods," or a resumptive sentence explaining their state in not benefiting or averting. His saying "will avail me nothing" is the answer to the condition. Talhah ibn Musarrif read "in yuridni" with a fat-hah on the yā'.

He said: ﴿Indeed, then I would be in clear error﴾, i.e., indeed, if I took gods besides Him, I would be in manifest and clear error. This is an allusion to them, as has preceded. "Error" means loss.

Then he declared his faith in a declaration after which no doubt remains, saying: ﴿Indeed I have believed in your Lord, so listen to me﴾. He addressed these words to the messengers.

The exegetes said: the people wanted to kill him, so he turned to the messengers and said: "Indeed I have believed in your Lord, O messengers, so listen to me," i.e., listen to my faith, and bear witness for me to it.

It has been said: he addressed these words to his people when they wanted to kill him, out of steadfastness in religion and rigor for the truth. When he said this and declared his faith, they rose against him and killed him. It is said (p-1222) that they trampled him with their feet. It is said that they burned him. It is said that they dug a pit for him and threw him into it. It is said that they did not kill him, but God raised him to heaven, so he is in Paradise, and Hasan said this. It is said that they sawed him with a saw.

It was said: "Enter Paradise," i.e., it was said to him this as an honour, that he would enter it after his killing, as is God's custom with His martyred servants.

According to the view of one who said he was raised to heaven and was not killed, the meaning is: when they wanted to kill him, God saved him from being killed. It was said to him: "Enter Paradise," and when he entered it and beheld it: ﴿It was said, "Enter Paradise." He said, "Would that my people knew what my Lord has forgiven me and made me among the honoured"﴾. The sentence is a resumptive answer to an implied question, i.e., what did he say after it was said to him, "Enter Paradise," and he entered it? So it was said: he said, "Would that my people knew," etc.

The "mā" in "bi-mā ghafara lī" is the verbal-source (maṣdariyya) "mā", i.e., "by the forgiveness of my Lord." It has been said it is the relative (mawṣūla), i.e., "by that which my Lord forgave me," the returning pronoun being omitted, i.e., "my Lord forgave it to me." This has been deemed weak, because there is no sense in his wishing that his people knew about his forgiven sins; what is meant is only his wish that his people would know of his Lord's forgiveness of him.

al-Farra' said: it is an interrogative meaning amazement, as if he said: "for what reason did my Lord forgive me?"

al-Kisa'i said: if this were correct, he would have said "bi-mā" without an alif.

This is answered by saying that it has been attested in the language of the Arabs to be used with the alif, even though it is less common than omitting it. Among that is the verse of the poet:

"On what grounds does a base fellow revile me, like a pig rolling in ash?"

In the meaning of his wishing (tamanni), there are two opinions. The first is that he wished they would know his condition, so that they would know the goodness of his end and the praiseworthy outcome of his affair, as a humiliation to them.

It has also been said that he wished they would know this so that they would believe as he believed and come to a state like his.

Al-Firyabi recorded from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿And set forth for them a parable: the companions of the town﴾, that he said: "It is Antioch." Ibn Abi Hatim recorded the same from Buraydah.

Ibn Sa'd and Ibn Asakir recorded, through the route of al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Between Musa ibn Imran and Isa ibn Maryam there were one thousand and nine hundred years, and there was no fatrah (a gap in which no prophet was sent) between them. Between the birth of Isa and the Prophet (ﷺ) there were five hundred and sixty-nine years. In the first part of that period three prophets were sent, and this is His saying: ﴿When We sent to them two, and they denied them, so We strengthened [them] with a third﴾. The one who was strengthened by them was Shim'un, and he was one of the Hawariyyun (the disciples). The fatrah during which Allah sent no messenger was four hundred and thirty-four years."

Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from him also, regarding His saying ﴿Your omen is with you﴾, that he said: "Your ill omen is with you."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from him also, regarding His saying ﴿And there came from the farthest part of the city a man﴾, that he said: "He is Habib the carpenter."

Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from him through another route that he said: "The name of the companion of Ya Sin was Habib, and leprosy had spread in him quickly."

Al-Hakim recorded from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "When the companion of Ya Sin said, ﴿O my people, follow the messengers﴾, they throttled him so that he would die. Then he turned to the prophets and said, ﴿Indeed I have believed in your Lord, so hear me﴾," meaning: "So bear witness for me."

On the first reading, when He, the Exalted, said ﴿Indeed, you are among the messengers﴾ [Ya-Sin: 3] and ﴿so that you may warn a people﴾ [Ya-Sin: 6], the meaning is: say to them, "I am not an innovation among the messengers. Before me, a short while ago, messengers came to the companions of the town, warned them as I have warned you, mentioned the Oneness of God, warned of the Resurrection, and gave good tidings of the bliss of the abode of permanence."

On the second reading, when He had said that warning does not benefit one whom God has led astray, and that He has decreed for him that he will not believe, the Prophet (ﷺ) was told: present to yourself and to your people a parable, i.e., liken for them, in your own mind, a parable of the companions of the town, where three messengers came to them and they did not believe. The messengers bore harm patiently, while you came to them alone, and your people are more numerous than the people of the three. For they (the messengers) came to the people of the town, whereas I have sent you to mankind entirely.

The meaning is: present to them a parable like the parable of the companions of the town, i.e., relate to them a wondrous story, the story of the companions of the town. The word "parable" has been omitted, and "the companions of the town" has been put in its place in terms of i'rab (grammatical case).

It has been said: there is no need for an implied word. Rather, the meaning is: make the companions of the town a parable for them, so that "a parable" and "the companions of the town" are two objects of "present" (iḍrib). Or "the companions of the town" is a substitute (badal) for "a parable." We have already discussed which of these two objects is the first: is it "a parable" or "the companions of the town"?

It has also been said: the striking of a parable (ḍarb al-mathal) is used at times to compare a strange situation with another similar to it, as in His saying: ﴿God presents as a parable for those who disbelieve the wife of Noah and the wife of Lot﴾ [al-Tahrim: 10]. And it is used at other times to mention a strange situation and explain it to people without intending to match it with a counterpart, as in His saying: ﴿and We presented to you the parables﴾ [Ibrahim: 45], i.e., We made clear to you wondrous and strange conditions, which in their strangeness are like parables. So His saying here, "and present to them a parable," admits of taking both senses into account.

Al-Qurtubi said: this town is Antioch according to the statement of all the exegetes. His saying ﴿when the messengers came to it﴾ is a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for "the companions of the town." The messengers were the disciples of Jesus, whom he sent to the people of Antioch to call them to God.

God, the Exalted, attributed the sending to Himself in His saying ﴿when We sent to them two﴾, because Jesus sent them by the command of God, the Exalted. It is also permissible that God sent them after Jesus was raised to heaven. They denied them regarding their message. It has been said: they struck them and imprisoned them.

It is said: the names of the two were Yuhanna and Sham'un. It is said: the names of the three were Sadiq, Masduq and Shalum, as stated by Ibn Jarir and others.

It is said: they were Sam'an, Yahya and Bulus. ﴿So We reinforced them with a third﴾. The majority read it with the shadda (doubled z), and Abu Bakr, from ʿAsim, read it with the z unshaddahed.

Al-Jawhari said: "fa-ʿazzaznā" may be pronounced with or without doubling, i.e., "we strengthened and fortified," so the two readings have the same meaning on this view.

It has been said: the unshaddahed form means "we overpowered and subdued," and from it is His saying ﴿and he overpowered me in the speech﴾ [Sad: 23]. The shaddahed form means "we strengthened and multiplied."

It is said: this third one was Shamʿun. It is said: it was someone else. They said, "Indeed we are sent to you," i.e., the three said it together, and they brought this statement (p-1221) emphatically, because the denial directed at the two had already preceded.

Denying the two is also denying the third, because they were all sent with one thing, namely calling to God, Mighty and Majestic. This sentence is a resumptive (mustaʾnafa) answer to an implied question, as if it were said: what did these messengers say after being reinforced with a third?

Likewise, the sentence ﴿They said, "You are only human beings like us"﴾ is a resumptive answer to an implied question: as if it were said: what did the people of Antioch say to them? So it was said: they said, "You are only human beings like us," i.e., you share with us in humanity, so you have no distinction over us in which you are singled out.

Then they openly denied the sending down of the heavenly scriptures, saying: ﴿and the Most Merciful has sent down nothing; you are only lying﴾, meaning: concerning what you claim, and what others among those before you, of the messengers and their followers, claim. So the messengers answered them by affirming their mission with a statement emphasized strongly, because the people of Antioch repeated the denial.

That is their saying: ﴿Our Lord knows that we are indeed sent to you﴾. They emphasized the answer with the oath that is understood from their saying "Our Lord knows," and with "inna," and with the lam.

﴿And we are not responsible except for clear conveyance﴾, i.e., what is incumbent upon us from our Lord is only to convey His message in a manner that is manifest and clear, and nothing beyond that is upon us. This sentence is resumptive, like the one before it.

Likewise the sentence ﴿They said, "Indeed we see an omen in you"﴾ is a resumptive answer to an implied question, i.e., "we consider you ill-omened." They found no answer to give to the messengers except this answer, which is founded on ignorance, indicating great stupidity, and the absence of any argument with which you could repel the messengers.

Muqatil said: rain was withheld from them for three years.

It has been said: they had been warning them for ten years. Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 36, verses 28–40 (part 1 of 2):

When what happened to them occurred with Habib al-Najjar, Allah became angry on his behalf, hastened punishment upon them, and destroyed them with the Shout. The meaning of ﴿Nor did We send down upon his people after him any host from heaven﴾ is: upon the people of Habib al-Najjar, after they killed him, or after Allah raised him up to the heavens, according to the earlier disagreement, any host from heaven to destroy them and to take vengeance upon them. That is, We did not need to send down hosts from heaven to destroy them, as happened to the Prophet (ﷺ) on the Day of Badr, when the angels were sent to support him and to fight his enemies. ﴿Nor were We ever going to send down﴾ means: it was not fitting in Our decree and Our wisdom that We should send down a host to destroy them, because Our decree and Our determination had already preceded that their destruction would be by the Shout and not by the sending down of an army.

Qatadah, Mujahid and al-Hasan said: that is, We did not send down upon them any message from heaven, nor any prophet after they killed him.

It is narrated from al-Hasan that he said: "They are the angels who descend with revelation upon the prophets." The apparent meaning of the Qur'anic wording, however, is to belittle their status and to diminish their affair, that is, they were not worthy that We should send down a host from heaven to destroy them. Rather, We destroyed them with one single Shout, as is indicated by His saying: ﴿It was but one shout﴾, that is: if the punishment, or the vengeance, or the seizure was but one shout, which Jibril (Gabriel) cried out, and so he destroyed them.

The exegetes said: Jibril took hold of the two door-posts of the city, then cried out to them with one shout, and behold, they were dead, with no sound heard from them, like a fire when it is extinguished. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿behold, they were extinguished﴾, that is: they were a people extinguished, dead. He likened them to a fire when it is put out, because life is like a blazing fire and death is like its extinguishing.

The majority of reciters read ﴿shout﴾ (ṣayḥatan) in the accusative, on the basis that kāna (was) is a defective (naqisah) verb, and its subject is a pronoun referring to what is understood from the context, as we have mentioned.

Abu Ja'far, Shayba, al-A'raj, Mu'adh and al-Qarri read it in the nominative (ṣayḥatun), on the basis that kāna is a complete (tammah) verb, meaning: "occurred and came about." Abu Hatim and many of the grammarians rejected this reading because of the feminine form in His saying ﴿if it was﴾ (in kānat). Abu Hatim said: "If it were as Abu Ja'far recited, it would have said: 'in kāna illā ṣayḥatun.'" Al-Zajjaj explained this reading by saying: "in kānat 'alayhim ṣayḥatun illā ṣayḥatan wāḥidatan," and others explained it as: "mā waqaʿat 'alayhim illā ṣayḥatun wāḥidatun."

Abdullah ibn Mas'ud read ﴿if it was but one zaqyah (cry)﴾, and the zaqyah is the shout. Al-Nahhas said: "This is contrary to the Mushaf (the written codex). Also, the well-known language is zaqā yazqū when one cries out, and from it comes the proverb 'heavier than the zawāqī' (cries), so on this basis it should have been zaqwah." This objection is answered by what al-Jawhari mentioned. He said: "al-zaqw and al-zaqy are a verbal noun, and zaqā al-ṣadā yazqū means the echo cried out; zaqā means shouted, and every crier is zāqin, and al-zaqyah is the shout."

﴿Alas for the servants!﴾ The majority read ḥasratan (alas) in the accusative, as an indefinite vocative (munādā munakkar), as if he called out to "Regret" and said to it: "This is your time, so come forth."

It was also said that it is accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), and the vocative particle is omitted, the implied meaning being: "O people, feel regret with regret."

Qatadah and Ubayy, in one narration from him, read ḥasratu in the nominative, as a direct address.

Al-Farra' said regarding the justification of this reading: "The preferred form is the accusative, but if the indefinite noun were in the nominative it would also be correct." He cited examples he heard from the Arabs, among them: "yā muhtammu bi-amrinā lā tahtamma" (O one concerned with our affair, do not be concerned), and he recited:

*"yā dāru ghayyarahā al-bilā taghyīran"*
(O abode, decay has altered you a great alteration.)

Al-Nahhas said: "In this there is an invalidation of the chapter of the vocative, or most of it." The implied wording of what he mentioned is: "yā ayyuhā al-muhtammu lā tahtamma bi-amrinā" (O you who are concerned, do not be concerned with our affair), and the implied wording of the verse is: "yā ayyatuhā al-dāru" (O abode).

The true meaning of ḥasrah is that a person is overcome by regret to the point that he becomes exhausted (ḥasīr).

Ibn Jarir said: the meaning is: "Alas, O regret, from the servants against themselves, and remorse and lament for their mocking of the messengers of Allah." This is supported by the reading of Ibn Abbas and Ali ibn al-Husayn: "yā ḥasrata al-ʿibād" in the genitive construction (iḍāfah), and this reading is also narrated from Ubayy.

Al-Dahhak said: it is the regret of the angels over the disbelievers when they denied the messengers. It was also said: it is the words of the man who came from the farthest part of the city. It was also said: the one who says "Alas for the servants!" is the disbelievers who denied, and the worshippers are the messengers, because when they saw the punishment they regretted killing them and wished for faith; this was said by Abu al-ʿĀliyah and Mujahid. It was also said: the regret over them is from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, by way of metaphor (istiʿārah), to magnify what they committed.

Ibn Hurmuz, Muslim ibn Jundub, Ikrimah and Abu al-Zinad read yā ḥasrah with the ha' silent, treating the connected speech as if it were a pause (ijrā' al-waṣl majrā al-waqf). It is also read as yā ḥasratā, as was recited in surah al-Zumar.

The clause ﴿No messenger comes to them but they mock him﴾ is a resumed sentence (mustaʾnafah) that explains what they were upon of denying the messengers and mocking them, and that this is the cause of the regret over them.

Then He, glory be to Him, marvelled at their condition, in that they did not take warning from the likes of them among the earlier nations, so He said: ﴿Have they not seen how many generations We destroyed before them﴾, that is: did they not know the multitude of those whom We destroyed before them of the generations, the earlier nations.

The clause ﴿that they do not return to them﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿how many We destroyed﴾ in meaning.

Sibawayh said: "anna (that) is a substitute for kam (how many), and it is the declarative kam (khabariyyah), therefore it was permissible to substitute from it something that is not an interrogative. The meaning is: 'Have they not seen that the generations whom We destroyed, that they do not return to them?'"

Al-Farra' said: kam is in the accusative position in two ways. The first is by the verb yarau (they see), and he cited as evidence that in the reading of Ibn Mas'ud it is: "alam yarawu man ahlaknā" (have they not seen whom We destroyed). The second way is that kam is in the accusative position by the verb ahlaknā (We destroyed).

Al-Nahhas said: "The first view is untenable, because kam cannot be governed by what precedes it, since it is an interrogative, and it is impossible for an interrogative to fall within the scope of what precedes it. The same applies when it is declarative." Although Sibawayh had alluded to part of this when he made anna a substitute for kam, al-Mubarrad rejected this with the strongest rejection.

﴿And all of them, every one, will be brought before Us﴾, that is: they will be brought before Us on the Day of Resurrection for recompense.

Ibn ʿAmir, ʿAsim and Hamzah read lammā with its shaddah (lammā), and the rest read it with the shaddah removed (lammā, lamā).

Al-Farra' said: whoever read it with the shaddah made lammā mean illā (except), and in (in) mean mā (not), that is: "mā kullun illā jamīʿun ladaynā muḥḍarūn" (none of them but will be brought before Us all together). The meaning of jamīʿ is majmūʿūn (gathered), so it is faʿīl in the sense of mafʿūl, and ladaynā is an adverbial complement of it. As for the reading with the shaddah removed, in is the light form (mukhaffafah) of the heavy form (thaqīlah), and what follows it is in the nominative by being the subject; the tanwīn on kull is a substitute for the genitive complement, and what follows is the predicate, and the lām is the distinguishing lām that separates the light form from the negative.

Abu ʿUbaydah said: "mā in this reading is superfluous, and its implied wording in his view is: 'wa-in kullun la-jamīʿun.'"

It was also said: the meaning of muḥḍarūn is "punished," but the better view is that it is according to its literal meaning of being brought forth for reckoning.

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned the proof for monotheism and resurrection together with enumerating the blessings and reminding of them, so He said: ﴿And a sign for them is the dead earth﴾. Ayah (sign) is the predicate placed first (khabar muqaddam), and its indefiniteness is for magnification, and lahum (for them) is its qualifier, or it is connected to āyah because it means "a sign." Al-ardu (the earth) is the subject. It is also permissible for āyah to be the subject, since it has been specified by the qualifier, and what follows is the predicate.

The people of Medina read al-mayyitah (dead) with the shaddah, and the rest read it without it. The clause ﴿We have revived it﴾ is a resumed sentence explaining how it is a sign. It was also said: it is a qualifier of the earth, so by this Allah drew their attention to the reviving of the dead, and reminded them of His blessings and the perfection of His power, for He, glory be to Him, revived the earth with vegetation and brought forth from it the grains which they eat and on which they nourish themselves. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿And We bring forth from it grain, and from it they eat﴾, that is, what they subsist on of grains. The placing first of ﴿from it﴾ indicates that grain is the main part of what is eaten and the most of what sustains livelihood.

﴿And We placed in it gardens of palms and grapes﴾, that is: We placed in the earth gardens of kinds of palm and grape. He specified these two for mention because they are the highest of fruits and the most beneficial to people. ﴿And We caused springs to gush forth in it﴾, that is: We caused some springs to gush forth in the earth. The object (mawsūf) is omitted and the qualifier is put in its place, or the object is al-ʿuyūn (springs), and min is extra (zā'idah) according to the view of those who permit its addition in affirmative speech, which is al-Akhfash and those who agree with him. By al-ʿuyūn is meant springs of water.

The majority read fajjarnā with the shaddah, and Jinah ibn Hubaysh read it without it. Al-fajr and al-tafjīr are like al-fatḥ and al-tafṭīḥ, both in wording and meaning.

The lām in ﴿so that they may eat of its fruit﴾ is connected to ﴿We placed﴾, and the pronoun in ﴿of its fruit﴾ refers to what was mentioned of the gardens and palms. It was also said: it refers to the water of the springs, because the fruit comes from it; this was said by al-Jurjani.

The majority read thamarihi with a fatḥah on the thāʾ and the mīm. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it with a ḍammah on both. Al-Aʿmash read it with a ḍammah on the thāʾ and sukūn on the mīm. This matter has already been discussed in surah al-Anʿam.

His saying ﴿and what their hands have made﴾ is conjoined to thamarihi, that is: so that they may eat of its fruit and eat of what their hands have made, such as juice and date syrup and the like. Likewise what they planted and dug out, on the basis that mā is a relative pronoun (mawṣūlah). It was also said: mā is negative, and the meaning is: they did not make it; rather the one who made it is Allah, that is: they found it already made, and they had no part in it. This is the view of al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Muqatil.

The majority read ʿamilathu (which they made, with the pronoun), and the Kufans read ʿamilat (without the pronoun), by omitting the pronoun. The interrogative in His saying ﴿Will they not then give thanks?﴾ is for rebuke and reproach of them for their not giving thanks for the blessings.

The clause ﴿Glory be to Him who created all the pairs﴾ is a resumed sentence, brought to declare Him, glory be to Him, free from what they did in abandoning thanks for His mentioned blessings, and to express wonder at their neglect of that. The discussion of the meaning of "Subhan" has already been fully covered. It has the force of a command to the servants that they should declare Him free from what is unfitting for Him. Al-azwāj (pairs) means kinds and species, because each species varies in colours, tastes and forms. ﴿Of what the earth grows﴾ is an explanation of al-azwāj, and what is meant is everything that grows in it of the things mentioned and others. ﴿And of themselves﴾, that is: He created the pairs from themselves, namely males and females. ﴿And of what they do not know﴾: of the kinds of His creation on land and sea, in heaven and earth.

﴿And a sign for them is the night: We strip from it the day﴾. What is said about this is as we have mentioned regarding His saying ﴿And a sign for them is the dead earth, We have revived it﴾. The meaning is that this is a sign indicating the oneness of Allah, His power, and the necessity of His divinity. Salkh (stripping) is removing and drawing off; one says: "Allah stripped him from his body." Then it is used in the sense of extraction. So He, glory be to Him, made the departure of light and the arrival of darkness like stripping something off, and this is an eloquent metaphor. ﴿Then behold, they are in darkness﴾, that is: they enter into darkness suddenly and abruptly. It is said: "aẓlamnā," meaning we entered into the darkness of the night, and "aẓharnā," meaning we entered the time of noon, and likewise "aṣbaḥnā" and "amsaynā." It was also said: min here means ʿan (from), and the meaning is: We strip from it the light of the day.

Al-Farra' said: He casts the day over the night, so it comes with darkness, because the original state is darkness and the day comes upon it. When the sun sets, the day is stripped from the night, that is, drawn off and removed, and then the darkness appears.

﴿And the sun runs on to a resting place for it﴾. The wāw may be conjunctive, connecting to the night, and the meaning would be: "and a sign for them is the sun." It is also permissible that the wāw is initial (ibtidāʾiyyah), with al-shams (the sun) as the subject and what follows as the predicate, and the speech is then resumed, containing mention of an independent sign.

It was said: in the speech there is an omission, and the meaning is: it runs toward a fixed course (limajrā mustaqarrin) for it, so the lām is for cause, that is: for a term (li-ajalin) fixed for it. It was also said: the lām has the meaning of "ilā" (to), and this has been read that way.

The meaning of *mustaqarr* (resting place) is said to be the Day of Resurrection, when the sun comes to rest and has no further movement. It is also said that its resting place is the furthest point it reaches, beyond which it does not go. It is said to be the limit of its rise in summer and the limit of its descent in winter. It is also said that its resting place is beneath the Throne ('Arsh), because it goes there, prostrates, asks permission to return, and is granted it. This last view is the preferred one.

Al-Hasan (al-Basri) said: The sun has three hundred and sixty risings in the year. It descends to a new rising each day and does not descend again until the year is complete. So it keeps moving through those stations, and that is its resting place. Other views have also been reported.

Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah, Zayn al-'Abidin, his son al-Baqir, and al-Sadiq ibn al-Baqir read *lā mustaqarra lahā* with *lā* for the negation of the whole category and *mustaqarr* built on the fatha.

Ibn Abi 'Ablah read *lā mustaqarrun lahā*, with *lā* in the sense of *laysa* (is not), *mustaqarrun* as its subject, and *lahā* as its predicate. The demonstrative in His words ﴿that﴾ refers to the sun's course, meaning: that course is the decree of ﴿the Mighty﴾, that is, the Dominant, the Subduer, ﴿the All-Knowing﴾, that is, whose knowledge encompasses everything. It is also possible that the demonstrative refers back to the *mustaqarr*, meaning: that resting place is the decree of Allah.

﴿And the moon — We have decreed for it stations﴾. Nafi', Ibn Kathir, and Abu 'Amr read *al-qamaru* in the nominative, as a new sentence. The rest read it in the accusative, by the construction of the verb being occupied (*ishtighāl*). The accusative of *manāzila* (stations) is as a second object, because *qaddarnā* means *ṣayyarnā* (We made). It may also be an accusative of circumstance, meaning: We decreed its course while it was in the state of having stations. It may also be an accusative of place, meaning: in stations.

Abu 'Ubayd preferred the accusative for *al-qamara*, saying: because before it there is a verb, *nasliku* (We strip away), and after it there is a verb, *qaddarnā*.

Al-Nahhas said: As far as I know, all the grammarians of Arabic disagree with what he said. Among them is al-Farra', who said: The nominative is more pleasing to me. He said: The nominative is preferred by them because it is coordinated with what precedes it, and its meaning is: and a sign for them is the moon.

Abu Hatim said: The nominative is preferred, because you have diverted the verb from it by the pronoun, so you have made it nominative by beginning the sentence with it.

The *manāzil* (stations) are the twenty-eight known mansions in which the moon lodges each night, one of them, and they are well known; their mention will come. When the moon reaches the last of them, it returns to the first. It traverses the orbit (*falak*) in twenty-eight nights, then it is hidden for two nights, then it appears as a crescent, and it returns to traverse those stations in the orbit.
