﴿Until it returns like the old 'urjūn﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: the *'urjūn* is the stalk of the bunch of dates on which the sprigs are. It is of the pattern *fu'lūn*, from *al-in'irāj*, which is bending. Its meaning is that it travels through its stations, and when it is at the end of them it becomes thin, curved, and small until it becomes like the old *'urjūn*. On this view, the *nūn* is an augmentative (extra) letter.

Qatadah said: It is the dry, bent palm-stalk of the date palm. Tha'lab said: The *'urjūn* is what remains on the palm when the bunch has been cut, and *al-qadīm* means the decayed. Al-Khalil said: The *'urjūn* is the base of the bunch, which is yellow and broad, and the crescent is compared to it when it bends. Likewise al-Jawhari said it is the base of the bunch which curves, and from which the sprigs are cut, and it remains dry on the palm. *'Arrajtuhu* means I struck him with the *'urjūn*. On this view, the *nūn* is radical.

The majority read *al-'urjūni* with a damma on the 'ayn and the jim. Sulayman al-Taymi read it with a kasra on the 'ayn and a fatha on the jim. Both are dialect forms. *Al-qadīm* means the old, the aged.

﴿The sun is not to overtake the moon﴾. *Al-shamsu* is in the nominative as the subject of a new sentence, because *lā* does not operate on a definite noun. That is: it is not valid, nor possible, for the sun to overtake the moon in its speed and descend into the station in which the moon is, because each of them has its own authority when alone, so neither of them can enter upon the other. Its authority would then cease until Allah permits the Resurrection, and the sun will rise from its west.

Al-Dahhak said: The meaning is that when the sun rises, there is no light for the moon, and when the moon rises, there is no light for the sun.

Mujahid said: That is, the light of one does not resemble the light of the other.

Al-Hasan said: They do not meet in the sky on the night of the crescent specifically, and Yahya ibn Salam said likewise.

It is also said: The meaning is that when they meet in the sky, one of them is in front of the other, in a station which they do not share.

It is also said: The moon is in the lowest heaven, and the sun is in the fourth heaven. This was reported by al-Nahhas and al-Mahdawi.

Al-Nahhas said: The best and clearest of what has been said about its meaning is that the moon's course is swift, and the sun cannot overtake it in travel.

As for His words ﴿And the sun and the moon are joined together﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 9], that is when He holds the sun back from rising, as explained earlier in al-An'am, and it will come also in Surah al-Qiyamah. Their joining is a sign of the end of this world and the establishment of the Hour.

﴿Nor does the night overtake the day﴾: that is, it does not precede it so as to outstrip it, but it follows it in succession, and each of them comes in its time without outstripping its companion. It is also said that by the night and the day are meant their two signs, which are the sun and the moon, so it is the reverse of His words: ﴿The sun is not to overtake the moon﴾; that is: nor does the moon outstrip the sun. The mention of "outstripping" instead of "overtaking" is because of the swiftness of the moon's course.

﴿And each in an orbit is swimming﴾. The tanwin on *kullun* is a replacement for the genitive noun that is omitted, meaning: and each one of them. *Falak* is either a rotating body, a rotating surface, or a circle. The disagreement about whether the sky is flat or spherical is well known. *Sabh* is movement with ease and smoothness. The plural in His words *yasbaḥūn* (they swim) is in view of the differing risings of the two, so it is as if they were many, according to the multiplicity of those risings. Or the intended meaning is: the sun, the moon, and the stars.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Mas'ud, concerning His words: ﴿And We did not send down upon his people after him...﴾ (the verse), he said: We did not strain against them with armies; that is, the matter is easier for Us than that.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His words: ﴿Alas, for the servants﴾, he said: it means: Woe to the servants.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him, concerning His words: ﴿Alas, for the servants﴾, he said: It is regret over the servants who ﴿no messenger came to them but they used to mock him﴾; that is, the regret over them on the Day of Resurrection.

Ibn Abi Hatim also reported from him, concerning His words: ﴿and what their hands had made﴾, he said: They found it made, which their hands had not made, meaning the Euphrates, the Tigris, the river of Balkh, and the like. ﴿Will they not then be thankful?﴾ for this.

al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others reported from Abu Dharr, who said: "I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about His words: ﴿And the sun runs on to its resting place﴾, and he said: 'Its resting place is beneath the Throne.'"

In another wording from al-Bukhari and others, from his narration, he said: "I was with the Prophet (ﷺ) in the mosque at the setting of the sun, and he said: 'O Abu Dharr, do you know where the sun sets?' I said: 'Allah and His Messenger know best.' He said: 'It goes on until it prostrates beneath the Throne, and that is His words: ﴿And the sun runs on to its resting place﴾.'"

In another wording from his narration, also in Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, and others, he said: "'O Abu Dharr, do you know where this goes?' I said: 'Allah and His Messenger know best.' He said: 'It goes on until it prostrates before its Lord, then it asks permission to return, and it is granted permission. It is as if it were said to it: Rise from where you came, and it rises from its west.'" Then he recited: "That is the resting place for it," and that is the reading of 'Abd Allah.

al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, and others reported something similar from the words of Ibn 'Umar.

al-Khatib, in his book *al-Nujum*, reported from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His words: ﴿And the moon — We have decreed for it stations﴾, the verse, he said: They are twenty-eight stations in which the moon lodges each month: fourteen of them are Syrian and fourteen are Yemeni. The first of them are al-Sharatan, al-Batin, al-Thurayya, al-Dabaran, al-Hak'a, al-Han'a, al-Dhira', al-Nathra, al-Tarf, al-Jabha, al-Zubra, al-Sarfa, al-'Awwa', al-Simak, which is the last of the Syrian, al-Ghafr, al-Zubana, al-Iklil, al-Qalb, al-Shawla, al-Na'a'im, al-Balda, Sa'd al-Dhabih, Sa'd Bula', Sa'd al-Su'ud, Sa'd al-Akhbiya, Muqaddam al-Dalw, Mu'akhkhar al-Dalw, and al-Hut, which is the last of the Yemeni. When it has traversed these twenty-eight stations, ﴿it returns like the old 'urjūn﴾, as it was at the beginning of the month.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him, concerning His words: ﴿like the old 'urjūn﴾: that is, the base of the ancient bunch.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 36, verses 28–40 (part 1 of 2):

When what happened to them occurred with Habib al-Najjar, Allah became angry on his behalf, hastened punishment upon them, and destroyed them with the Shout. The meaning of ﴿Nor did We send down upon his people after him any host from heaven﴾ is: upon the people of Habib al-Najjar, after they killed him, or after Allah raised him up to the heavens, according to the earlier disagreement, any host from heaven to destroy them and to take vengeance upon them. That is, We did not need to send down hosts from heaven to destroy them, as happened to the Prophet (ﷺ) on the Day of Badr, when the angels were sent to support him and to fight his enemies. ﴿Nor were We ever going to send down﴾ means: it was not fitting in Our decree and Our wisdom that We should send down a host to destroy them, because Our decree and Our determination had already preceded that their destruction would be by the Shout and not by the sending down of an army.

Qatadah, Mujahid and al-Hasan said: that is, We did not send down upon them any message from heaven, nor any prophet after they killed him.

It is narrated from al-Hasan that he said: "They are the angels who descend with revelation upon the prophets." The apparent meaning of the Qur'anic wording, however, is to belittle their status and to diminish their affair, that is, they were not worthy that We should send down a host from heaven to destroy them. Rather, We destroyed them with one single Shout, as is indicated by His saying: ﴿It was but one shout﴾, that is: if the punishment, or the vengeance, or the seizure was but one shout, which Jibril (Gabriel) cried out, and so he destroyed them.

The exegetes said: Jibril took hold of the two door-posts of the city, then cried out to them with one shout, and behold, they were dead, with no sound heard from them, like a fire when it is extinguished. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿behold, they were extinguished﴾, that is: they were a people extinguished, dead. He likened them to a fire when it is put out, because life is like a blazing fire and death is like its extinguishing.

The majority of reciters read ﴿shout﴾ (ṣayḥatan) in the accusative, on the basis that kāna (was) is a defective (naqisah) verb, and its subject is a pronoun referring to what is understood from the context, as we have mentioned.

Abu Ja'far, Shayba, al-A'raj, Mu'adh and al-Qarri read it in the nominative (ṣayḥatun), on the basis that kāna is a complete (tammah) verb, meaning: "occurred and came about." Abu Hatim and many of the grammarians rejected this reading because of the feminine form in His saying ﴿if it was﴾ (in kānat). Abu Hatim said: "If it were as Abu Ja'far recited, it would have said: 'in kāna illā ṣayḥatun.'" Al-Zajjaj explained this reading by saying: "in kānat 'alayhim ṣayḥatun illā ṣayḥatan wāḥidatan," and others explained it as: "mā waqaʿat 'alayhim illā ṣayḥatun wāḥidatun."

Abdullah ibn Mas'ud read ﴿if it was but one zaqyah (cry)﴾, and the zaqyah is the shout. Al-Nahhas said: "This is contrary to the Mushaf (the written codex). Also, the well-known language is zaqā yazqū when one cries out, and from it comes the proverb 'heavier than the zawāqī' (cries), so on this basis it should have been zaqwah." This objection is answered by what al-Jawhari mentioned. He said: "al-zaqw and al-zaqy are a verbal noun, and zaqā al-ṣadā yazqū means the echo cried out; zaqā means shouted, and every crier is zāqin, and al-zaqyah is the shout."

﴿Alas for the servants!﴾ The majority read ḥasratan (alas) in the accusative, as an indefinite vocative (munādā munakkar), as if he called out to "Regret" and said to it: "This is your time, so come forth."

It was also said that it is accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), and the vocative particle is omitted, the implied meaning being: "O people, feel regret with regret."

Qatadah and Ubayy, in one narration from him, read ḥasratu in the nominative, as a direct address.

Al-Farra' said regarding the justification of this reading: "The preferred form is the accusative, but if the indefinite noun were in the nominative it would also be correct." He cited examples he heard from the Arabs, among them: "yā muhtammu bi-amrinā lā tahtamma" (O one concerned with our affair, do not be concerned), and he recited:

*"yā dāru ghayyarahā al-bilā taghyīran"*
(O abode, decay has altered you a great alteration.)

Al-Nahhas said: "In this there is an invalidation of the chapter of the vocative, or most of it." The implied wording of what he mentioned is: "yā ayyuhā al-muhtammu lā tahtamma bi-amrinā" (O you who are concerned, do not be concerned with our affair), and the implied wording of the verse is: "yā ayyatuhā al-dāru" (O abode).

The true meaning of ḥasrah is that a person is overcome by regret to the point that he becomes exhausted (ḥasīr).

Ibn Jarir said: the meaning is: "Alas, O regret, from the servants against themselves, and remorse and lament for their mocking of the messengers of Allah." This is supported by the reading of Ibn Abbas and Ali ibn al-Husayn: "yā ḥasrata al-ʿibād" in the genitive construction (iḍāfah), and this reading is also narrated from Ubayy.

Al-Dahhak said: it is the regret of the angels over the disbelievers when they denied the messengers. It was also said: it is the words of the man who came from the farthest part of the city. It was also said: the one who says "Alas for the servants!" is the disbelievers who denied, and the worshippers are the messengers, because when they saw the punishment they regretted killing them and wished for faith; this was said by Abu al-ʿĀliyah and Mujahid. It was also said: the regret over them is from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, by way of metaphor (istiʿārah), to magnify what they committed.

Ibn Hurmuz, Muslim ibn Jundub, Ikrimah and Abu al-Zinad read yā ḥasrah with the ha' silent, treating the connected speech as if it were a pause (ijrā' al-waṣl majrā al-waqf). It is also read as yā ḥasratā, as was recited in surah al-Zumar.

The clause ﴿No messenger comes to them but they mock him﴾ is a resumed sentence (mustaʾnafah) that explains what they were upon of denying the messengers and mocking them, and that this is the cause of the regret over them.

Then He, glory be to Him, marvelled at their condition, in that they did not take warning from the likes of them among the earlier nations, so He said: ﴿Have they not seen how many generations We destroyed before them﴾, that is: did they not know the multitude of those whom We destroyed before them of the generations, the earlier nations.

The clause ﴿that they do not return to them﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿how many We destroyed﴾ in meaning.

Sibawayh said: "anna (that) is a substitute for kam (how many), and it is the declarative kam (khabariyyah), therefore it was permissible to substitute from it something that is not an interrogative. The meaning is: 'Have they not seen that the generations whom We destroyed, that they do not return to them?'"

Al-Farra' said: kam is in the accusative position in two ways. The first is by the verb yarau (they see), and he cited as evidence that in the reading of Ibn Mas'ud it is: "alam yarawu man ahlaknā" (have they not seen whom We destroyed). The second way is that kam is in the accusative position by the verb ahlaknā (We destroyed).

Al-Nahhas said: "The first view is untenable, because kam cannot be governed by what precedes it, since it is an interrogative, and it is impossible for an interrogative to fall within the scope of what precedes it. The same applies when it is declarative." Although Sibawayh had alluded to part of this when he made anna a substitute for kam, al-Mubarrad rejected this with the strongest rejection.

﴿And all of them, every one, will be brought before Us﴾, that is: they will be brought before Us on the Day of Resurrection for recompense.

Ibn ʿAmir, ʿAsim and Hamzah read lammā with its shaddah (lammā), and the rest read it with the shaddah removed (lammā, lamā).

Al-Farra' said: whoever read it with the shaddah made lammā mean illā (except), and in (in) mean mā (not), that is: "mā kullun illā jamīʿun ladaynā muḥḍarūn" (none of them but will be brought before Us all together). The meaning of jamīʿ is majmūʿūn (gathered), so it is faʿīl in the sense of mafʿūl, and ladaynā is an adverbial complement of it. As for the reading with the shaddah removed, in is the light form (mukhaffafah) of the heavy form (thaqīlah), and what follows it is in the nominative by being the subject; the tanwīn on kull is a substitute for the genitive complement, and what follows is the predicate, and the lām is the distinguishing lām that separates the light form from the negative.

Abu ʿUbaydah said: "mā in this reading is superfluous, and its implied wording in his view is: 'wa-in kullun la-jamīʿun.'"

It was also said: the meaning of muḥḍarūn is "punished," but the better view is that it is according to its literal meaning of being brought forth for reckoning.

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned the proof for monotheism and resurrection together with enumerating the blessings and reminding of them, so He said: ﴿And a sign for them is the dead earth﴾. Ayah (sign) is the predicate placed first (khabar muqaddam), and its indefiniteness is for magnification, and lahum (for them) is its qualifier, or it is connected to āyah because it means "a sign." Al-ardu (the earth) is the subject. It is also permissible for āyah to be the subject, since it has been specified by the qualifier, and what follows is the predicate.

The people of Medina read al-mayyitah (dead) with the shaddah, and the rest read it without it. The clause ﴿We have revived it﴾ is a resumed sentence explaining how it is a sign. It was also said: it is a qualifier of the earth, so by this Allah drew their attention to the reviving of the dead, and reminded them of His blessings and the perfection of His power, for He, glory be to Him, revived the earth with vegetation and brought forth from it the grains which they eat and on which they nourish themselves. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿And We bring forth from it grain, and from it they eat﴾, that is, what they subsist on of grains. The placing first of ﴿from it﴾ indicates that grain is the main part of what is eaten and the most of what sustains livelihood.

﴿And We placed in it gardens of palms and grapes﴾, that is: We placed in the earth gardens of kinds of palm and grape. He specified these two for mention because they are the highest of fruits and the most beneficial to people. ﴿And We caused springs to gush forth in it﴾, that is: We caused some springs to gush forth in the earth. The object (mawsūf) is omitted and the qualifier is put in its place, or the object is al-ʿuyūn (springs), and min is extra (zā'idah) according to the view of those who permit its addition in affirmative speech, which is al-Akhfash and those who agree with him. By al-ʿuyūn is meant springs of water.

The majority read fajjarnā with the shaddah, and Jinah ibn Hubaysh read it without it. Al-fajr and al-tafjīr are like al-fatḥ and al-tafṭīḥ, both in wording and meaning.

The lām in ﴿so that they may eat of its fruit﴾ is connected to ﴿We placed﴾, and the pronoun in ﴿of its fruit﴾ refers to what was mentioned of the gardens and palms. It was also said: it refers to the water of the springs, because the fruit comes from it; this was said by al-Jurjani.

The majority read thamarihi with a fatḥah on the thāʾ and the mīm. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it with a ḍammah on both. Al-Aʿmash read it with a ḍammah on the thāʾ and sukūn on the mīm. This matter has already been discussed in surah al-Anʿam.

His saying ﴿and what their hands have made﴾ is conjoined to thamarihi, that is: so that they may eat of its fruit and eat of what their hands have made, such as juice and date syrup and the like. Likewise what they planted and dug out, on the basis that mā is a relative pronoun (mawṣūlah). It was also said: mā is negative, and the meaning is: they did not make it; rather the one who made it is Allah, that is: they found it already made, and they had no part in it. This is the view of al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Muqatil.

The majority read ʿamilathu (which they made, with the pronoun), and the Kufans read ʿamilat (without the pronoun), by omitting the pronoun. The interrogative in His saying ﴿Will they not then give thanks?﴾ is for rebuke and reproach of them for their not giving thanks for the blessings.

The clause ﴿Glory be to Him who created all the pairs﴾ is a resumed sentence, brought to declare Him, glory be to Him, free from what they did in abandoning thanks for His mentioned blessings, and to express wonder at their neglect of that. The discussion of the meaning of "Subhan" has already been fully covered. It has the force of a command to the servants that they should declare Him free from what is unfitting for Him. Al-azwāj (pairs) means kinds and species, because each species varies in colours, tastes and forms. ﴿Of what the earth grows﴾ is an explanation of al-azwāj, and what is meant is everything that grows in it of the things mentioned and others. ﴿And of themselves﴾, that is: He created the pairs from themselves, namely males and females. ﴿And of what they do not know﴾: of the kinds of His creation on land and sea, in heaven and earth.

﴿And a sign for them is the night: We strip from it the day﴾. What is said about this is as we have mentioned regarding His saying ﴿And a sign for them is the dead earth, We have revived it﴾. The meaning is that this is a sign indicating the oneness of Allah, His power, and the necessity of His divinity. Salkh (stripping) is removing and drawing off; one says: "Allah stripped him from his body." Then it is used in the sense of extraction. So He, glory be to Him, made the departure of light and the arrival of darkness like stripping something off, and this is an eloquent metaphor. ﴿Then behold, they are in darkness﴾, that is: they enter into darkness suddenly and abruptly. It is said: "aẓlamnā," meaning we entered into the darkness of the night, and "aẓharnā," meaning we entered the time of noon, and likewise "aṣbaḥnā" and "amsaynā." It was also said: min here means ʿan (from), and the meaning is: We strip from it the light of the day.

Al-Farra' said: He casts the day over the night, so it comes with darkness, because the original state is darkness and the day comes upon it. When the sun sets, the day is stripped from the night, that is, drawn off and removed, and then the darkness appears.

﴿And the sun runs on to a resting place for it﴾. The wāw may be conjunctive, connecting to the night, and the meaning would be: "and a sign for them is the sun." It is also permissible that the wāw is initial (ibtidāʾiyyah), with al-shams (the sun) as the subject and what follows as the predicate, and the speech is then resumed, containing mention of an independent sign.

It was said: in the speech there is an omission, and the meaning is: it runs toward a fixed course (limajrā mustaqarrin) for it, so the lām is for cause, that is: for a term (li-ajalin) fixed for it. It was also said: the lām has the meaning of "ilā" (to), and this has been read that way.

The meaning of *mustaqarr* (resting place) is said to be the Day of Resurrection, when the sun comes to rest and has no further movement. It is also said that its resting place is the furthest point it reaches, beyond which it does not go. It is said to be the limit of its rise in summer and the limit of its descent in winter. It is also said that its resting place is beneath the Throne ('Arsh), because it goes there, prostrates, asks permission to return, and is granted it. This last view is the preferred one.

Al-Hasan (al-Basri) said: The sun has three hundred and sixty risings in the year. It descends to a new rising each day and does not descend again until the year is complete. So it keeps moving through those stations, and that is its resting place. Other views have also been reported.

Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah, Zayn al-'Abidin, his son al-Baqir, and al-Sadiq ibn al-Baqir read *lā mustaqarra lahā* with *lā* for the negation of the whole category and *mustaqarr* built on the fatha.

Ibn Abi 'Ablah read *lā mustaqarrun lahā*, with *lā* in the sense of *laysa* (is not), *mustaqarrun* as its subject, and *lahā* as its predicate. The demonstrative in His words ﴿that﴾ refers to the sun's course, meaning: that course is the decree of ﴿the Mighty﴾, that is, the Dominant, the Subduer, ﴿the All-Knowing﴾, that is, whose knowledge encompasses everything. It is also possible that the demonstrative refers back to the *mustaqarr*, meaning: that resting place is the decree of Allah.

﴿And the moon — We have decreed for it stations﴾. Nafi', Ibn Kathir, and Abu 'Amr read *al-qamaru* in the nominative, as a new sentence. The rest read it in the accusative, by the construction of the verb being occupied (*ishtighāl*). The accusative of *manāzila* (stations) is as a second object, because *qaddarnā* means *ṣayyarnā* (We made). It may also be an accusative of circumstance, meaning: We decreed its course while it was in the state of having stations. It may also be an accusative of place, meaning: in stations.

Abu 'Ubayd preferred the accusative for *al-qamara*, saying: because before it there is a verb, *nasliku* (We strip away), and after it there is a verb, *qaddarnā*.

Al-Nahhas said: As far as I know, all the grammarians of Arabic disagree with what he said. Among them is al-Farra', who said: The nominative is more pleasing to me. He said: The nominative is preferred by them because it is coordinated with what precedes it, and its meaning is: and a sign for them is the moon.

Abu Hatim said: The nominative is preferred, because you have diverted the verb from it by the pronoun, so you have made it nominative by beginning the sentence with it.

The *manāzil* (stations) are the twenty-eight known mansions in which the moon lodges each night, one of them, and they are well known; their mention will come. When the moon reaches the last of them, it returns to the first. It traverses the orbit (*falak*) in twenty-eight nights, then it is hidden for two nights, then it appears as a crescent, and it returns to traverse those stations in the orbit.

﴿Until it returns like the old 'urjūn﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: the *'urjūn* is the stalk of the bunch of dates on which the sprigs are. It is of the pattern *fu'lūn*, from *al-in'irāj*, which is bending. Its meaning is that it travels through its stations, and when it is at the end of them it becomes thin, curved, and small until it becomes like the old *'urjūn*. On this view, the *nūn* is an augmentative (extra) letter.

Qatadah said: It is the dry, bent palm-stalk of the date palm. Tha'lab said: The *'urjūn* is what remains on the palm when the bunch has been cut, and *al-qadīm* means the decayed. Al-Khalil said: The *'urjūn* is the base of the bunch, which is yellow and broad, and the crescent is compared to it when it bends. Likewise al-Jawhari said it is the base of the bunch which curves, and from which the sprigs are cut, and it remains dry on the palm. *'Arrajtuhu* means I struck him with the *'urjūn*. On this view, the *nūn* is radical.

The majority read *al-'urjūni* with a damma on the 'ayn and the jim. Sulayman al-Taymi read it with a kasra on the 'ayn and a fatha on the jim. Both are dialect forms. *Al-qadīm* means the old, the aged.

﴿The sun is not to overtake the moon﴾. *Al-shamsu* is in the nominative as the subject of a new sentence, because *lā* does not operate on a definite noun. That is: it is not valid, nor possible, for the sun to overtake the moon in its speed and descend into the station in which the moon is, because each of them has its own authority when alone, so neither of them can enter upon the other. Its authority would then cease until Allah permits the Resurrection, and the sun will rise from its west.

Al-Dahhak said: The meaning is that when the sun rises, there is no light for the moon, and when the moon rises, there is no light for the sun.

Mujahid said: That is, the light of one does not resemble the light of the other.

Al-Hasan said: They do not meet in the sky on the night of the crescent specifically, and Yahya ibn Salam said likewise.

It is also said: The meaning is that when they meet in the sky, one of them is in front of the other, in a station which they do not share.

It is also said: The moon is in the lowest heaven, and the sun is in the fourth heaven. This was reported by al-Nahhas and al-Mahdawi.

Al-Nahhas said: The best and clearest of what has been said about its meaning is that the moon's course is swift, and the sun cannot overtake it in travel.

As for His words ﴿And the sun and the moon are joined together﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 9], that is when He holds the sun back from rising, as explained earlier in al-An'am, and it will come also in Surah al-Qiyamah. Their joining is a sign of the end of this world and the establishment of the Hour.

﴿Nor does the night overtake the day﴾: that is, it does not precede it so as to outstrip it, but it follows it in succession, and each of them comes in its time without outstripping its companion. It is also said that by the night and the day are meant their two signs, which are the sun and the moon, so it is the reverse of His words: ﴿The sun is not to overtake the moon﴾; that is: nor does the moon outstrip the sun. The mention of "outstripping" instead of "overtaking" is because of the swiftness of the moon's course.

﴿And each in an orbit is swimming﴾. The tanwin on *kullun* is a replacement for the genitive noun that is omitted, meaning: and each one of them. *Falak* is either a rotating body, a rotating surface, or a circle. The disagreement about whether the sky is flat or spherical is well known. *Sabh* is movement with ease and smoothness. The plural in His words *yasbaḥūn* (they swim) is in view of the differing risings of the two, so it is as if they were many, according to the multiplicity of those risings. Or the intended meaning is: the sun, the moon, and the stars.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Mas'ud, concerning His words: ﴿And We did not send down upon his people after him...﴾ (the verse), he said: We did not strain against them with armies; that is, the matter is easier for Us than that.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His words: ﴿Alas, for the servants﴾, he said: it means: Woe to the servants.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him, concerning His words: ﴿Alas, for the servants﴾, he said: It is regret over the servants who ﴿no messenger came to them but they used to mock him﴾; that is, the regret over them on the Day of Resurrection.

Ibn Abi Hatim also reported from him, concerning His words: ﴿and what their hands had made﴾, he said: They found it made, which their hands had not made, meaning the Euphrates, the Tigris, the river of Balkh, and the like. ﴿Will they not then be thankful?﴾ for this.

al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others reported from Abu Dharr, who said: "I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about His words: ﴿And the sun runs on to its resting place﴾, and he said: 'Its resting place is beneath the Throne.'"

In another wording from al-Bukhari and others, from his narration, he said: "I was with the Prophet (ﷺ) in the mosque at the setting of the sun, and he said: 'O Abu Dharr, do you know where the sun sets?' I said: 'Allah and His Messenger know best.' He said: 'It goes on until it prostrates beneath the Throne, and that is His words: ﴿And the sun runs on to its resting place﴾.'"

In another wording from his narration, also in Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, and others, he said: "'O Abu Dharr, do you know where this goes?' I said: 'Allah and His Messenger know best.' He said: 'It goes on until it prostrates before its Lord, then it asks permission to return, and it is granted permission. It is as if it were said to it: Rise from where you came, and it rises from its west.'" Then he recited: "That is the resting place for it," and that is the reading of 'Abd Allah.

al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, and others reported something similar from the words of Ibn 'Umar.

al-Khatib, in his book *al-Nujum*, reported from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His words: ﴿And the moon — We have decreed for it stations﴾, the verse, he said: They are twenty-eight stations in which the moon lodges each month: fourteen of them are Syrian and fourteen are Yemeni. The first of them are al-Sharatan, al-Batin, al-Thurayya, al-Dabaran, al-Hak'a, al-Han'a, al-Dhira', al-Nathra, al-Tarf, al-Jabha, al-Zubra, al-Sarfa, al-'Awwa', al-Simak, which is the last of the Syrian, al-Ghafr, al-Zubana, al-Iklil, al-Qalb, al-Shawla, al-Na'a'im, al-Balda, Sa'd al-Dhabih, Sa'd Bula', Sa'd al-Su'ud, Sa'd al-Akhbiya, Muqaddam al-Dalw, Mu'akhkhar al-Dalw, and al-Hut, which is the last of the Yemeni. When it has traversed these twenty-eight stations, ﴿it returns like the old 'urjūn﴾, as it was at the beginning of the month.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him, concerning His words: ﴿like the old 'urjūn﴾: that is, the base of the ancient bunch.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 36, verses 28–40 (part 1 of 2):

When what happened to them occurred with Habib al-Najjar, Allah became angry on his behalf, hastened punishment upon them, and destroyed them with the Shout. The meaning of ﴿Nor did We send down upon his people after him any host from heaven﴾ is: upon the people of Habib al-Najjar, after they killed him, or after Allah raised him up to the heavens, according to the earlier disagreement, any host from heaven to destroy them and to take vengeance upon them. That is, We did not need to send down hosts from heaven to destroy them, as happened to the Prophet (ﷺ) on the Day of Badr, when the angels were sent to support him and to fight his enemies. ﴿Nor were We ever going to send down﴾ means: it was not fitting in Our decree and Our wisdom that We should send down a host to destroy them, because Our decree and Our determination had already preceded that their destruction would be by the Shout and not by the sending down of an army.

Qatadah, Mujahid and al-Hasan said: that is, We did not send down upon them any message from heaven, nor any prophet after they killed him.

It is narrated from al-Hasan that he said: "They are the angels who descend with revelation upon the prophets." The apparent meaning of the Qur'anic wording, however, is to belittle their status and to diminish their affair, that is, they were not worthy that We should send down a host from heaven to destroy them. Rather, We destroyed them with one single Shout, as is indicated by His saying: ﴿It was but one shout﴾, that is: if the punishment, or the vengeance, or the seizure was but one shout, which Jibril (Gabriel) cried out, and so he destroyed them.

The exegetes said: Jibril took hold of the two door-posts of the city, then cried out to them with one shout, and behold, they were dead, with no sound heard from them, like a fire when it is extinguished. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿behold, they were extinguished﴾, that is: they were a people extinguished, dead. He likened them to a fire when it is put out, because life is like a blazing fire and death is like its extinguishing.

The majority of reciters read ﴿shout﴾ (ṣayḥatan) in the accusative, on the basis that kāna (was) is a defective (naqisah) verb, and its subject is a pronoun referring to what is understood from the context, as we have mentioned.

Abu Ja'far, Shayba, al-A'raj, Mu'adh and al-Qarri read it in the nominative (ṣayḥatun), on the basis that kāna is a complete (tammah) verb, meaning: "occurred and came about." Abu Hatim and many of the grammarians rejected this reading because of the feminine form in His saying ﴿if it was﴾ (in kānat). Abu Hatim said: "If it were as Abu Ja'far recited, it would have said: 'in kāna illā ṣayḥatun.'" Al-Zajjaj explained this reading by saying: "in kānat 'alayhim ṣayḥatun illā ṣayḥatan wāḥidatan," and others explained it as: "mā waqaʿat 'alayhim illā ṣayḥatun wāḥidatun."

Abdullah ibn Mas'ud read ﴿if it was but one zaqyah (cry)﴾, and the zaqyah is the shout. Al-Nahhas said: "This is contrary to the Mushaf (the written codex). Also, the well-known language is zaqā yazqū when one cries out, and from it comes the proverb 'heavier than the zawāqī' (cries), so on this basis it should have been zaqwah." This objection is answered by what al-Jawhari mentioned. He said: "al-zaqw and al-zaqy are a verbal noun, and zaqā al-ṣadā yazqū means the echo cried out; zaqā means shouted, and every crier is zāqin, and al-zaqyah is the shout."

﴿Alas for the servants!﴾ The majority read ḥasratan (alas) in the accusative, as an indefinite vocative (munādā munakkar), as if he called out to "Regret" and said to it: "This is your time, so come forth."

It was also said that it is accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), and the vocative particle is omitted, the implied meaning being: "O people, feel regret with regret."

Qatadah and Ubayy, in one narration from him, read ḥasratu in the nominative, as a direct address.

Al-Farra' said regarding the justification of this reading: "The preferred form is the accusative, but if the indefinite noun were in the nominative it would also be correct." He cited examples he heard from the Arabs, among them: "yā muhtammu bi-amrinā lā tahtamma" (O one concerned with our affair, do not be concerned), and he recited:

*"yā dāru ghayyarahā al-bilā taghyīran"*
(O abode, decay has altered you a great alteration.)

Al-Nahhas said: "In this there is an invalidation of the chapter of the vocative, or most of it." The implied wording of what he mentioned is: "yā ayyuhā al-muhtammu lā tahtamma bi-amrinā" (O you who are concerned, do not be concerned with our affair), and the implied wording of the verse is: "yā ayyatuhā al-dāru" (O abode).

The true meaning of ḥasrah is that a person is overcome by regret to the point that he becomes exhausted (ḥasīr).

Ibn Jarir said: the meaning is: "Alas, O regret, from the servants against themselves, and remorse and lament for their mocking of the messengers of Allah." This is supported by the reading of Ibn Abbas and Ali ibn al-Husayn: "yā ḥasrata al-ʿibād" in the genitive construction (iḍāfah), and this reading is also narrated from Ubayy.

Al-Dahhak said: it is the regret of the angels over the disbelievers when they denied the messengers. It was also said: it is the words of the man who came from the farthest part of the city. It was also said: the one who says "Alas for the servants!" is the disbelievers who denied, and the worshippers are the messengers, because when they saw the punishment they regretted killing them and wished for faith; this was said by Abu al-ʿĀliyah and Mujahid. It was also said: the regret over them is from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, by way of metaphor (istiʿārah), to magnify what they committed.

Ibn Hurmuz, Muslim ibn Jundub, Ikrimah and Abu al-Zinad read yā ḥasrah with the ha' silent, treating the connected speech as if it were a pause (ijrā' al-waṣl majrā al-waqf). It is also read as yā ḥasratā, as was recited in surah al-Zumar.

The clause ﴿No messenger comes to them but they mock him﴾ is a resumed sentence (mustaʾnafah) that explains what they were upon of denying the messengers and mocking them, and that this is the cause of the regret over them.

Then He, glory be to Him, marvelled at their condition, in that they did not take warning from the likes of them among the earlier nations, so He said: ﴿Have they not seen how many generations We destroyed before them﴾, that is: did they not know the multitude of those whom We destroyed before them of the generations, the earlier nations.

The clause ﴿that they do not return to them﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿how many We destroyed﴾ in meaning.

Sibawayh said: "anna (that) is a substitute for kam (how many), and it is the declarative kam (khabariyyah), therefore it was permissible to substitute from it something that is not an interrogative. The meaning is: 'Have they not seen that the generations whom We destroyed, that they do not return to them?'"

Al-Farra' said: kam is in the accusative position in two ways. The first is by the verb yarau (they see), and he cited as evidence that in the reading of Ibn Mas'ud it is: "alam yarawu man ahlaknā" (have they not seen whom We destroyed). The second way is that kam is in the accusative position by the verb ahlaknā (We destroyed).

Al-Nahhas said: "The first view is untenable, because kam cannot be governed by what precedes it, since it is an interrogative, and it is impossible for an interrogative to fall within the scope of what precedes it. The same applies when it is declarative." Although Sibawayh had alluded to part of this when he made anna a substitute for kam, al-Mubarrad rejected this with the strongest rejection.

﴿And all of them, every one, will be brought before Us﴾, that is: they will be brought before Us on the Day of Resurrection for recompense.

Ibn ʿAmir, ʿAsim and Hamzah read lammā with its shaddah (lammā), and the rest read it with the shaddah removed (lammā, lamā).

Al-Farra' said: whoever read it with the shaddah made lammā mean illā (except), and in (in) mean mā (not), that is: "mā kullun illā jamīʿun ladaynā muḥḍarūn" (none of them but will be brought before Us all together). The meaning of jamīʿ is majmūʿūn (gathered), so it is faʿīl in the sense of mafʿūl, and ladaynā is an adverbial complement of it. As for the reading with the shaddah removed, in is the light form (mukhaffafah) of the heavy form (thaqīlah), and what follows it is in the nominative by being the subject; the tanwīn on kull is a substitute for the genitive complement, and what follows is the predicate, and the lām is the distinguishing lām that separates the light form from the negative.

Abu ʿUbaydah said: "mā in this reading is superfluous, and its implied wording in his view is: 'wa-in kullun la-jamīʿun.'"

It was also said: the meaning of muḥḍarūn is "punished," but the better view is that it is according to its literal meaning of being brought forth for reckoning.

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned the proof for monotheism and resurrection together with enumerating the blessings and reminding of them, so He said: ﴿And a sign for them is the dead earth﴾. Ayah (sign) is the predicate placed first (khabar muqaddam), and its indefiniteness is for magnification, and lahum (for them) is its qualifier, or it is connected to āyah because it means "a sign." Al-ardu (the earth) is the subject. It is also permissible for āyah to be the subject, since it has been specified by the qualifier, and what follows is the predicate.

The people of Medina read al-mayyitah (dead) with the shaddah, and the rest read it without it. The clause ﴿We have revived it﴾ is a resumed sentence explaining how it is a sign. It was also said: it is a qualifier of the earth, so by this Allah drew their attention to the reviving of the dead, and reminded them of His blessings and the perfection of His power, for He, glory be to Him, revived the earth with vegetation and brought forth from it the grains which they eat and on which they nourish themselves. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿And We bring forth from it grain, and from it they eat﴾, that is, what they subsist on of grains. The placing first of ﴿from it﴾ indicates that grain is the main part of what is eaten and the most of what sustains livelihood.

﴿And We placed in it gardens of palms and grapes﴾, that is: We placed in the earth gardens of kinds of palm and grape. He specified these two for mention because they are the highest of fruits and the most beneficial to people. ﴿And We caused springs to gush forth in it﴾, that is: We caused some springs to gush forth in the earth. The object (mawsūf) is omitted and the qualifier is put in its place, or the object is al-ʿuyūn (springs), and min is extra (zā'idah) according to the view of those who permit its addition in affirmative speech, which is al-Akhfash and those who agree with him. By al-ʿuyūn is meant springs of water.

The majority read fajjarnā with the shaddah, and Jinah ibn Hubaysh read it without it. Al-fajr and al-tafjīr are like al-fatḥ and al-tafṭīḥ, both in wording and meaning.

The lām in ﴿so that they may eat of its fruit﴾ is connected to ﴿We placed﴾, and the pronoun in ﴿of its fruit﴾ refers to what was mentioned of the gardens and palms. It was also said: it refers to the water of the springs, because the fruit comes from it; this was said by al-Jurjani.

The majority read thamarihi with a fatḥah on the thāʾ and the mīm. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it with a ḍammah on both. Al-Aʿmash read it with a ḍammah on the thāʾ and sukūn on the mīm. This matter has already been discussed in surah al-Anʿam.

His saying ﴿and what their hands have made﴾ is conjoined to thamarihi, that is: so that they may eat of its fruit and eat of what their hands have made, such as juice and date syrup and the like. Likewise what they planted and dug out, on the basis that mā is a relative pronoun (mawṣūlah). It was also said: mā is negative, and the meaning is: they did not make it; rather the one who made it is Allah, that is: they found it already made, and they had no part in it. This is the view of al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Muqatil.

The majority read ʿamilathu (which they made, with the pronoun), and the Kufans read ʿamilat (without the pronoun), by omitting the pronoun. The interrogative in His saying ﴿Will they not then give thanks?﴾ is for rebuke and reproach of them for their not giving thanks for the blessings.

The clause ﴿Glory be to Him who created all the pairs﴾ is a resumed sentence, brought to declare Him, glory be to Him, free from what they did in abandoning thanks for His mentioned blessings, and to express wonder at their neglect of that. The discussion of the meaning of "Subhan" has already been fully covered. It has the force of a command to the servants that they should declare Him free from what is unfitting for Him. Al-azwāj (pairs) means kinds and species, because each species varies in colours, tastes and forms. ﴿Of what the earth grows﴾ is an explanation of al-azwāj, and what is meant is everything that grows in it of the things mentioned and others. ﴿And of themselves﴾, that is: He created the pairs from themselves, namely males and females. ﴿And of what they do not know﴾: of the kinds of His creation on land and sea, in heaven and earth.

﴿And a sign for them is the night: We strip from it the day﴾. What is said about this is as we have mentioned regarding His saying ﴿And a sign for them is the dead earth, We have revived it﴾. The meaning is that this is a sign indicating the oneness of Allah, His power, and the necessity of His divinity. Salkh (stripping) is removing and drawing off; one says: "Allah stripped him from his body." Then it is used in the sense of extraction. So He, glory be to Him, made the departure of light and the arrival of darkness like stripping something off, and this is an eloquent metaphor. ﴿Then behold, they are in darkness﴾, that is: they enter into darkness suddenly and abruptly. It is said: "aẓlamnā," meaning we entered into the darkness of the night, and "aẓharnā," meaning we entered the time of noon, and likewise "aṣbaḥnā" and "amsaynā." It was also said: min here means ʿan (from), and the meaning is: We strip from it the light of the day.

Al-Farra' said: He casts the day over the night, so it comes with darkness, because the original state is darkness and the day comes upon it. When the sun sets, the day is stripped from the night, that is, drawn off and removed, and then the darkness appears.

﴿And the sun runs on to a resting place for it﴾. The wāw may be conjunctive, connecting to the night, and the meaning would be: "and a sign for them is the sun." It is also permissible that the wāw is initial (ibtidāʾiyyah), with al-shams (the sun) as the subject and what follows as the predicate, and the speech is then resumed, containing mention of an independent sign.

It was said: in the speech there is an omission, and the meaning is: it runs toward a fixed course (limajrā mustaqarrin) for it, so the lām is for cause, that is: for a term (li-ajalin) fixed for it. It was also said: the lām has the meaning of "ilā" (to), and this has been read that way.

The meaning of *mustaqarr* (resting place) is said to be the Day of Resurrection, when the sun comes to rest and has no further movement. It is also said that its resting place is the furthest point it reaches, beyond which it does not go. It is said to be the limit of its rise in summer and the limit of its descent in winter. It is also said that its resting place is beneath the Throne ('Arsh), because it goes there, prostrates, asks permission to return, and is granted it. This last view is the preferred one.

Al-Hasan (al-Basri) said: The sun has three hundred and sixty risings in the year. It descends to a new rising each day and does not descend again until the year is complete. So it keeps moving through those stations, and that is its resting place. Other views have also been reported.

Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah, Zayn al-'Abidin, his son al-Baqir, and al-Sadiq ibn al-Baqir read *lā mustaqarra lahā* with *lā* for the negation of the whole category and *mustaqarr* built on the fatha.

Ibn Abi 'Ablah read *lā mustaqarrun lahā*, with *lā* in the sense of *laysa* (is not), *mustaqarrun* as its subject, and *lahā* as its predicate. The demonstrative in His words ﴿that﴾ refers to the sun's course, meaning: that course is the decree of ﴿the Mighty﴾, that is, the Dominant, the Subduer, ﴿the All-Knowing﴾, that is, whose knowledge encompasses everything. It is also possible that the demonstrative refers back to the *mustaqarr*, meaning: that resting place is the decree of Allah.

﴿And the moon — We have decreed for it stations﴾. Nafi', Ibn Kathir, and Abu 'Amr read *al-qamaru* in the nominative, as a new sentence. The rest read it in the accusative, by the construction of the verb being occupied (*ishtighāl*). The accusative of *manāzila* (stations) is as a second object, because *qaddarnā* means *ṣayyarnā* (We made). It may also be an accusative of circumstance, meaning: We decreed its course while it was in the state of having stations. It may also be an accusative of place, meaning: in stations.

Abu 'Ubayd preferred the accusative for *al-qamara*, saying: because before it there is a verb, *nasliku* (We strip away), and after it there is a verb, *qaddarnā*.

Al-Nahhas said: As far as I know, all the grammarians of Arabic disagree with what he said. Among them is al-Farra', who said: The nominative is more pleasing to me. He said: The nominative is preferred by them because it is coordinated with what precedes it, and its meaning is: and a sign for them is the moon.

Abu Hatim said: The nominative is preferred, because you have diverted the verb from it by the pronoun, so you have made it nominative by beginning the sentence with it.

The *manāzil* (stations) are the twenty-eight known mansions in which the moon lodges each night, one of them, and they are well known; their mention will come. When the moon reaches the last of them, it returns to the first. It traverses the orbit (*falak*) in twenty-eight nights, then it is hidden for two nights, then it appears as a crescent, and it returns to traverse those stations in the orbit.

﴿Until it returns like the old 'urjūn﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: the *'urjūn* is the stalk of the bunch of dates on which the sprigs are. It is of the pattern *fu'lūn*, from *al-in'irāj*, which is bending. Its meaning is that it travels through its stations, and when it is at the end of them it becomes thin, curved, and small until it becomes like the old *'urjūn*. On this view, the *nūn* is an augmentative (extra) letter.

Qatadah said: It is the dry, bent palm-stalk of the date palm. Tha'lab said: The *'urjūn* is what remains on the palm when the bunch has been cut, and *al-qadīm* means the decayed. Al-Khalil said: The *'urjūn* is the base of the bunch, which is yellow and broad, and the crescent is compared to it when it bends. Likewise al-Jawhari said it is the base of the bunch which curves, and from which the sprigs are cut, and it remains dry on the palm. *'Arrajtuhu* means I struck him with the *'urjūn*. On this view, the *nūn* is radical.

The majority read *al-'urjūni* with a damma on the 'ayn and the jim. Sulayman al-Taymi read it with a kasra on the 'ayn and a fatha on the jim. Both are dialect forms. *Al-qadīm* means the old, the aged.

﴿The sun is not to overtake the moon﴾. *Al-shamsu* is in the nominative as the subject of a new sentence, because *lā* does not operate on a definite noun. That is: it is not valid, nor possible, for the sun to overtake the moon in its speed and descend into the station in which the moon is, because each of them has its own authority when alone, so neither of them can enter upon the other. Its authority would then cease until Allah permits the Resurrection, and the sun will rise from its west.

Al-Dahhak said: The meaning is that when the sun rises, there is no light for the moon, and when the moon rises, there is no light for the sun.

Mujahid said: That is, the light of one does not resemble the light of the other.

Al-Hasan said: They do not meet in the sky on the night of the crescent specifically, and Yahya ibn Salam said likewise.

It is also said: The meaning is that when they meet in the sky, one of them is in front of the other, in a station which they do not share.

It is also said: The moon is in the lowest heaven, and the sun is in the fourth heaven. This was reported by al-Nahhas and al-Mahdawi.

Al-Nahhas said: The best and clearest of what has been said about its meaning is that the moon's course is swift, and the sun cannot overtake it in travel.

As for His words ﴿And the sun and the moon are joined together﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 9], that is when He holds the sun back from rising, as explained earlier in al-An'am, and it will come also in Surah al-Qiyamah. Their joining is a sign of the end of this world and the establishment of the Hour.

﴿Nor does the night overtake the day﴾: that is, it does not precede it so as to outstrip it, but it follows it in succession, and each of them comes in its time without outstripping its companion. It is also said that by the night and the day are meant their two signs, which are the sun and the moon, so it is the reverse of His words: ﴿The sun is not to overtake the moon﴾; that is: nor does the moon outstrip the sun. The mention of "outstripping" instead of "overtaking" is because of the swiftness of the moon's course.

﴿And each in an orbit is swimming﴾. The tanwin on *kullun* is a replacement for the genitive noun that is omitted, meaning: and each one of them. *Falak* is either a rotating body, a rotating surface, or a circle. The disagreement about whether the sky is flat or spherical is well known. *Sabh* is movement with ease and smoothness. The plural in His words *yasbaḥūn* (they swim) is in view of the differing risings of the two, so it is as if they were many, according to the multiplicity of those risings. Or the intended meaning is: the sun, the moon, and the stars.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Mas'ud, concerning His words: ﴿And We did not send down upon his people after him...﴾ (the verse), he said: We did not strain against them with armies; that is, the matter is easier for Us than that.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His words: ﴿Alas, for the servants﴾, he said: it means: Woe to the servants.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him, concerning His words: ﴿Alas, for the servants﴾, he said: It is regret over the servants who ﴿no messenger came to them but they used to mock him﴾; that is, the regret over them on the Day of Resurrection.

Ibn Abi Hatim also reported from him, concerning His words: ﴿and what their hands had made﴾, he said: They found it made, which their hands had not made, meaning the Euphrates, the Tigris, the river of Balkh, and the like. ﴿Will they not then be thankful?﴾ for this.

al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others reported from Abu Dharr, who said: "I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about His words: ﴿And the sun runs on to its resting place﴾, and he said: 'Its resting place is beneath the Throne.'"

In another wording from al-Bukhari and others, from his narration, he said: "I was with the Prophet (ﷺ) in the mosque at the setting of the sun, and he said: 'O Abu Dharr, do you know where the sun sets?' I said: 'Allah and His Messenger know best.' He said: 'It goes on until it prostrates beneath the Throne, and that is His words: ﴿And the sun runs on to its resting place﴾.'"

In another wording from his narration, also in Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, and others, he said: "'O Abu Dharr, do you know where this goes?' I said: 'Allah and His Messenger know best.' He said: 'It goes on until it prostrates before its Lord, then it asks permission to return, and it is granted permission. It is as if it were said to it: Rise from where you came, and it rises from its west.'" Then he recited: "That is the resting place for it," and that is the reading of 'Abd Allah.

al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, and others reported something similar from the words of Ibn 'Umar.

al-Khatib, in his book *al-Nujum*, reported from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His words: ﴿And the moon — We have decreed for it stations﴾, the verse, he said: They are twenty-eight stations in which the moon lodges each month: fourteen of them are Syrian and fourteen are Yemeni. The first of them are al-Sharatan, al-Batin, al-Thurayya, al-Dabaran, al-Hak'a, al-Han'a, al-Dhira', al-Nathra, al-Tarf, al-Jabha, al-Zubra, al-Sarfa, al-'Awwa', al-Simak, which is the last of the Syrian, al-Ghafr, al-Zubana, al-Iklil, al-Qalb, al-Shawla, al-Na'a'im, al-Balda, Sa'd al-Dhabih, Sa'd Bula', Sa'd al-Su'ud, Sa'd al-Akhbiya, Muqaddam al-Dalw, Mu'akhkhar al-Dalw, and al-Hut, which is the last of the Yemeni. When it has traversed these twenty-eight stations, ﴿it returns like the old 'urjūn﴾, as it was at the beginning of the month.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him, concerning His words: ﴿like the old 'urjūn﴾: that is, the base of the ancient bunch.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 36, verses 28–40 (part 1 of 2):

When what happened to them occurred with Habib al-Najjar, Allah became angry on his behalf, hastened punishment upon them, and destroyed them with the Shout. The meaning of ﴿Nor did We send down upon his people after him any host from heaven﴾ is: upon the people of Habib al-Najjar, after they killed him, or after Allah raised him up to the heavens, according to the earlier disagreement, any host from heaven to destroy them and to take vengeance upon them. That is, We did not need to send down hosts from heaven to destroy them, as happened to the Prophet (ﷺ) on the Day of Badr, when the angels were sent to support him and to fight his enemies. ﴿Nor were We ever going to send down﴾ means: it was not fitting in Our decree and Our wisdom that We should send down a host to destroy them, because Our decree and Our determination had already preceded that their destruction would be by the Shout and not by the sending down of an army.

Qatadah, Mujahid and al-Hasan said: that is, We did not send down upon them any message from heaven, nor any prophet after they killed him.

It is narrated from al-Hasan that he said: "They are the angels who descend with revelation upon the prophets." The apparent meaning of the Qur'anic wording, however, is to belittle their status and to diminish their affair, that is, they were not worthy that We should send down a host from heaven to destroy them. Rather, We destroyed them with one single Shout, as is indicated by His saying: ﴿It was but one shout﴾, that is: if the punishment, or the vengeance, or the seizure was but one shout, which Jibril (Gabriel) cried out, and so he destroyed them.

The exegetes said: Jibril took hold of the two door-posts of the city, then cried out to them with one shout, and behold, they were dead, with no sound heard from them, like a fire when it is extinguished. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿behold, they were extinguished﴾, that is: they were a people extinguished, dead. He likened them to a fire when it is put out, because life is like a blazing fire and death is like its extinguishing.

The majority of reciters read ﴿shout﴾ (ṣayḥatan) in the accusative, on the basis that kāna (was) is a defective (naqisah) verb, and its subject is a pronoun referring to what is understood from the context, as we have mentioned.

Abu Ja'far, Shayba, al-A'raj, Mu'adh and al-Qarri read it in the nominative (ṣayḥatun), on the basis that kāna is a complete (tammah) verb, meaning: "occurred and came about." Abu Hatim and many of the grammarians rejected this reading because of the feminine form in His saying ﴿if it was﴾ (in kānat). Abu Hatim said: "If it were as Abu Ja'far recited, it would have said: 'in kāna illā ṣayḥatun.'" Al-Zajjaj explained this reading by saying: "in kānat 'alayhim ṣayḥatun illā ṣayḥatan wāḥidatan," and others explained it as: "mā waqaʿat 'alayhim illā ṣayḥatun wāḥidatun."

Abdullah ibn Mas'ud read ﴿if it was but one zaqyah (cry)﴾, and the zaqyah is the shout. Al-Nahhas said: "This is contrary to the Mushaf (the written codex). Also, the well-known language is zaqā yazqū when one cries out, and from it comes the proverb 'heavier than the zawāqī' (cries), so on this basis it should have been zaqwah." This objection is answered by what al-Jawhari mentioned. He said: "al-zaqw and al-zaqy are a verbal noun, and zaqā al-ṣadā yazqū means the echo cried out; zaqā means shouted, and every crier is zāqin, and al-zaqyah is the shout."

﴿Alas for the servants!﴾ The majority read ḥasratan (alas) in the accusative, as an indefinite vocative (munādā munakkar), as if he called out to "Regret" and said to it: "This is your time, so come forth."

It was also said that it is accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), and the vocative particle is omitted, the implied meaning being: "O people, feel regret with regret."

Qatadah and Ubayy, in one narration from him, read ḥasratu in the nominative, as a direct address.

Al-Farra' said regarding the justification of this reading: "The preferred form is the accusative, but if the indefinite noun were in the nominative it would also be correct." He cited examples he heard from the Arabs, among them: "yā muhtammu bi-amrinā lā tahtamma" (O one concerned with our affair, do not be concerned), and he recited:

*"yā dāru ghayyarahā al-bilā taghyīran"*
(O abode, decay has altered you a great alteration.)

Al-Nahhas said: "In this there is an invalidation of the chapter of the vocative, or most of it." The implied wording of what he mentioned is: "yā ayyuhā al-muhtammu lā tahtamma bi-amrinā" (O you who are concerned, do not be concerned with our affair), and the implied wording of the verse is: "yā ayyatuhā al-dāru" (O abode).

The true meaning of ḥasrah is that a person is overcome by regret to the point that he becomes exhausted (ḥasīr).

Ibn Jarir said: the meaning is: "Alas, O regret, from the servants against themselves, and remorse and lament for their mocking of the messengers of Allah." This is supported by the reading of Ibn Abbas and Ali ibn al-Husayn: "yā ḥasrata al-ʿibād" in the genitive construction (iḍāfah), and this reading is also narrated from Ubayy.

Al-Dahhak said: it is the regret of the angels over the disbelievers when they denied the messengers. It was also said: it is the words of the man who came from the farthest part of the city. It was also said: the one who says "Alas for the servants!" is the disbelievers who denied, and the worshippers are the messengers, because when they saw the punishment they regretted killing them and wished for faith; this was said by Abu al-ʿĀliyah and Mujahid. It was also said: the regret over them is from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, by way of metaphor (istiʿārah), to magnify what they committed.

Ibn Hurmuz, Muslim ibn Jundub, Ikrimah and Abu al-Zinad read yā ḥasrah with the ha' silent, treating the connected speech as if it were a pause (ijrā' al-waṣl majrā al-waqf). It is also read as yā ḥasratā, as was recited in surah al-Zumar.

The clause ﴿No messenger comes to them but they mock him﴾ is a resumed sentence (mustaʾnafah) that explains what they were upon of denying the messengers and mocking them, and that this is the cause of the regret over them.

Then He, glory be to Him, marvelled at their condition, in that they did not take warning from the likes of them among the earlier nations, so He said: ﴿Have they not seen how many generations We destroyed before them﴾, that is: did they not know the multitude of those whom We destroyed before them of the generations, the earlier nations.

The clause ﴿that they do not return to them﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿how many We destroyed﴾ in meaning.

Sibawayh said: "anna (that) is a substitute for kam (how many), and it is the declarative kam (khabariyyah), therefore it was permissible to substitute from it something that is not an interrogative. The meaning is: 'Have they not seen that the generations whom We destroyed, that they do not return to them?'"

Al-Farra' said: kam is in the accusative position in two ways. The first is by the verb yarau (they see), and he cited as evidence that in the reading of Ibn Mas'ud it is: "alam yarawu man ahlaknā" (have they not seen whom We destroyed). The second way is that kam is in the accusative position by the verb ahlaknā (We destroyed).

Al-Nahhas said: "The first view is untenable, because kam cannot be governed by what precedes it, since it is an interrogative, and it is impossible for an interrogative to fall within the scope of what precedes it. The same applies when it is declarative." Although Sibawayh had alluded to part of this when he made anna a substitute for kam, al-Mubarrad rejected this with the strongest rejection.

﴿And all of them, every one, will be brought before Us﴾, that is: they will be brought before Us on the Day of Resurrection for recompense.

Ibn ʿAmir, ʿAsim and Hamzah read lammā with its shaddah (lammā), and the rest read it with the shaddah removed (lammā, lamā).

Al-Farra' said: whoever read it with the shaddah made lammā mean illā (except), and in (in) mean mā (not), that is: "mā kullun illā jamīʿun ladaynā muḥḍarūn" (none of them but will be brought before Us all together). The meaning of jamīʿ is majmūʿūn (gathered), so it is faʿīl in the sense of mafʿūl, and ladaynā is an adverbial complement of it. As for the reading with the shaddah removed, in is the light form (mukhaffafah) of the heavy form (thaqīlah), and what follows it is in the nominative by being the subject; the tanwīn on kull is a substitute for the genitive complement, and what follows is the predicate, and the lām is the distinguishing lām that separates the light form from the negative.

Abu ʿUbaydah said: "mā in this reading is superfluous, and its implied wording in his view is: 'wa-in kullun la-jamīʿun.'"

It was also said: the meaning of muḥḍarūn is "punished," but the better view is that it is according to its literal meaning of being brought forth for reckoning.

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned the proof for monotheism and resurrection together with enumerating the blessings and reminding of them, so He said: ﴿And a sign for them is the dead earth﴾. Ayah (sign) is the predicate placed first (khabar muqaddam), and its indefiniteness is for magnification, and lahum (for them) is its qualifier, or it is connected to āyah because it means "a sign." Al-ardu (the earth) is the subject. It is also permissible for āyah to be the subject, since it has been specified by the qualifier, and what follows is the predicate.

The people of Medina read al-mayyitah (dead) with the shaddah, and the rest read it without it. The clause ﴿We have revived it﴾ is a resumed sentence explaining how it is a sign. It was also said: it is a qualifier of the earth, so by this Allah drew their attention to the reviving of the dead, and reminded them of His blessings and the perfection of His power, for He, glory be to Him, revived the earth with vegetation and brought forth from it the grains which they eat and on which they nourish themselves. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿And We bring forth from it grain, and from it they eat﴾, that is, what they subsist on of grains. The placing first of ﴿from it﴾ indicates that grain is the main part of what is eaten and the most of what sustains livelihood.

﴿And We placed in it gardens of palms and grapes﴾, that is: We placed in the earth gardens of kinds of palm and grape. He specified these two for mention because they are the highest of fruits and the most beneficial to people. ﴿And We caused springs to gush forth in it﴾, that is: We caused some springs to gush forth in the earth. The object (mawsūf) is omitted and the qualifier is put in its place, or the object is al-ʿuyūn (springs), and min is extra (zā'idah) according to the view of those who permit its addition in affirmative speech, which is al-Akhfash and those who agree with him. By al-ʿuyūn is meant springs of water.

The majority read fajjarnā with the shaddah, and Jinah ibn Hubaysh read it without it. Al-fajr and al-tafjīr are like al-fatḥ and al-tafṭīḥ, both in wording and meaning.

The lām in ﴿so that they may eat of its fruit﴾ is connected to ﴿We placed﴾, and the pronoun in ﴿of its fruit﴾ refers to what was mentioned of the gardens and palms. It was also said: it refers to the water of the springs, because the fruit comes from it; this was said by al-Jurjani.

The majority read thamarihi with a fatḥah on the thāʾ and the mīm. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it with a ḍammah on both. Al-Aʿmash read it with a ḍammah on the thāʾ and sukūn on the mīm. This matter has already been discussed in surah al-Anʿam.

His saying ﴿and what their hands have made﴾ is conjoined to thamarihi, that is: so that they may eat of its fruit and eat of what their hands have made, such as juice and date syrup and the like. Likewise what they planted and dug out, on the basis that mā is a relative pronoun (mawṣūlah). It was also said: mā is negative, and the meaning is: they did not make it; rather the one who made it is Allah, that is: they found it already made, and they had no part in it. This is the view of al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Muqatil.

The majority read ʿamilathu (which they made, with the pronoun), and the Kufans read ʿamilat (without the pronoun), by omitting the pronoun. The interrogative in His saying ﴿Will they not then give thanks?﴾ is for rebuke and reproach of them for their not giving thanks for the blessings.

The clause ﴿Glory be to Him who created all the pairs﴾ is a resumed sentence, brought to declare Him, glory be to Him, free from what they did in abandoning thanks for His mentioned blessings, and to express wonder at their neglect of that. The discussion of the meaning of "Subhan" has already been fully covered. It has the force of a command to the servants that they should declare Him free from what is unfitting for Him. Al-azwāj (pairs) means kinds and species, because each species varies in colours, tastes and forms. ﴿Of what the earth grows﴾ is an explanation of al-azwāj, and what is meant is everything that grows in it of the things mentioned and others. ﴿And of themselves﴾, that is: He created the pairs from themselves, namely males and females. ﴿And of what they do not know﴾: of the kinds of His creation on land and sea, in heaven and earth.

﴿And a sign for them is the night: We strip from it the day﴾. What is said about this is as we have mentioned regarding His saying ﴿And a sign for them is the dead earth, We have revived it﴾. The meaning is that this is a sign indicating the oneness of Allah, His power, and the necessity of His divinity. Salkh (stripping) is removing and drawing off; one says: "Allah stripped him from his body." Then it is used in the sense of extraction. So He, glory be to Him, made the departure of light and the arrival of darkness like stripping something off, and this is an eloquent metaphor. ﴿Then behold, they are in darkness﴾, that is: they enter into darkness suddenly and abruptly. It is said: "aẓlamnā," meaning we entered into the darkness of the night, and "aẓharnā," meaning we entered the time of noon, and likewise "aṣbaḥnā" and "amsaynā." It was also said: min here means ʿan (from), and the meaning is: We strip from it the light of the day.

Al-Farra' said: He casts the day over the night, so it comes with darkness, because the original state is darkness and the day comes upon it. When the sun sets, the day is stripped from the night, that is, drawn off and removed, and then the darkness appears.

﴿And the sun runs on to a resting place for it﴾. The wāw may be conjunctive, connecting to the night, and the meaning would be: "and a sign for them is the sun." It is also permissible that the wāw is initial (ibtidāʾiyyah), with al-shams (the sun) as the subject and what follows as the predicate, and the speech is then resumed, containing mention of an independent sign.

It was said: in the speech there is an omission, and the meaning is: it runs toward a fixed course (limajrā mustaqarrin) for it, so the lām is for cause, that is: for a term (li-ajalin) fixed for it. It was also said: the lām has the meaning of "ilā" (to), and this has been read that way.

The meaning of *mustaqarr* (resting place) is said to be the Day of Resurrection, when the sun comes to rest and has no further movement. It is also said that its resting place is the furthest point it reaches, beyond which it does not go. It is said to be the limit of its rise in summer and the limit of its descent in winter. It is also said that its resting place is beneath the Throne ('Arsh), because it goes there, prostrates, asks permission to return, and is granted it. This last view is the preferred one.

Al-Hasan (al-Basri) said: The sun has three hundred and sixty risings in the year. It descends to a new rising each day and does not descend again until the year is complete. So it keeps moving through those stations, and that is its resting place. Other views have also been reported.

Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah, Zayn al-'Abidin, his son al-Baqir, and al-Sadiq ibn al-Baqir read *lā mustaqarra lahā* with *lā* for the negation of the whole category and *mustaqarr* built on the fatha.

Ibn Abi 'Ablah read *lā mustaqarrun lahā*, with *lā* in the sense of *laysa* (is not), *mustaqarrun* as its subject, and *lahā* as its predicate. The demonstrative in His words ﴿that﴾ refers to the sun's course, meaning: that course is the decree of ﴿the Mighty﴾, that is, the Dominant, the Subduer, ﴿the All-Knowing﴾, that is, whose knowledge encompasses everything. It is also possible that the demonstrative refers back to the *mustaqarr*, meaning: that resting place is the decree of Allah.

﴿And the moon — We have decreed for it stations﴾. Nafi', Ibn Kathir, and Abu 'Amr read *al-qamaru* in the nominative, as a new sentence. The rest read it in the accusative, by the construction of the verb being occupied (*ishtighāl*). The accusative of *manāzila* (stations) is as a second object, because *qaddarnā* means *ṣayyarnā* (We made). It may also be an accusative of circumstance, meaning: We decreed its course while it was in the state of having stations. It may also be an accusative of place, meaning: in stations.

Abu 'Ubayd preferred the accusative for *al-qamara*, saying: because before it there is a verb, *nasliku* (We strip away), and after it there is a verb, *qaddarnā*.

Al-Nahhas said: As far as I know, all the grammarians of Arabic disagree with what he said. Among them is al-Farra', who said: The nominative is more pleasing to me. He said: The nominative is preferred by them because it is coordinated with what precedes it, and its meaning is: and a sign for them is the moon.

Abu Hatim said: The nominative is preferred, because you have diverted the verb from it by the pronoun, so you have made it nominative by beginning the sentence with it.

The *manāzil* (stations) are the twenty-eight known mansions in which the moon lodges each night, one of them, and they are well known; their mention will come. When the moon reaches the last of them, it returns to the first. It traverses the orbit (*falak*) in twenty-eight nights, then it is hidden for two nights, then it appears as a crescent, and it returns to traverse those stations in the orbit.

﴿Until it returns like the old 'urjūn﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: the *'urjūn* is the stalk of the bunch of dates on which the sprigs are. It is of the pattern *fu'lūn*, from *al-in'irāj*, which is bending. Its meaning is that it travels through its stations, and when it is at the end of them it becomes thin, curved, and small until it becomes like the old *'urjūn*. On this view, the *nūn* is an augmentative (extra) letter.

Qatadah said: It is the dry, bent palm-stalk of the date palm. Tha'lab said: The *'urjūn* is what remains on the palm when the bunch has been cut, and *al-qadīm* means the decayed. Al-Khalil said: The *'urjūn* is the base of the bunch, which is yellow and broad, and the crescent is compared to it when it bends. Likewise al-Jawhari said it is the base of the bunch which curves, and from which the sprigs are cut, and it remains dry on the palm. *'Arrajtuhu* means I struck him with the *'urjūn*. On this view, the *nūn* is radical.

The majority read *al-'urjūni* with a damma on the 'ayn and the jim. Sulayman al-Taymi read it with a kasra on the 'ayn and a fatha on the jim. Both are dialect forms. *Al-qadīm* means the old, the aged.

﴿The sun is not to overtake the moon﴾. *Al-shamsu* is in the nominative as the subject of a new sentence, because *lā* does not operate on a definite noun. That is: it is not valid, nor possible, for the sun to overtake the moon in its speed and descend into the station in which the moon is, because each of them has its own authority when alone, so neither of them can enter upon the other. Its authority would then cease until Allah permits the Resurrection, and the sun will rise from its west.

Al-Dahhak said: The meaning is that when the sun rises, there is no light for the moon, and when the moon rises, there is no light for the sun.

Mujahid said: That is, the light of one does not resemble the light of the other.

Al-Hasan said: They do not meet in the sky on the night of the crescent specifically, and Yahya ibn Salam said likewise.

It is also said: The meaning is that when they meet in the sky, one of them is in front of the other, in a station which they do not share.

It is also said: The moon is in the lowest heaven, and the sun is in the fourth heaven. This was reported by al-Nahhas and al-Mahdawi.

Al-Nahhas said: The best and clearest of what has been said about its meaning is that the moon's course is swift, and the sun cannot overtake it in travel.

As for His words ﴿And the sun and the moon are joined together﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 9], that is when He holds the sun back from rising, as explained earlier in al-An'am, and it will come also in Surah al-Qiyamah. Their joining is a sign of the end of this world and the establishment of the Hour.

﴿Nor does the night overtake the day﴾: that is, it does not precede it so as to outstrip it, but it follows it in succession, and each of them comes in its time without outstripping its companion. It is also said that by the night and the day are meant their two signs, which are the sun and the moon, so it is the reverse of His words: ﴿The sun is not to overtake the moon﴾; that is: nor does the moon outstrip the sun. The mention of "outstripping" instead of "overtaking" is because of the swiftness of the moon's course.

﴿And each in an orbit is swimming﴾. The tanwin on *kullun* is a replacement for the genitive noun that is omitted, meaning: and each one of them. *Falak* is either a rotating body, a rotating surface, or a circle. The disagreement about whether the sky is flat or spherical is well known. *Sabh* is movement with ease and smoothness. The plural in His words *yasbaḥūn* (they swim) is in view of the differing risings of the two, so it is as if they were many, according to the multiplicity of those risings. Or the intended meaning is: the sun, the moon, and the stars.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Mas'ud, concerning His words: ﴿And We did not send down upon his people after him...﴾ (the verse), he said: We did not strain against them with armies; that is, the matter is easier for Us than that.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His words: ﴿Alas, for the servants﴾, he said: it means: Woe to the servants.
