And al-nasl and al-naslān mean hastening in walking. It is said: nasala yansilu, like ḍaraba yaḍribu; and it is said yansulu with ḍammah. And from it is the statement of Imru' al-Qays:

So slip my garments from your garments, and they slip off.

And the statement of another:

Like the wolf's stealthy approach, when the night came upon him in cold, so he crept.

﴿They will say: "Woe to us! Who has raised us from our sleeping place?"﴾ That is: they will say at their resurrection from the graves by the blast: "Woe to us!" They call out "woe" to themselves, as if they were saying to it: "Come, for this is the time of your presence." These who speak are the disbelievers.

Ibn al-Anbari said: The pause at "Woe to us!" is a good pause. Then the speech begins with His words: "Who has raised us from our sleeping place?" They thought, because their minds were confused by what they witnessed of the terror, and what entered them of fear, that they had been asleep.

The Jumhur (majority of reciters) read ﴿Ya waylana﴾, while Ibn Abi Layla read *yā waylatanā*, with the added *tāʾ*.

The Jumhur read ﴿man baʿathanā﴾ with the *mīm* of *man* fathah, as an interrogative (*istifhām*, question). Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Dahhak, and Abu Nahik read it with the *mīm* kasrah, making it a preposition (*ḥarf jarr*). This reading is also narrated from ʿAli ibn Abi Talib.

On this reading, *min* is connected to *al-waylu* (woe), and the Jumhur read ﴿man baʿathanā﴾ [as above].

In Ubayy's reading, it is *man ahabbanā*, from *habba min nawmihi*, meaning he woke up from his sleep. Thaʿlab recited the following verse as evidence for this reading:

*"A blaming woman who rose in the night to rebuke me, and no blamer had reproached me before that."*

It is also said that they say this when they see Hell.

Abu Salih said: when the first blast is sounded, the punishment is lifted from the people of the graves, and they rest in a sleep until the second blast.

The clause ﴿This is what the Most Merciful promised, and the messengers spoke the truth﴾ is a reply to them from the angels or from the believers.

It is also said that it is from the speech of the disbelievers, with some of them answering others.

Al-Farraʾ held the first view, and Mujahid the second.

Qatadah said: it is from the words of Allah, glory be to Him. The *mā* in ﴿what the Most Merciful promised﴾ is a relative pronoun (*ism mawṣūl*), and its returning pronoun is omitted. The meaning is: this is what the Most Merciful promised, and in which the messengers spoke the truth. It has already been decreed against you and has come upon you. The two objects of *waʿd* (promise) and *ṣidq* (truth) are omitted, meaning: the Most Merciful promised it to you, and the messengers told you the truth about it. The original form is: "He promised you it and spoke truly to you about it," or "the Most Merciful promised it to us and the messengers spoke truly to us about it," with this being the speech of the believers, or of the disbelievers.

﴿It was but a single blast﴾, meaning that the blast mentioned was only a single cry that Israfil uttered by blowing into the Trumpet. ﴿Then, behold, they will all be brought before Us﴾, meaning they will all be gathered and brought swiftly before Us for reckoning and retribution.

﴿So on that Day no soul will be wronged﴾ in any way, ﴿in anything﴾ that it deserves. That is, nothing will be diminished from the reward of its deeds, and it will not be wronged in any form of injustice. ﴿And you will not be recompensed except for what you used to do﴾, meaning except the recompense for what you used to do in the world, or except for what you used to do, that is, because of it, or in exchange for it.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Abu Malik, concerning His words: "We carried their offspring..." (the verse), that he said: in the ship of Noah, in which He carried of every pair two. ﴿And We created for them from the like of it that they ride﴾: the ships that are in the sea and the rivers, in which people ride.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir recorded similarly from Abu Salih.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Ibn ʿAbbas, concerning His words: ﴿And We created for them from the like of it that they ride﴾, that he said: these are ships, made after the ship of Noah.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also recorded from him concerning the verse, that he said: it means camels, which Allah created as you see. They are the "ships of the desert," on which they carry loads and ride.

Similar was said by al-Hasan, ʿIkrimah, ʿAbd Allah ibn Shaddad, and Mujahid.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Mardawayh recorded from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), concerning His words: ﴿So they will not be able to make a bequest﴾ (the verse), that he said: The Hour will be established while people are in their markets, trading, measuring cloth, milking the she-camels, and occupied with their needs, so they will not be able to make a bequest ﴿nor return to their families﴾.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and ʿAbd Allah ibn Ahmad in *Zawaʾid al-Zuhd*, and Ibn al-Mundhir, recorded from al-Zubayr ibn al-ʿAwwam, who said: The Hour will be established while a man is measuring out cloth and a man is milking a she-camel. Then he recited: ﴿So they will not be able to make a bequest﴾ (the verse).

al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others recorded from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The Hour will certainly be established while two men have spread out their garment, but they will not trade it nor fold it. The Hour will certainly be established while a man is plastering his cistern and will not drink from it. The Hour will certainly be established while a man has departed with the milk of his she-camel and will not taste it. The Hour will certainly be established while a man has raised his morsel to his mouth and will not eat it."

al-Firyabi, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb concerning His words: ﴿Who has raised us from our resting place?﴾, that he said: they sleep a sleep before the resurrection.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 36, verses 41–54 (part 1 of 2):

Then He, glory be to Him and exalted, mentioned another kind of the blessings with which He favoured His servants, and said: ﴿And a sign for them is that We carried their offspring in the laden ship.﴾ That is, a proof and an indication. It has also been said that the meaning of "sign" (āyah) here is a lesson ('ibrah), and it has been said it is a blessing (ni'mah), and it has been said it is a warning (nidhārah).

There is disagreement about the meaning of ﴿that We carried their offspring﴾ and to whom the pronoun refers, since the first pronoun, in His words ﴿And a sign for them﴾, refers either to the people of Makkah, or to the disbelieving Arabs, or to the disbelievers in general who lived in the time of Muhammad (ﷺ). It has been said that the pronoun refers to the past generations, and the meaning is that God carried the offspring of the past generations in the laden ship, so the two pronouns are different.

This was related by al-Nahhas from ʿAli ibn Sulayman al-Akhfash.

It has also been said that both pronouns refer to the disbelievers of Makkah and those like them. The meaning is that God carried their offspring, their children and their weak ones, in the ship, and God bestowed favour upon them by this; that is, they carry them with them in the ships when they travel, or they send their children for trade on their behalf in them.

It has also been said that "offspring" (dhurriyyah) means the fathers and grandfathers, and "the ship" is the ship of Noah. That is, God carried the fathers and grandfathers of these people in the ship of Noah.

Al-Wahidi said: The word dhurriyyah applies to fathers as it applies to children.

Abu ʿUthman said: The fathers were called dhurriyyah because from them comes the begetting of the sons (dharʾ al-abnāʾ). It has also been said that dhurriyyah means the sperm-drops present in the wombs of women, and the wombs are likened to the laden ship. The preferred view is the second, then the first, then the third; as for the fourth, it is extremely remote and strange.

The discussion of dhurriyyah and its derivation has already been treated in full in Surat al-Baqarah. Mashḥūn means filled, loaded. Al-fulk (the ship) is used for the singular and the plural, as has been mentioned in Surat Yunus. The word āyah is in the nominative as a predicate that has been placed first (khabar muqaddam), and the subject is ﴿that We carried﴾, or the reverse, as we have said before.

It has also been said that the pronoun in His words ﴿And a sign for them﴾ refers to the servants mentioned in His words ﴿Alas for the servants!﴾ [Yasin: 30], because after that He said ﴿And a sign for them is the dead earth﴾ [Yasin: 33], and He said ﴿And a sign for them is the night﴾ [Yasin: 37]. Then He said ﴿And a sign for them is that We carried their offspring﴾. It is as if He said: "And a sign for the servants is that We carried the offspring of the servants." It does not necessarily follow that by one of the two pronouns is meant some of them, and by the other pronoun another part of them. This is a good view.

﴿And We created for them of its likeness that which they ride﴾. That is, We created for them, from what resembles the ship, that which they ride; here "mā" is a relative pronoun.

Mujahid, Qatadah, and a group of the people of tafsir said: It is the camels, which He created for them to ride on land, like the ships that are ridden on the sea. The Arabs call camels "the ships of the land." It has also been said that the meaning is: We created for them ships like those ships which they ride. This was said by al-Hasan, al-Dahhak, and Abu Malik.

Al-Nahhas said: This is more correct, because its chain of transmission (ittiṣāl al-isnād) from Ibn ʿAbbas is continuous. It has also been said that it means the ships made after the ship of Noah.

﴿And if We will, We drown them, and there is no one to cry out for them, nor are they rescued﴾. This is part of the same verse in which God bestowed favour upon them. The aspect of the favour is that He did not drown them in the深 depths of the seas, though He is capable of that. The pronoun refers either to the owners of the offspring, or to the offspring, or to all of them, according to the differing views. Al-ṣarīkh means al-muṣrikh (one who cries out for help), and al-muṣrikh is the one who gives aid; that is, there is no helper for them who would aid them if We willed to drown them. It has also been said that al-ṣarīkh means protection.

The meaning of yunqadhūn is: they are delivered. It is said: anqadhahu and istanqadhahu, when he delivered him from something disliked.

﴿Except as a mercy from Us﴾. This is an exception of the type called istithnāʾ mufarragh (an exception in which the excepted element is left unstated), from the most general of the causes; that is: there is no one to cry out for them, and they are not rescued for anything at all, except by a mercy from Us. Thus said al-Kisaʾi, al-Zajjaj, and others. It has also been said that it is an istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ (disjunctive exception), that is: but by a mercy from Us.

It has also been said that it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdariyyah) governed by a verb understood, and the accusative of matāʿan (as a provision) is by conjunction to raḥmatan (mercy), that is: We let them enjoy the life of this world ﴿for a time﴾, and this is death, said Qatadah. Yahya ibn Salam said: until the Resurrection.

﴿And when it is said to them: "Fear what is before you and what is behind you"﴾. That is: what is before you of calamities and misfortunes, for they encompass you, and what is behind you of them.

Qatadah said the meaning of ﴿Fear what is before you﴾ is: of the events concerning those who were before you of the nations, ﴿and what is behind you﴾ is in the Hereafter.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Mujahid said: ﴿what is before you﴾ is what has passed of sins, ﴿and what is behind you﴾ is what remains of them.

It has been said: ﴿what is before you﴾ is the world, ﴿and what is behind you﴾ is the Hereafter; this was said by Sufyan.

al-Tha'labi related the reverse of this view from Ibn ʿAbbas.

It has been said: ﴿what is before you﴾ is what is manifest to you, ﴿and what is behind you﴾ is what is hidden from you. The answer to idhā (when) is omitted, and the estimate is: when it is said to them that, they turn away, as is indicated by ﴿except that they were turning away from them﴾. ﴿So that you may be shown mercy﴾, that is: in hope that you will be shown mercy, or in order that you may be shown mercy, or hoping that you will be shown mercy.

﴿And no sign comes to them from the signs of their Lord except that they were turning away from it﴾. Here mā is negative, and the form of the present tense indicates renewal. The first min is extra for emphasis, and the second min is partitive. The meaning: no sign comes to them, indicating the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) and the soundness of what he called to of monotheism, in any state, except that they were turning away from it.

Its apparent meaning includes both the revealed signs and the cosmic signs. The clause ﴿except that they were turning away from it﴾ is in the place of the accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), as its explanation has passed in more than one place.

What is meant by turning away is not giving attention to it, and abandoning correct reflection upon it. This verse is connected to His words ﴿Alas for the servants! No messenger comes to them except that they used to mock him﴾ [Yasin: 30]; that is: when the messengers came to them they denied them, and when the signs were brought to them they turned away from them.

﴿And when it is said to them: "Spend from what Allah has provided you"﴾. That is: give charity to the poor from what Allah has given you and bestowed upon you of wealth. al-Hasan said: He means the Jews, who were commanded to feed the poor.

Muqatil said: The believers said to the disbelievers of Quraysh: "Spend on the needy from what you claim belongs to Allah of your wealth, of crops and livestock," as in His words: ﴿And they assigned to Allah a share of what He created of crops and livestock﴾ [al-Anʿam: 136]. So their answer was what Allah related about them in His words: ﴿Those who disbelieved said to those who believed﴾, mocking them, and deriding their words: ﴿Shall we feed one whom, if Allah willed, He would feed?﴾ That is: one whom, if Allah willed, He would provide for. They had heard the Muslims saying that the Provider is Allah, and that He enriches whom He wills and impoverishes whom He wills. So it seems they attempted by this statement to put the Muslims in a difficult position, and said: "We agree with the will of Allah, so we do not feed the one whom Allah has not fed." This was an error on their part, and obstinacy, and disputation with falsehood, for Allah, glory be to Him, made some of His creatures rich and some poor, and commanded the rich to feed the poor, and tested them with it in what He obligated them to give from their wealth as charity.

Their saying ﴿One whom, if Allah willed, He would feed﴾, although it is in itself a true statement, yet because they intended by it the denial of the power of Allah, or the denial of the permissibility of commanding spending while Allah has power, their argument from this standpoint was false.

His words ﴿You are not but in manifest error﴾ are part of the speech of the disbelievers. The meaning: you, O Muslims, in asking for wealth and in commanding us to feed the poor, are in error most clear and evident.

It has also been said that it is part of the speech of Allah, glory be to Him, as an answer to this statement that the disbelievers made.

al-Qushayri and al-Mawardi said: the verse was revealed concerning a people of the zindiqs (heretics).

Among the disbelievers of Quraysh and others among the rest of the Arabs there were people who were heretics, who did not believe in the Creator, so they made this statement mockingly at the Muslims and in opposition to them.

al-Qurtubi related something similar to this from Ibn ʿAbbas.

﴿And they say: "When is this promise?"﴾ That is, the promise you make to us of punishment, and the Resurrection, and the return to Paradise or to Hell. ﴿If you are truthful﴾ in what you say and what you promise us. They said this mockingly and derisively toward the believers, and their intent was to deny that entirely, to negate its realization, and to reject its occurrence.

So Allah, glory be to Him, answered them with His words: (p. 1227) ﴿They await only one shout, which will seize them while they are disputing﴾. That is: they are not waiting for anything but one shout, which is the blast of Israfil in the Trumpet. ﴿Which will seize them while they are disputing﴾, that is: they will be disputing among themselves about trade and buying and selling and similar matters of the worldly life. This is the first blast, the blast of swooning.

The readers differed concerning yakhiṣṣimūn. Ḥamzah read it with the vowel of the kh sukūn and the ṣ light, from khaṣama, yakhṣimu, and the meaning: some of them dispute with others, so the object is omitted.

Abu ʿAmr and Qalun read it with the vowel of the kh hidden and the ṣ doubled. Nafiʿ, Ibn Kathir, and Hisham did likewise, except that they purified the fatḥah of the kh. The rest read it with a kasrah on the kh and the ṣ doubled.

The original form in all three readings is yakhtaṣimūn, then the tā was assimilated into the ṣād. Nafiʿ, Ibn Kathir, and Hisham fully transferred the fatḥah of the tā to the sākin before it. Abu ʿAmr and Qalun made the vowel of it slight, to indicate that the original of the kh is sukūn. The rest dropped its vowel, so two sākins met, and they gave the first of them a kasrah.

It is related from Abu ʿAmr and Qalun that they both read with the kh sukūn and the ṣ doubled, and this is a problematic reading because two sākins come together in it.

Ubayy read yakhtaṣimūn according to what is the original.

﴿So they will not be able to make a bequest﴾. That is: none of them will be able to bequeath to another his wealth and what is upon him, or he will not be able to instruct him to repent and to desist from sins; rather they will die in their markets and their places. ﴿Nor to their families will they return﴾. That is: to their homes from which they died outside. It has also been said that the meaning is: they will not return to their families with speech. This is information about what will befall them at the first blast.

Then, glory be to Him, informed about what will befall them at the second blast, and He said: ﴿And the Trumpet will be blown, and at once they will be out of their graves to their Lord, hastening﴾. That is, the graves. ﴿Hastening to their Lord﴾, that is, hurrying. Between the two blasts there are forty years.

He expressed the future with the past form when He said ﴿And the Trumpet will be blown﴾, to indicate the certainty of its occurrence, as the people of rhetoric (ahl al-bayān) mentioned, and they made this verse an example of it. And al-ṣūr with the wāw sukūn is the horn into which Israfil blows, as the Sunnah has reported. The application of this name to a horn is well known in the Arabic language, and from it is the statement of the poet:

We struck them on the morning of al-Ghawrayn, a fierce striking, not like the striking of the two horns.

That is: the two horns.

This has passed in Surat al-Anʿam. Qatadah said: al-ṣūr is the plural of ṣūrah, that is: the Trumpet blew the spirits into the forms.

al-Ajdāth is the plural of jadath, which is the grave. It was read al-ajdāf with fāʾ, and that is a dialect, while the eloquent dialect is with the thāʾ (ṯ). And al-nasl and al-naslān mean hastening in walking. It is said: nasala yansilu, like ḍaraba yaḍribu; and it is said yansulu with ḍammah. And from it is the statement of Imru' al-Qays:

So slip my garments from your garments, and they slip off.

And the statement of another:

Like the wolf's stealthy approach, when the night came upon him in cold, so he crept.

It has also been said that "offspring" (dhurriyyah) means the fathers and grandfathers, and "the ship" is the ship of Noah. That is, God carried the fathers and grandfathers of these people in the ship of Noah.

Al-Wahidi said: The word dhurriyyah applies to fathers as it applies to children.

Abu ʿUthman said: The fathers were called dhurriyyah because from them comes the begetting of the sons (dharʾ al-abnāʾ). It has also been said that dhurriyyah means the sperm-drops present in the wombs of women, and the wombs are likened to the laden ship. The preferred view is the second, then the first, then the third; as for the fourth, it is extremely remote and strange.

The discussion of dhurriyyah and its derivation has already been treated in full in Surat al-Baqarah. Mashḥūn means filled, loaded. Al-fulk (the ship) is used for the singular and the plural, as has been mentioned in Surat Yunus. The word āyah is in the nominative as a predicate that has been placed first (khabar muqaddam), and the subject is ﴿that We carried﴾, or the reverse, as we have said before.

It has also been said that the pronoun in His words ﴿And a sign for them﴾ refers to the servants mentioned in His words ﴿Alas for the servants!﴾ [Yasin: 30], because after that He said ﴿And a sign for them is the dead earth﴾ [Yasin: 33], and He said ﴿And a sign for them is the night﴾ [Yasin: 37]. Then He said ﴿And a sign for them is that We carried their offspring﴾. It is as if He said: "And a sign for the servants is that We carried the offspring of the servants." It does not necessarily follow that by one of the two pronouns is meant some of them, and by the other pronoun another part of them. This is a good view.

﴿And We created for them of its likeness that which they ride﴾. That is, We created for them, from what resembles the ship, that which they ride; here "mā" is a relative pronoun.

Mujahid, Qatadah, and a group of the people of tafsir said: It is the camels, which He created for them to ride on land, like the ships that are ridden on the sea. The Arabs call camels "the ships of the land." It has also been said that the meaning is: We created for them ships like those ships which they ride. This was said by al-Hasan, al-Dahhak, and Abu Malik.

Al-Nahhas said: This is more correct, because its chain of transmission (ittiṣāl al-isnād) from Ibn ʿAbbas is continuous. It has also been said that it means the ships made after the ship of Noah.

﴿And if We will, We drown them, and there is no one to cry out for them, nor are they rescued﴾. This is part of the same verse in which God bestowed favour upon them. The aspect of the favour is that He did not drown them in the深 depths of the seas, though He is capable of that. The pronoun refers either to the owners of the offspring, or to the offspring, or to all of them, according to the differing views. Al-ṣarīkh means al-muṣrikh (one who cries out for help), and al-muṣrikh is the one who gives aid; that is, there is no helper for them who would aid them if We willed to drown them. It has also been said that al-ṣarīkh means protection.

The meaning of yunqadhūn is: they are delivered. It is said: anqadhahu and istanqadhahu, when he delivered him from something disliked.

﴿Except as a mercy from Us﴾. This is an exception of the type called istithnāʾ mufarragh (an exception in which the excepted element is left unstated), from the most general of the causes; that is: there is no one to cry out for them, and they are not rescued for anything at all, except by a mercy from Us. Thus said al-Kisaʾi, al-Zajjaj, and others. It has also been said that it is an istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ (disjunctive exception), that is: but by a mercy from Us.

It has also been said that it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdariyyah) governed by a verb understood, and the accusative of matāʿan (as a provision) is by conjunction to raḥmatan (mercy), that is: We let them enjoy the life of this world ﴿for a time﴾, and this is death, said Qatadah. Yahya ibn Salam said: until the Resurrection.

﴿And when it is said to them: "Fear what is before you and what is behind you"﴾. That is: what is before you of calamities and misfortunes, for they encompass you, and what is behind you of them.

Qatadah said the meaning of ﴿Fear what is before you﴾ is: of the events concerning those who were before you of the nations, ﴿and what is behind you﴾ is in the Hereafter.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Mujahid said: ﴿what is before you﴾ is what has passed of sins, ﴿and what is behind you﴾ is what remains of them.

It has been said: ﴿what is before you﴾ is the world, ﴿and what is behind you﴾ is the Hereafter; this was said by Sufyan.

al-Tha'labi related the reverse of this view from Ibn ʿAbbas.

It has been said: ﴿what is before you﴾ is what is manifest to you, ﴿and what is behind you﴾ is what is hidden from you. The answer to idhā (when) is omitted, and the estimate is: when it is said to them that, they turn away, as is indicated by ﴿except that they were turning away from them﴾. ﴿So that you may be shown mercy﴾, that is: in hope that you will be shown mercy, or in order that you may be shown mercy, or hoping that you will be shown mercy.

﴿And no sign comes to them from the signs of their Lord except that they were turning away from it﴾. Here mā is negative, and the form of the present tense indicates renewal. The first min is extra for emphasis, and the second min is partitive. The meaning: no sign comes to them, indicating the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) and the soundness of what he called to of monotheism, in any state, except that they were turning away from it.

Its apparent meaning includes both the revealed signs and the cosmic signs. The clause ﴿except that they were turning away from it﴾ is in the place of the accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), as its explanation has passed in more than one place.

What is meant by turning away is not giving attention to it, and abandoning correct reflection upon it. This verse is connected to His words ﴿Alas for the servants! No messenger comes to them except that they used to mock him﴾ [Yasin: 30]; that is: when the messengers came to them they denied them, and when the signs were brought to them they turned away from them.

﴿And when it is said to them: "Spend from what Allah has provided you"﴾. That is: give charity to the poor from what Allah has given you and bestowed upon you of wealth. al-Hasan said: He means the Jews, who were commanded to feed the poor.

Muqatil said: The believers said to the disbelievers of Quraysh: "Spend on the needy from what you claim belongs to Allah of your wealth, of crops and livestock," as in His words: ﴿And they assigned to Allah a share of what He created of crops and livestock﴾ [al-Anʿam: 136]. So their answer was what Allah related about them in His words: ﴿Those who disbelieved said to those who believed﴾, mocking them, and deriding their words: ﴿Shall we feed one whom, if Allah willed, He would feed?﴾ That is: one whom, if Allah willed, He would provide for. They had heard the Muslims saying that the Provider is Allah, and that He enriches whom He wills and impoverishes whom He wills. So it seems they attempted by this statement to put the Muslims in a difficult position, and said: "We agree with the will of Allah, so we do not feed the one whom Allah has not fed." This was an error on their part, and obstinacy, and disputation with falsehood, for Allah, glory be to Him, made some of His creatures rich and some poor, and commanded the rich to feed the poor, and tested them with it in what He obligated them to give from their wealth as charity.

Their saying ﴿One whom, if Allah willed, He would feed﴾, although it is in itself a true statement, yet because they intended by it the denial of the power of Allah, or the denial of the permissibility of commanding spending while Allah has power, their argument from this standpoint was false.

His words ﴿You are not but in manifest error﴾ are part of the speech of the disbelievers. The meaning: you, O Muslims, in asking for wealth and in commanding us to feed the poor, are in error most clear and evident.

It has also been said that it is part of the speech of Allah, glory be to Him, as an answer to this statement that the disbelievers made.

al-Qushayri and al-Mawardi said: the verse was revealed concerning a people of the zindiqs (heretics).

Among the disbelievers of Quraysh and others among the rest of the Arabs there were people who were heretics, who did not believe in the Creator, so they made this statement mockingly at the Muslims and in opposition to them.

al-Qurtubi related something similar to this from Ibn ʿAbbas.

﴿And they say: "When is this promise?"﴾ That is, the promise you make to us of punishment, and the Resurrection, and the return to Paradise or to Hell. ﴿If you are truthful﴾ in what you say and what you promise us. They said this mockingly and derisively toward the believers, and their intent was to deny that entirely, to negate its realization, and to reject its occurrence.

So Allah, glory be to Him, answered them with His words: (p. 1227) ﴿They await only one shout, which will seize them while they are disputing﴾. That is: they are not waiting for anything but one shout, which is the blast of Israfil in the Trumpet. ﴿Which will seize them while they are disputing﴾, that is: they will be disputing among themselves about trade and buying and selling and similar matters of the worldly life. This is the first blast, the blast of swooning.

The readers differed concerning yakhiṣṣimūn. Ḥamzah read it with the vowel of the kh sukūn and the ṣ light, from khaṣama, yakhṣimu, and the meaning: some of them dispute with others, so the object is omitted.

Abu ʿAmr and Qalun read it with the vowel of the kh hidden and the ṣ doubled. Nafiʿ, Ibn Kathir, and Hisham did likewise, except that they purified the fatḥah of the kh. The rest read it with a kasrah on the kh and the ṣ doubled.

The original form in all three readings is yakhtaṣimūn, then the tā was assimilated into the ṣād. Nafiʿ, Ibn Kathir, and Hisham fully transferred the fatḥah of the tā to the sākin before it. Abu ʿAmr and Qalun made the vowel of it slight, to indicate that the original of the kh is sukūn. The rest dropped its vowel, so two sākins met, and they gave the first of them a kasrah.

It is related from Abu ʿAmr and Qalun that they both read with the kh sukūn and the ṣ doubled, and this is a problematic reading because two sākins come together in it.

Ubayy read yakhtaṣimūn according to what is the original.

﴿So they will not be able to make a bequest﴾. That is: none of them will be able to bequeath to another his wealth and what is upon him, or he will not be able to instruct him to repent and to desist from sins; rather they will die in their markets and their places. ﴿Nor to their families will they return﴾. That is: to their homes from which they died outside. It has also been said that the meaning is: they will not return to their families with speech. This is information about what will befall them at the first blast.

Then, glory be to Him, informed about what will befall them at the second blast, and He said: ﴿And the Trumpet will be blown, and at once they will be out of their graves to their Lord, hastening﴾. That is, the graves. ﴿Hastening to their Lord﴾, that is, hurrying. Between the two blasts there are forty years.

He expressed the future with the past form when He said ﴿And the Trumpet will be blown﴾, to indicate the certainty of its occurrence, as the people of rhetoric (ahl al-bayān) mentioned, and they made this verse an example of it. And al-ṣūr with the wāw sukūn is the horn into which Israfil blows, as the Sunnah has reported. The application of this name to a horn is well known in the Arabic language, and from it is the statement of the poet:

We struck them on the morning of al-Ghawrayn, a fierce striking, not like the striking of the two horns.

That is: the two horns.

This has passed in Surat al-Anʿam. Qatadah said: al-ṣūr is the plural of ṣūrah, that is: the Trumpet blew the spirits into the forms.

al-Ajdāth is the plural of jadath, which is the grave. It was read al-ajdāf with fāʾ, and that is a dialect, while the eloquent dialect is with the thāʾ (ṯ). And al-nasl and al-naslān mean hastening in walking. It is said: nasala yansilu, like ḍaraba yaḍribu; and it is said yansulu with ḍammah. And from it is the statement of Imru' al-Qays:

So slip my garments from your garments, and they slip off.

And the statement of another:

Like the wolf's stealthy approach, when the night came upon him in cold, so he crept.

﴿They will say: "Woe to us! Who has raised us from our sleeping place?"﴾ That is: they will say at their resurrection from the graves by the blast: "Woe to us!" They call out "woe" to themselves, as if they were saying to it: "Come, for this is the time of your presence." These who speak are the disbelievers.

Ibn al-Anbari said: The pause at "Woe to us!" is a good pause. Then the speech begins with His words: "Who has raised us from our sleeping place?" They thought, because their minds were confused by what they witnessed of the terror, and what entered them of fear, that they had been asleep.

The Jumhur (majority of reciters) read ﴿Ya waylana﴾, while Ibn Abi Layla read *yā waylatanā*, with the added *tāʾ*.

The Jumhur read ﴿man baʿathanā﴾ with the *mīm* of *man* fathah, as an interrogative (*istifhām*, question). Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Dahhak, and Abu Nahik read it with the *mīm* kasrah, making it a preposition (*ḥarf jarr*). This reading is also narrated from ʿAli ibn Abi Talib.

On this reading, *min* is connected to *al-waylu* (woe), and the Jumhur read ﴿man baʿathanā﴾ [as above].

In Ubayy's reading, it is *man ahabbanā*, from *habba min nawmihi*, meaning he woke up from his sleep. Thaʿlab recited the following verse as evidence for this reading:

*"A blaming woman who rose in the night to rebuke me, and no blamer had reproached me before that."*

It is also said that they say this when they see Hell.

Abu Salih said: when the first blast is sounded, the punishment is lifted from the people of the graves, and they rest in a sleep until the second blast.

The clause ﴿This is what the Most Merciful promised, and the messengers spoke the truth﴾ is a reply to them from the angels or from the believers.

It is also said that it is from the speech of the disbelievers, with some of them answering others.

Al-Farraʾ held the first view, and Mujahid the second.

Qatadah said: it is from the words of Allah, glory be to Him. The *mā* in ﴿what the Most Merciful promised﴾ is a relative pronoun (*ism mawṣūl*), and its returning pronoun is omitted. The meaning is: this is what the Most Merciful promised, and in which the messengers spoke the truth. It has already been decreed against you and has come upon you. The two objects of *waʿd* (promise) and *ṣidq* (truth) are omitted, meaning: the Most Merciful promised it to you, and the messengers told you the truth about it. The original form is: "He promised you it and spoke truly to you about it," or "the Most Merciful promised it to us and the messengers spoke truly to us about it," with this being the speech of the believers, or of the disbelievers.

﴿It was but a single blast﴾, meaning that the blast mentioned was only a single cry that Israfil uttered by blowing into the Trumpet. ﴿Then, behold, they will all be brought before Us﴾, meaning they will all be gathered and brought swiftly before Us for reckoning and retribution.

﴿So on that Day no soul will be wronged﴾ in any way, ﴿in anything﴾ that it deserves. That is, nothing will be diminished from the reward of its deeds, and it will not be wronged in any form of injustice. ﴿And you will not be recompensed except for what you used to do﴾, meaning except the recompense for what you used to do in the world, or except for what you used to do, that is, because of it, or in exchange for it.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Abu Malik, concerning His words: "We carried their offspring..." (the verse), that he said: in the ship of Noah, in which He carried of every pair two. ﴿And We created for them from the like of it that they ride﴾: the ships that are in the sea and the rivers, in which people ride.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir recorded similarly from Abu Salih.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Ibn ʿAbbas, concerning His words: ﴿And We created for them from the like of it that they ride﴾, that he said: these are ships, made after the ship of Noah.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also recorded from him concerning the verse, that he said: it means camels, which Allah created as you see. They are the "ships of the desert," on which they carry loads and ride.

Similar was said by al-Hasan, ʿIkrimah, ʿAbd Allah ibn Shaddad, and Mujahid.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Mardawayh recorded from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), concerning His words: ﴿So they will not be able to make a bequest﴾ (the verse), that he said: The Hour will be established while people are in their markets, trading, measuring cloth, milking the she-camels, and occupied with their needs, so they will not be able to make a bequest ﴿nor return to their families﴾.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and ʿAbd Allah ibn Ahmad in *Zawaʾid al-Zuhd*, and Ibn al-Mundhir, recorded from al-Zubayr ibn al-ʿAwwam, who said: The Hour will be established while a man is measuring out cloth and a man is milking a she-camel. Then he recited: ﴿So they will not be able to make a bequest﴾ (the verse).

al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others recorded from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The Hour will certainly be established while two men have spread out their garment, but they will not trade it nor fold it. The Hour will certainly be established while a man is plastering his cistern and will not drink from it. The Hour will certainly be established while a man has departed with the milk of his she-camel and will not taste it. The Hour will certainly be established while a man has raised his morsel to his mouth and will not eat it."

al-Firyabi, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb concerning His words: ﴿Who has raised us from our resting place?﴾, that he said: they sleep a sleep before the resurrection.

There is disagreement about the meaning of ﴿that We carried their offspring﴾ and to whom the pronoun refers, since the first pronoun, in His words ﴿And a sign for them﴾, refers either to the people of Makkah, or to the disbelieving Arabs, or to the disbelievers in general who lived in the time of Muhammad (ﷺ). It has been said that the pronoun refers to the past generations, and the meaning is that God carried the offspring of the past generations in the laden ship, so the two pronouns are different.

His words ﴿You are not but in manifest error﴾ are part of the speech of the disbelievers. The meaning: you, O Muslims, in asking for wealth and in commanding us to feed the poor, are in error most clear and evident.

It has also been said that it is part of the speech of Allah, glory be to Him, as an answer to this statement that the disbelievers made.

al-Qushayri and al-Mawardi said: the verse was revealed concerning a people of the zindiqs (heretics).

Among the disbelievers of Quraysh and others among the rest of the Arabs there were people who were heretics, who did not believe in the Creator, so they made this statement mockingly at the Muslims and in opposition to them.

al-Qurtubi related something similar to this from Ibn ʿAbbas.

﴿And they say: "When is this promise?"﴾ That is, the promise you make to us of punishment, and the Resurrection, and the return to Paradise or to Hell. ﴿If you are truthful﴾ in what you say and what you promise us. They said this mockingly and derisively toward the believers, and their intent was to deny that entirely, to negate its realization, and to reject its occurrence.

So Allah, glory be to Him, answered them with His words: (p. 1227) ﴿They await only one shout, which will seize them while they are disputing﴾. That is: they are not waiting for anything but one shout, which is the blast of Israfil in the Trumpet. ﴿Which will seize them while they are disputing﴾, that is: they will be disputing among themselves about trade and buying and selling and similar matters of the worldly life. This is the first blast, the blast of swooning.

The readers differed concerning yakhiṣṣimūn. Ḥamzah read it with the vowel of the kh sukūn and the ṣ light, from khaṣama, yakhṣimu, and the meaning: some of them dispute with others, so the object is omitted.

Abu ʿAmr and Qalun read it with the vowel of the kh hidden and the ṣ doubled. Nafiʿ, Ibn Kathir, and Hisham did likewise, except that they purified the fatḥah of the kh. The rest read it with a kasrah on the kh and the ṣ doubled.

The original form in all three readings is yakhtaṣimūn, then the tā was assimilated into the ṣād. Nafiʿ, Ibn Kathir, and Hisham fully transferred the fatḥah of the tā to the sākin before it. Abu ʿAmr and Qalun made the vowel of it slight, to indicate that the original of the kh is sukūn. The rest dropped its vowel, so two sākins met, and they gave the first of them a kasrah.

It is related from Abu ʿAmr and Qalun that they both read with the kh sukūn and the ṣ doubled, and this is a problematic reading because two sākins come together in it.

Ubayy read yakhtaṣimūn according to what is the original.

﴿So they will not be able to make a bequest﴾. That is: none of them will be able to bequeath to another his wealth and what is upon him, or he will not be able to instruct him to repent and to desist from sins; rather they will die in their markets and their places. ﴿Nor to their families will they return﴾. That is: to their homes from which they died outside. It has also been said that the meaning is: they will not return to their families with speech. This is information about what will befall them at the first blast.

Then, glory be to Him, informed about what will befall them at the second blast, and He said: ﴿And the Trumpet will be blown, and at once they will be out of their graves to their Lord, hastening﴾. That is, the graves. ﴿Hastening to their Lord﴾, that is, hurrying. Between the two blasts there are forty years.

He expressed the future with the past form when He said ﴿And the Trumpet will be blown﴾, to indicate the certainty of its occurrence, as the people of rhetoric (ahl al-bayān) mentioned, and they made this verse an example of it. And al-ṣūr with the wāw sukūn is the horn into which Israfil blows, as the Sunnah has reported. The application of this name to a horn is well known in the Arabic language, and from it is the statement of the poet:

We struck them on the morning of al-Ghawrayn, a fierce striking, not like the striking of the two horns.

That is: the two horns.

This has passed in Surat al-Anʿam. Qatadah said: al-ṣūr is the plural of ṣūrah, that is: the Trumpet blew the spirits into the forms.

al-Ajdāth is the plural of jadath, which is the grave. It was read al-ajdāf with fāʾ, and that is a dialect, while the eloquent dialect is with the thāʾ (ṯ). And al-nasl and al-naslān mean hastening in walking. It is said: nasala yansilu, like ḍaraba yaḍribu; and it is said yansulu with ḍammah. And from it is the statement of Imru' al-Qays:

So slip my garments from your garments, and they slip off.

And the statement of another:

Like the wolf's stealthy approach, when the night came upon him in cold, so he crept.

﴿They will say: "Woe to us! Who has raised us from our sleeping place?"﴾ That is: they will say at their resurrection from the graves by the blast: "Woe to us!" They call out "woe" to themselves, as if they were saying to it: "Come, for this is the time of your presence." These who speak are the disbelievers.

Ibn al-Anbari said: The pause at "Woe to us!" is a good pause. Then the speech begins with His words: "Who has raised us from our sleeping place?" They thought, because their minds were confused by what they witnessed of the terror, and what entered them of fear, that they had been asleep.

The Jumhur (majority of reciters) read ﴿Ya waylana﴾, while Ibn Abi Layla read *yā waylatanā*, with the added *tāʾ*.

The Jumhur read ﴿man baʿathanā﴾ with the *mīm* of *man* fathah, as an interrogative (*istifhām*, question). Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Dahhak, and Abu Nahik read it with the *mīm* kasrah, making it a preposition (*ḥarf jarr*). This reading is also narrated from ʿAli ibn Abi Talib.

On this reading, *min* is connected to *al-waylu* (woe), and the Jumhur read ﴿man baʿathanā﴾ [as above].

In Ubayy's reading, it is *man ahabbanā*, from *habba min nawmihi*, meaning he woke up from his sleep. Thaʿlab recited the following verse as evidence for this reading:

*"A blaming woman who rose in the night to rebuke me, and no blamer had reproached me before that."*

It is also said that they say this when they see Hell.

Abu Salih said: when the first blast is sounded, the punishment is lifted from the people of the graves, and they rest in a sleep until the second blast.

The clause ﴿This is what the Most Merciful promised, and the messengers spoke the truth﴾ is a reply to them from the angels or from the believers.

It is also said that it is from the speech of the disbelievers, with some of them answering others.

Al-Farraʾ held the first view, and Mujahid the second.

Qatadah said: it is from the words of Allah, glory be to Him. The *mā* in ﴿what the Most Merciful promised﴾ is a relative pronoun (*ism mawṣūl*), and its returning pronoun is omitted. The meaning is: this is what the Most Merciful promised, and in which the messengers spoke the truth. It has already been decreed against you and has come upon you. The two objects of *waʿd* (promise) and *ṣidq* (truth) are omitted, meaning: the Most Merciful promised it to you, and the messengers told you the truth about it. The original form is: "He promised you it and spoke truly to you about it," or "the Most Merciful promised it to us and the messengers spoke truly to us about it," with this being the speech of the believers, or of the disbelievers.

﴿It was but a single blast﴾, meaning that the blast mentioned was only a single cry that Israfil uttered by blowing into the Trumpet. ﴿Then, behold, they will all be brought before Us﴾, meaning they will all be gathered and brought swiftly before Us for reckoning and retribution.

﴿So on that Day no soul will be wronged﴾ in any way, ﴿in anything﴾ that it deserves. That is, nothing will be diminished from the reward of its deeds, and it will not be wronged in any form of injustice. ﴿And you will not be recompensed except for what you used to do﴾, meaning except the recompense for what you used to do in the world, or except for what you used to do, that is, because of it, or in exchange for it.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Abu Malik, concerning His words: "We carried their offspring..." (the verse), that he said: in the ship of Noah, in which He carried of every pair two. ﴿And We created for them from the like of it that they ride﴾: the ships that are in the sea and the rivers, in which people ride.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir recorded similarly from Abu Salih.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Ibn ʿAbbas, concerning His words: ﴿And We created for them from the like of it that they ride﴾, that he said: these are ships, made after the ship of Noah.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also recorded from him concerning the verse, that he said: it means camels, which Allah created as you see. They are the "ships of the desert," on which they carry loads and ride.

Similar was said by al-Hasan, ʿIkrimah, ʿAbd Allah ibn Shaddad, and Mujahid.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Mardawayh recorded from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), concerning His words: ﴿So they will not be able to make a bequest﴾ (the verse), that he said: The Hour will be established while people are in their markets, trading, measuring cloth, milking the she-camels, and occupied with their needs, so they will not be able to make a bequest ﴿nor return to their families﴾.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and ʿAbd Allah ibn Ahmad in *Zawaʾid al-Zuhd*, and Ibn al-Mundhir, recorded from al-Zubayr ibn al-ʿAwwam, who said: The Hour will be established while a man is measuring out cloth and a man is milking a she-camel. Then he recited: ﴿So they will not be able to make a bequest﴾ (the verse).

al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others recorded from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The Hour will certainly be established while two men have spread out their garment, but they will not trade it nor fold it. The Hour will certainly be established while a man is plastering his cistern and will not drink from it. The Hour will certainly be established while a man has departed with the milk of his she-camel and will not taste it. The Hour will certainly be established while a man has raised his morsel to his mouth and will not eat it."

al-Firyabi, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb concerning His words: ﴿Who has raised us from our resting place?﴾, that he said: they sleep a sleep before the resurrection.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 36, verses 41–54 (part 1 of 2):

Then He, glory be to Him and exalted, mentioned another kind of the blessings with which He favoured His servants, and said: ﴿And a sign for them is that We carried their offspring in the laden ship.﴾ That is, a proof and an indication. It has also been said that the meaning of "sign" (āyah) here is a lesson ('ibrah), and it has been said it is a blessing (ni'mah), and it has been said it is a warning (nidhārah).

There is disagreement about the meaning of ﴿that We carried their offspring﴾ and to whom the pronoun refers, since the first pronoun, in His words ﴿And a sign for them﴾, refers either to the people of Makkah, or to the disbelieving Arabs, or to the disbelievers in general who lived in the time of Muhammad (ﷺ). It has been said that the pronoun refers to the past generations, and the meaning is that God carried the offspring of the past generations in the laden ship, so the two pronouns are different.

This was related by al-Nahhas from ʿAli ibn Sulayman al-Akhfash.

It has also been said that both pronouns refer to the disbelievers of Makkah and those like them. The meaning is that God carried their offspring, their children and their weak ones, in the ship, and God bestowed favour upon them by this; that is, they carry them with them in the ships when they travel, or they send their children for trade on their behalf in them.

It has also been said that "offspring" (dhurriyyah) means the fathers and grandfathers, and "the ship" is the ship of Noah. That is, God carried the fathers and grandfathers of these people in the ship of Noah.

Al-Wahidi said: The word dhurriyyah applies to fathers as it applies to children.

Abu ʿUthman said: The fathers were called dhurriyyah because from them comes the begetting of the sons (dharʾ al-abnāʾ). It has also been said that dhurriyyah means the sperm-drops present in the wombs of women, and the wombs are likened to the laden ship. The preferred view is the second, then the first, then the third; as for the fourth, it is extremely remote and strange.

The discussion of dhurriyyah and its derivation has already been treated in full in Surat al-Baqarah. Mashḥūn means filled, loaded. Al-fulk (the ship) is used for the singular and the plural, as has been mentioned in Surat Yunus. The word āyah is in the nominative as a predicate that has been placed first (khabar muqaddam), and the subject is ﴿that We carried﴾, or the reverse, as we have said before.

It has also been said that the pronoun in His words ﴿And a sign for them﴾ refers to the servants mentioned in His words ﴿Alas for the servants!﴾ [Yasin: 30], because after that He said ﴿And a sign for them is the dead earth﴾ [Yasin: 33], and He said ﴿And a sign for them is the night﴾ [Yasin: 37]. Then He said ﴿And a sign for them is that We carried their offspring﴾. It is as if He said: "And a sign for the servants is that We carried the offspring of the servants." It does not necessarily follow that by one of the two pronouns is meant some of them, and by the other pronoun another part of them. This is a good view.

﴿And We created for them of its likeness that which they ride﴾. That is, We created for them, from what resembles the ship, that which they ride; here "mā" is a relative pronoun.

Mujahid, Qatadah, and a group of the people of tafsir said: It is the camels, which He created for them to ride on land, like the ships that are ridden on the sea. The Arabs call camels "the ships of the land." It has also been said that the meaning is: We created for them ships like those ships which they ride. This was said by al-Hasan, al-Dahhak, and Abu Malik.

Al-Nahhas said: This is more correct, because its chain of transmission (ittiṣāl al-isnād) from Ibn ʿAbbas is continuous. It has also been said that it means the ships made after the ship of Noah.

﴿And if We will, We drown them, and there is no one to cry out for them, nor are they rescued﴾. This is part of the same verse in which God bestowed favour upon them. The aspect of the favour is that He did not drown them in the深 depths of the seas, though He is capable of that. The pronoun refers either to the owners of the offspring, or to the offspring, or to all of them, according to the differing views. Al-ṣarīkh means al-muṣrikh (one who cries out for help), and al-muṣrikh is the one who gives aid; that is, there is no helper for them who would aid them if We willed to drown them. It has also been said that al-ṣarīkh means protection.

The meaning of yunqadhūn is: they are delivered. It is said: anqadhahu and istanqadhahu, when he delivered him from something disliked.

﴿Except as a mercy from Us﴾. This is an exception of the type called istithnāʾ mufarragh (an exception in which the excepted element is left unstated), from the most general of the causes; that is: there is no one to cry out for them, and they are not rescued for anything at all, except by a mercy from Us. Thus said al-Kisaʾi, al-Zajjaj, and others. It has also been said that it is an istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ (disjunctive exception), that is: but by a mercy from Us.

It has also been said that it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdariyyah) governed by a verb understood, and the accusative of matāʿan (as a provision) is by conjunction to raḥmatan (mercy), that is: We let them enjoy the life of this world ﴿for a time﴾, and this is death, said Qatadah. Yahya ibn Salam said: until the Resurrection.

﴿And when it is said to them: "Fear what is before you and what is behind you"﴾. That is: what is before you of calamities and misfortunes, for they encompass you, and what is behind you of them.

Qatadah said the meaning of ﴿Fear what is before you﴾ is: of the events concerning those who were before you of the nations, ﴿and what is behind you﴾ is in the Hereafter.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Mujahid said: ﴿what is before you﴾ is what has passed of sins, ﴿and what is behind you﴾ is what remains of them.

It has been said: ﴿what is before you﴾ is the world, ﴿and what is behind you﴾ is the Hereafter; this was said by Sufyan.

al-Tha'labi related the reverse of this view from Ibn ʿAbbas.

It has been said: ﴿what is before you﴾ is what is manifest to you, ﴿and what is behind you﴾ is what is hidden from you. The answer to idhā (when) is omitted, and the estimate is: when it is said to them that, they turn away, as is indicated by ﴿except that they were turning away from them﴾. ﴿So that you may be shown mercy﴾, that is: in hope that you will be shown mercy, or in order that you may be shown mercy, or hoping that you will be shown mercy.

﴿And no sign comes to them from the signs of their Lord except that they were turning away from it﴾. Here mā is negative, and the form of the present tense indicates renewal. The first min is extra for emphasis, and the second min is partitive. The meaning: no sign comes to them, indicating the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) and the soundness of what he called to of monotheism, in any state, except that they were turning away from it.

Its apparent meaning includes both the revealed signs and the cosmic signs. The clause ﴿except that they were turning away from it﴾ is in the place of the accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), as its explanation has passed in more than one place.

What is meant by turning away is not giving attention to it, and abandoning correct reflection upon it. This verse is connected to His words ﴿Alas for the servants! No messenger comes to them except that they used to mock him﴾ [Yasin: 30]; that is: when the messengers came to them they denied them, and when the signs were brought to them they turned away from them.

So their answer was what Allah related about them in His words: ﴿Those who disbelieved said to those who believed﴾, mocking them, and deriding their words: ﴿Shall we feed one whom, if Allah willed, He would feed?﴾ That is: one whom, if Allah willed, He would provide for. They had heard the Muslims saying that the Provider is Allah, and that He enriches whom He wills and impoverishes whom He wills. So it seems they attempted by this statement to put the Muslims in a difficult position, and said: "We agree with the will of Allah, so we do not feed the one whom Allah has not fed." The two objects of *waʿd* (promise) and *ṣidq* (truth) are omitted, meaning: the Most Merciful promised it to you, and the messengers told you the truth about it. The original form is: "He promised you it and spoke truly to you about it," or "the Most Merciful promised it to us and the messengers spoke truly to us about it," with this being the speech of the believers, or of the disbelievers.

﴿It was but a single blast﴾, meaning that the blast mentioned was only a single cry that Israfil uttered by blowing into the Trumpet. ﴿Then, behold, they will all be brought before Us﴾, meaning they will all be gathered and brought swiftly before Us for reckoning and retribution.

﴿So on that Day no soul will be wronged﴾ in any way, ﴿in anything﴾ that it deserves. That is, nothing will be diminished from the reward of its deeds, and it will not be wronged in any form of injustice. ﴿And you will not be recompensed except for what you used to do﴾, meaning except the recompense for what you used to do in the world, or except for what you used to do, that is, because of it, or in exchange for it.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Abu Malik, concerning His words: "We carried their offspring..." (the verse), that he said: in the ship of Noah, in which He carried of every pair two. ﴿And We created for them from the like of it that they ride﴾: the ships that are in the sea and the rivers, in which people ride.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir recorded similarly from Abu Salih.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Ibn ʿAbbas, concerning His words: ﴿And We created for them from the like of it that they ride﴾, that he said: these are ships, made after the ship of Noah.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also recorded from him concerning the verse, that he said: it means camels, which Allah created as you see. They are the "ships of the desert," on which they carry loads and ride.

Similar was said by al-Hasan, ʿIkrimah, ʿAbd Allah ibn Shaddad, and Mujahid.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Mardawayh recorded from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), concerning His words: ﴿So they will not be able to make a bequest﴾ (the verse), that he said: The Hour will be established while people are in their markets, trading, measuring cloth, milking the she-camels, and occupied with their needs, so they will not be able to make a bequest ﴿nor return to their families﴾.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and ʿAbd Allah ibn Ahmad in *Zawaʾid al-Zuhd*, and Ibn al-Mundhir, recorded from al-Zubayr ibn al-ʿAwwam, who said: The Hour will be established while a man is measuring out cloth and a man is milking a she-camel. Then he recited: ﴿So they will not be able to make a bequest﴾ (the verse).

al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others recorded from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The Hour will certainly be established while two men have spread out their garment, but they will not trade it nor fold it. The Hour will certainly be established while a man is plastering his cistern and will not drink from it. The Hour will certainly be established while a man has departed with the milk of his she-camel and will not taste it. The Hour will certainly be established while a man has raised his morsel to his mouth and will not eat it."

al-Firyabi, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb concerning His words: ﴿Who has raised us from our resting place?﴾, that he said: they sleep a sleep before the resurrection.

When God, glory be to Him, mentioned the state of the disbelievers, He followed it with a description of the state of His righteous servants. He placed this among what will be said to the disbelievers on that Day, as an increase in their regret, a completion of their distress, and a completion of the affliction that has befallen them and the misery they have witnessed. When they see what God has prepared for them of various kinds of punishment, and what He has prepared for His friends of various kinds of bliss, this reaches their hearts to a great degree, and it increases the tightness of their chests by an increase that cannot be measured.

The meaning is: the people of the Garden on that Day are occupied with the pleasures they are in, which are such that "no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and it has not occurred to the heart of any human" (cf. Hadith), so they are diverted from concern for the disbelievers and their destination to the Fire, even if they were their relatives.

It is preferable not to restrict the occupation (shughl) to any specific thing.

Qatadah and Mujahid said: their occupation that Day is the deflowering of virgins. Waki' said: their occupation is listening (to music).

Ibn Kaysan said: it is visiting one another. It was also said: their occupation is that they are, that Day, as guests of God.

The Kufans and Ibn 'Amir recited *shughulin* with two dammahs. The rest recited it with a dammah on the shin and a sukun on the ghayn. Both are dialects, as al-Farra' said. Mujahid and Abu al-Simak recited it with two fathahs.

Yazid al-Nahwi and Ibn Hubayrah recited it with a fathah on the shin and a sukun on the ghayn.

The recitation of the majority is *fakihun* with a raf' (nominative), as the predicate of *inna*, with *fi shughulin* (in occupation) related to it, or in a place of nasb as a circumstantial (ḥāl). It is permissible that *fi shughulin* be in a place of raf' as the predicate of *inna*, with *fakihun* as a second predicate.

Al-A'mash and Talhah ibn Musarrif recited *fakihina* with a nasb, as a circumstantial (ḥāl), and *fi shughulin* is the predicate.

Al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far, Abu Haywah, Abu Raja', Shaybah, Qatadah and Mujahid recited *fakuhun*. Al-Farra' said: they are two dialects, like *al-fari-hu* and *al-farihu*, and *al-hadhiru* and *al-hadharu*.

Al-Kisa'i and Abu 'Ubaydah said: *al-fakih* means one who possesses fruit, like *tamir* and *labin*, while *al-fakih* means one who enjoys himself and lives in comfort. Qatadah said: *al-fakihun* means those who are amazed (or pleased with themselves).

Abu Zayd said: it is said, "a man is *fakih*" when he is good-natured and cheerful.

Mujahid and al-Dahhak said as Qatadah said.

Al-Suddi said as al-Kisa'i said.

﴿They and their spouses are in shade, reclining on couches﴾. This sentence is a new (independent) sentence, brought to explain the manner of their occupation and their enjoyment, and to complete it with what increases their joy and delight, namely that their spouses are with them in this same state of reclining on couches. The pronoun *hum* is a subject (mubtada'), *azwajuhum* is conjoined to it, and the predicate is *muttaki'un* (reclining). It is permissible that *hum* be an emphatic pronoun for the pronoun in *fakihun*, with *azwajuhum* conjoined to that pronoun, and the raf' of *muttaki'un* as the predicate of an omitted subject. *Fi zilalin* is related to it or is a circumstantial, and likewise *'ala al-ara'iki*. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that *fi zilalin* be the predicate and *'ala al-ara'iki* be a new sentence.

The majority recited *fi zilalin* with a kasrah on the ẓa' and an alif, which is the plural of *zill* (shade). Ibn Mas'ud, 'Abd ibn 'Umayr, al-A'mash, Yahya ibn Wathhab, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf recited *fi ẓulalin* with a dammah on the ẓa' and without an alif, the plural of *ẓullah* (canopy). On both recitations, what is meant is the furnishings and curtains that shade them like tents and canopied beds. *Al-ara'ik* is the plural of *arikah*, like *safa'in* is the plural of *safinah*, and what is meant by it is the couches that are inside the canopied beds.

Ahmad ibn Yahya Tha'lab said: *al-arikah* is only a couch within a dome.

Muqatil said: what is meant by the shades is the shelters of palaces.

The clause ﴿For them therein is fruit﴾ explains what they enjoy in the Garden of food, drink and the like.

What is meant is abundant fruit of every kind of fruit. ﴿And for them is whatever they ask for﴾. *Ma* here is either the relative pronoun with an omitted returning pronoun, or a qualifying (descriptive) *ma*, or a verbal *ma*. *Yaddda'una* is the present tense of *idda'a*.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: *yaddda'una* means "they wish for" (yatamannawn). The Arabs say, "ask of me whatever you wish," meaning "wish." And "so-and-so is in the best of what he wishes for," meaning "what he desires."

Al-Zajjaj said: it is from *du'a'* (calling), meaning what the people of the Garden call for, and it comes to them, from "I called my servant," so the *iftial* form is in the sense of the simple verb, like *al-ihtimal* in the sense of *al-haml* (carrying) and *al-irtihal* in the sense of *al-rahl* (departing).

It was said: *if'ala* is in the sense of *tafa'ala*, meaning they call one another to it, like their saying *irtamaw* and *taramaw* (they threw at one another).

It was said: the meaning is that whoever among them claims something, it is his, because God has (p-1229) imprinted upon them that none of them claims anything except what is fitting and becoming for him to claim. *Ma* is the subject, its predicate is *lahum* (for them), and the clause is conjoined to what precedes it.

*Yad'una*, with lightening (takhfif), was also recited, and its meaning is clear.

Ibn al-Anbari said: stopping at *yaddda'una* is a good pause.

Then a new start: *salamun* (peace), in the sense of: for them is peace. It was said: *salamun* is the predicate of *ma*, meaning: what is granted is pure, or possessing safety.

Al-Zajjaj said: *salamun* is in the nominative as a substitute (badal) for *ma*, meaning: and for them is that God sends peace upon them, and this is the wish of the people of the Garden. The preferable view is that His saying ﴿and for them is whatever they ask for﴾ be understood in its generality, and this peace enters under it as a primary inclusion, and there is no basis for restricting it to a particular type, even if it is the noblest of its types, in order to realize the sense of generality and to respect what the Qur'anic composition requires.

It was also said: *salamun* is raised as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "peace" is said to them as speech. It was also said: *salamun* is the subject, and its predicate is the verbal noun that governs *qawlan* (speech), meaning: "peace" is said to them as speech. It was also said: its predicate is ﴿from a Lord, Most Merciful﴾. It was also said: the estimation is: "Peace be upon you." This is according to the recitation of the majority.

Ubayy, Ibn Mas'ud and 'Isa recited *salaman* with a nasb, either as a verbal noun (masdar) or as a circumstantial in the sense of "pure." *Al-salam* is either from greeting (tahiyyah) or from safety (salamah).

Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi recited *salmun*, as if he said: "peace" (salm) is theirs, without dispute over it. *Qawlan* is in the accusative as a verbal noun, with an omitted verb, in the sense of: God said that to them as speech, or He says it to them as speech, or it is said to them as speech. ﴿From a Lord, Most Merciful﴾ means: from His side. It was said: God sends a cloud to them with the peace.

Muqatil said: the angels enter upon the people of the Garden from every gate, saying: "Peace be upon you, O people of the Garden, from a Lord, Most Merciful."

﴿And separate yourselves today, O guilty ones﴾. This is by the omission of a verb of speech, corresponding to what was said to the believers. That is: it is said to the guilty: "Separate yourselves," meaning: withdraw, from *maza hu ghayrahu*. It is said: "I separated the thing from the thing" when you isolate it from it and remove it.

Muqatil said: its meaning is: withdraw today, meaning in the Hereafter, from the righteous. Al-Suddi said: be apart. Al-Zajjaj said: stand apart from the believers. Qatadah said: they are removed from every good. Al-Dahhak said: the guilty are separated from one another, so the Jews form one group, the Christians a group, the Magians a group, the Sabians a group, and the idol-worshippers a group. Dawud ibn al-Jarrah said: the Muslims are separated from the guilty, except the people of desires (ahl al-ahwa'), for they will be with the guilty.

Then God rebuked and reproached them with His saying: ﴿Did I not charge you, O children of Adam, that you should not worship Satan﴾. This is among what is said to them.

*Al-'ahd* means charge (wasiyyah), meaning: Did I not command you and inform you, through the tongues of My messengers, that you should not worship Satan, meaning: that you should not obey him.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: Did I not send forth to you, through the tongue of the messengers, O children of Adam? Muqatil said: he means those who were commanded to withdraw. Al-Kisa'i said: *la* is for prohibition. It was also said: what is meant by the covenant here is the pledge taken from them when they were brought forth from the loins of Adam. It was also said: it is what God set up for them of rational proofs in His heavens and His earth.

﴿Indeed he is to you a clear enemy﴾ is a justification for what precedes it, namely the prohibition against obeying Satan and accepting his whispering. ﴿And that worship Me﴾ is conjoined to *an la ta'budu* (that you should not worship). *An* in both places is either explanatory of the covenant, which contains the sense of speech, or it may be verbal in both places, meaning: I did not charge you that you should not worship and that you should worship Me, or: Did I not charge you regarding abandoning the worship of Satan and regarding worshipping Me? ﴿This is a straight path﴾, meaning: the worship of God and His monotheism, or the reference is to the religion of Islam.

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned Satan's enmity toward the children of Adam, saying: ﴿And he has certainly led astray from among you a great multitude﴾. The *lam* is the one that prepares for an oath, and the sentence is a new sentence for rebuke and reproach, meaning: "By God, he has certainly led astray," etc.

Nafi' and 'Asim recited *jibillan* with a kasrah on the jim and the ba', and a shaddah on the lam. Ibn Abi Ishaq, al-Zuhri and Ibn Hurmuz recited it with two dammahs and a shaddah on the lam. Likewise al-Hasan, 'Isa ibn 'Umar and al-Nadr ibn Anas recited it.

Abu Yahya, Hammad ibn Salamah and al-Ashhab al-'Uqayli recited it with a kasrah on the jim, a sukun on the ba', and a lightening of the lam. Al-Nahhas said: the first recitation is the clearest.

The proof of this is that they all recited: ﴿and the earlier generations (al-jibillata al-awwalin)﴾ with a kasrah on the jim and the ba' and a shaddah on the lam.

So *jibillan* is the plural of *jibillah*, and all of them derive from *jabala Allahu al-khalq*, meaning God created them. The meaning of the verse is that Satan has led astray a great many creatures, as Mujahid said.

Qatadah said: large multitudes. Al-Kalbi said: many nations.

Tha'labi said: all the recitations have the same meaning, creation. It was recited *jilan* with a jim and a yā' with two dots below (ya' tahtiyyah).

Al-Dahhak said: a single *jil* is ten thousand, and the many is what no one counts except God, Mighty and Majestic. This recitation was also narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib.

The interrogative particle in His saying ﴿Did you not then use your reason?﴾ is for rebuke and reproach, and the *fa'* is for conjunction with an implied element demanded by the context, as was mentioned in its parallels: meaning, do you witness the traces of punishments? Did you not then use your reason? Or: Did you not use your reason regarding Satan's enmity toward you? Or: Did you not use your reason at all? The majority recited *a-fa-lam takununa ta'qilun* with the second-person address. Talhah and 'Isa recited it in the third person.

﴿This is Gehenna, which you were promised﴾, meaning: it will be said to them when they approach the Fire: "This is Gehenna, which you were promised in the world through the tongues of the messengers." The one who says it to them is the angels.

Then they will say to them: ﴿Burn therein today for what you used to disbelieve﴾, meaning: taste its heat today, enter it, and taste therein various kinds of punishment for what you used to disbelieve, meaning because of your disbelief in God in the world, your obedience to Satan, and your worship of idols. This command is one of humiliation and degradation, like His saying: ﴿Taste, indeed you are the mighty, the noble﴾ [al-Dukhan: 49].

﴿Today We will seal over their mouths﴾. *Al-yawm* is an adverbial complement for what follows it. It was recited *yukhtamu* in the passive voice, and the agent is the prepositional phrase after it.

The commentators said: they deny polytheism and the denial of the messengers, as in their saying: ﴿By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ [al-An'am: 23]. So God will seal their mouths with a seal such that they will not be able to speak. In this there is a shift (iltifat) from address to the third person, to signal that their vile deeds call for turning away from addressing them. Then He said: ﴿And their hands will speak to Us, and their feet will bear witness to what they used to earn﴾, meaning: their hands will speak of what they used to do, and their feet will bear witness against them to what they used to commit.

Al-Jumhur recited *tukallimuna* and *tashhadu*. Talhah ibn Musarrif recited *wa-li-tukallimana* and *wa-li-tashhada* with the *lam* of purpose (lam kay).

The Prophet's (ﷺ) speech in the hadiths and the poetry are translated as they stand.

Some say the purpose of the sealing upon their mouths is that the people of the place of standing (al-mawqif) may recognise them. Others say their mouths were sealed so that the confession would come from their limbs, since the testimony of one who does not speak is more forceful as proof than the testimony of one who does, because it comes in the manner of a miracle. Others say: so that they would know that their limbs, which had been helpers to them in disobeying God, became witnesses against them. What the hands speak is treated as speech and confession, because they were the direct agents of most sins, and the speech of the feet is treated as testimony, because they are present at every act of disobedience. The speech of the doer is a confession, and the speech of one present is testimony. This is a reasoning based on what is most common, for otherwise the feet may also be direct agents of disobedience, just as the hands may be.

﴿And if We willed, We would have obliterated their eyes﴾, meaning: We would have removed their eyes and made them such that no slit and no eyelid would appear on them.

Al-Kisa'i said: "ṭamasa, yaṭmusu, and yaṭmisu; the maṭmūs and the ṭamīs, according to the lexicographers, is the one who has no slit in his eyes," as in His words: ﴿And if God had willed, He would have taken away their hearing and their sight﴾ [al-Baqarah: 20]. The object of the willing is omitted: that is, if We willed to obliterate their eyes, We would have obliterated them.

Al-Suddi and al-Hasan said: the meaning is that We would have left them blind, wandering, unable to see the path of guidance. Ibn Jarir chose this view. ﴿So they would race toward the path﴾ is coordinated with "We would have obliterated" — that is, they would hasten to the path to cross it and proceed along it. The word "al-ṣirāṭ" (the path) is in the accusative by the removal of the preposition, meaning: they would race toward it. ʿAṭāʾ, Muqātil and Qatādah said: the meaning is, if We willed, We would have gouged out their eyes and blinded them to their error.

And We would have turned their sight from misguidance to guidance, so they would see their right course, be guided, and hasten to the path of the Hereafter. The meaning of ﴿Then how would they see?﴾ is: how would they see the path and handle its travel well, when they have no sight?

ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar read "fa-istabaqū" in the imperative form, meaning: it will be said to them, "Race!" In this there is a threat to them.

Then He repeated the threat to them, saying: ﴿And if We willed, We would have transformed them in their places﴾. Al-maskh is the alteration of the creation into a stone or something else of inanimate matter, or into a beast. Al-makāna means the place; that is, if We willed, We would have changed their form in the place where they are.

It is said: al-makāna is more specific than al-makān, like al-muqāma and al-muqām.

Al-Hasan said: that is, We would have made them sit still. ﴿So they would not be able to advance or return﴾: that is, they would not be able to go or come.

Al-Hasan said: they would not be able to move forward before them, nor turn back behind them, and likewise inanimate matter does not advance or retreat.

It is said: the meaning is, if We willed, We would have destroyed them in their dwellings. It is also said: We would have transformed them in the place where they committed the disobedience.

Yahya ibn Sallam said: all of this is on the Day of Resurrection.

The majority read ﴿ʿalā makānatihim﴾ in the singular. Al-Hasan, al-Sulamī, Zirr ibn Ḥubaysh and Abū Bakr (on the authority of ʿĀṣim) read "makānātihim" in the plural.

The majority read "muḍiyyan" with a ḍammah on the mīm. Abū Ḥaywah read "maḍiyyan" with a fatḥah on it, and it is narrated from him that he read it with a kasrah; this reading is also reported from al-Kisa'i.

It is said: the meaning is, they would not be able to return, so the verb was placed in the position of the verbal noun for the sake of the rhyming verse-ending (fāṣila). It is said: maḍā yamḍī muḍiyyan, when he went along the earth; and rajaʿa yarjiʿu rujūʿan, when he came back from where he had come.

﴿And whomever We grant long life, We reverse him in creation﴾. The majority read "nankusuhu" with a fatḥah on the first nūn, sukūn on the second, and a ḍammah on the kāf, lightened. ʿĀṣim and Ḥamzah read it with a ḍammah on the first nūn, a fatḥah on the second, and a kasrah on the kāf, doubled.
