Ibn Mas'ud, 'Abd ibn 'Umayr, al-A'mash, Yahya ibn Wathhab, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf recited *fi ẓulalin* with a dammah on the ẓa' and without an alif, the plural of *ẓullah* (canopy). On both recitations, what is meant is the furnishings and curtains that shade them like tents and canopied beds. *Al-ara'ik* is the plural of *arikah*, like *safa'in* is the plural of *safinah*, and what is meant by it is the couches that are inside the canopied beds.

Ahmad ibn Yahya Tha'lab said: *al-arikah* is only a couch within a dome.

Muqatil said: what is meant by the shades is the shelters of palaces.

The clause ﴿For them therein is fruit﴾ explains what they enjoy in the Garden of food, drink and the like.

What is meant is abundant fruit of every kind of fruit. ﴿And for them is whatever they ask for﴾. *Ma* here is either the relative pronoun with an omitted returning pronoun, or a qualifying (descriptive) *ma*, or a verbal *ma*. *Yaddda'una* is the present tense of *idda'a*.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: *yaddda'una* means "they wish for" (yatamannawn). The Arabs say, "ask of me whatever you wish," meaning "wish." And "so-and-so is in the best of what he wishes for," meaning "what he desires."

Al-Zajjaj said: it is from *du'a'* (calling), meaning what the people of the Garden call for, and it comes to them, from "I called my servant," so the *iftial* form is in the sense of the simple verb, like *al-ihtimal* in the sense of *al-haml* (carrying) and *al-irtihal* in the sense of *al-rahl* (departing).

It was said: *if'ala* is in the sense of *tafa'ala*, meaning they call one another to it, like their saying *irtamaw* and *taramaw* (they threw at one another).

It was said: the meaning is that whoever among them claims something, it is his, because God has (p-1229) imprinted upon them that none of them claims anything except what is fitting and becoming for him to claim. *Ma* is the subject, its predicate is *lahum* (for them), and the clause is conjoined to what precedes it.

*Yad'una*, with lightening (takhfif), was also recited, and its meaning is clear.

Ibn al-Anbari said: stopping at *yaddda'una* is a good pause.

Then a new start: *salamun* (peace), in the sense of: for them is peace. It was said: *salamun* is the predicate of *ma*, meaning: what is granted is pure, or possessing safety.

Al-Zajjaj said: *salamun* is in the nominative as a substitute (badal) for *ma*, meaning: and for them is that God sends peace upon them, and this is the wish of the people of the Garden. The preferable view is that His saying ﴿and for them is whatever they ask for﴾ be understood in its generality, and this peace enters under it as a primary inclusion, and there is no basis for restricting it to a particular type, even if it is the noblest of its types, in order to realize the sense of generality and to respect what the Qur'anic composition requires.

It was also said: *salamun* is raised as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "peace" is said to them as speech. It was also said: *salamun* is the subject, and its predicate is the verbal noun that governs *qawlan* (speech), meaning: "peace" is said to them as speech. It was also said: its predicate is ﴿from a Lord, Most Merciful﴾. It was also said: the estimation is: "Peace be upon you." This is according to the recitation of the majority.

Ubayy, Ibn Mas'ud and 'Isa recited *salaman* with a nasb, either as a verbal noun (masdar) or as a circumstantial in the sense of "pure." *Al-salam* is either from greeting (tahiyyah) or from safety (salamah).

Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi recited *salmun*, as if he said: "peace" (salm) is theirs, without dispute over it. *Qawlan* is in the accusative as a verbal noun, with an omitted verb, in the sense of: God said that to them as speech, or He says it to them as speech, or it is said to them as speech. ﴿From a Lord, Most Merciful﴾ means: from His side. It was said: God sends a cloud to them with the peace.

Muqatil said: the angels enter upon the people of the Garden from every gate, saying: "Peace be upon you, O people of the Garden, from a Lord, Most Merciful."

﴿And separate yourselves today, O guilty ones﴾. This is by the omission of a verb of speech, corresponding to what was said to the believers. That is: it is said to the guilty: "Separate yourselves," meaning: withdraw, from *maza hu ghayrahu*. It is said: "I separated the thing from the thing" when you isolate it from it and remove it.

Muqatil said: its meaning is: withdraw today, meaning in the Hereafter, from the righteous. Al-Suddi said: be apart. Al-Zajjaj said: stand apart from the believers. Qatadah said: they are removed from every good. Al-Dahhak said: the guilty are separated from one another, so the Jews form one group, the Christians a group, the Magians a group, the Sabians a group, and the idol-worshippers a group. Dawud ibn al-Jarrah said: the Muslims are separated from the guilty, except the people of desires (ahl al-ahwa'), for they will be with the guilty.

Then God rebuked and reproached them with His saying: ﴿Did I not charge you, O children of Adam, that you should not worship Satan﴾. This is among what is said to them.

*Al-'ahd* means charge (wasiyyah), meaning: Did I not command you and inform you, through the tongues of My messengers, that you should not worship Satan, meaning: that you should not obey him.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: Did I not send forth to you, through the tongue of the messengers, O children of Adam? Muqatil said: he means those who were commanded to withdraw. Al-Kisa'i said: *la* is for prohibition. It was also said: what is meant by the covenant here is the pledge taken from them when they were brought forth from the loins of Adam. It was also said: it is what God set up for them of rational proofs in His heavens and His earth.

﴿Indeed he is to you a clear enemy﴾ is a justification for what precedes it, namely the prohibition against obeying Satan and accepting his whispering. ﴿And that worship Me﴾ is conjoined to *an la ta'budu* (that you should not worship). *An* in both places is either explanatory of the covenant, which contains the sense of speech, or it may be verbal in both places, meaning: I did not charge you that you should not worship and that you should worship Me, or: Did I not charge you regarding abandoning the worship of Satan and regarding worshipping Me? ﴿This is a straight path﴾, meaning: the worship of God and His monotheism, or the reference is to the religion of Islam.

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned Satan's enmity toward the children of Adam, saying: ﴿And he has certainly led astray from among you a great multitude﴾. The *lam* is the one that prepares for an oath, and the sentence is a new sentence for rebuke and reproach, meaning: "By God, he has certainly led astray," etc.

Nafi' and 'Asim recited *jibillan* with a kasrah on the jim and the ba', and a shaddah on the lam. Ibn Abi Ishaq, al-Zuhri and Ibn Hurmuz recited it with two dammahs and a shaddah on the lam. Likewise al-Hasan, 'Isa ibn 'Umar and al-Nadr ibn Anas recited it.

Abu Yahya, Hammad ibn Salamah and al-Ashhab al-'Uqayli recited it with a kasrah on the jim, a sukun on the ba', and a lightening of the lam. Al-Nahhas said: the first recitation is the clearest.

The proof of this is that they all recited: ﴿and the earlier generations (al-jibillata al-awwalin)﴾ with a kasrah on the jim and the ba' and a shaddah on the lam.

So *jibillan* is the plural of *jibillah*, and all of them derive from *jabala Allahu al-khalq*, meaning God created them. The meaning of the verse is that Satan has led astray a great many creatures, as Mujahid said.

Qatadah said: large multitudes. Al-Kalbi said: many nations.

Tha'labi said: all the recitations have the same meaning, creation. It was recited *jilan* with a jim and a yā' with two dots below (ya' tahtiyyah).

Al-Dahhak said: a single *jil* is ten thousand, and the many is what no one counts except God, Mighty and Majestic. This recitation was also narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib.

The interrogative particle in His saying ﴿Did you not then use your reason?﴾ is for rebuke and reproach, and the *fa'* is for conjunction with an implied element demanded by the context, as was mentioned in its parallels: meaning, do you witness the traces of punishments? Did you not then use your reason? Or: Did you not use your reason regarding Satan's enmity toward you? Or: Did you not use your reason at all? The majority recited *a-fa-lam takununa ta'qilun* with the second-person address. Talhah and 'Isa recited it in the third person.

﴿This is Gehenna, which you were promised﴾, meaning: it will be said to them when they approach the Fire: "This is Gehenna, which you were promised in the world through the tongues of the messengers." The one who says it to them is the angels.

Then they will say to them: ﴿Burn therein today for what you used to disbelieve﴾, meaning: taste its heat today, enter it, and taste therein various kinds of punishment for what you used to disbelieve, meaning because of your disbelief in God in the world, your obedience to Satan, and your worship of idols. This command is one of humiliation and degradation, like His saying: ﴿Taste, indeed you are the mighty, the noble﴾ [al-Dukhan: 49].

﴿Today We will seal over their mouths﴾. *Al-yawm* is an adverbial complement for what follows it. It was recited *yukhtamu* in the passive voice, and the agent is the prepositional phrase after it.

The commentators said: they deny polytheism and the denial of the messengers, as in their saying: ﴿By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ [al-An'am: 23]. So God will seal their mouths with a seal such that they will not be able to speak. In this there is a shift (iltifat) from address to the third person, to signal that their vile deeds call for turning away from addressing them. Then He said: ﴿And their hands will speak to Us, and their feet will bear witness to what they used to earn﴾, meaning: their hands will speak of what they used to do, and their feet will bear witness against them to what they used to commit.

Al-Jumhur recited *tukallimuna* and *tashhadu*. Talhah ibn Musarrif recited *wa-li-tukallimana* and *wa-li-tashhada* with the *lam* of purpose (lam kay).

The Prophet's (ﷺ) speech in the hadiths and the poetry are translated as they stand.

Some say the purpose of the sealing upon their mouths is that the people of the place of standing (al-mawqif) may recognise them. Others say their mouths were sealed so that the confession would come from their limbs, since the testimony of one who does not speak is more forceful as proof than the testimony of one who does, because it comes in the manner of a miracle. Others say: so that they would know that their limbs, which had been helpers to them in disobeying God, became witnesses against them. What the hands speak is treated as speech and confession, because they were the direct agents of most sins, and the speech of the feet is treated as testimony, because they are present at every act of disobedience. The speech of the doer is a confession, and the speech of one present is testimony. This is a reasoning based on what is most common, for otherwise the feet may also be direct agents of disobedience, just as the hands may be.

﴿And if We willed, We would have obliterated their eyes﴾, meaning: We would have removed their eyes and made them such that no slit and no eyelid would appear on them.

Al-Kisa'i said: "ṭamasa, yaṭmusu, and yaṭmisu; the maṭmūs and the ṭamīs, according to the lexicographers, is the one who has no slit in his eyes," as in His words: ﴿And if God had willed, He would have taken away their hearing and their sight﴾ [al-Baqarah: 20]. The object of the willing is omitted: that is, if We willed to obliterate their eyes, We would have obliterated them.

Al-Suddi and al-Hasan said: the meaning is that We would have left them blind, wandering, unable to see the path of guidance. Ibn Jarir chose this view. ﴿So they would race toward the path﴾ is coordinated with "We would have obliterated" — that is, they would hasten to the path to cross it and proceed along it. The word "al-ṣirāṭ" (the path) is in the accusative by the removal of the preposition, meaning: they would race toward it. ʿAṭāʾ, Muqātil and Qatādah said: the meaning is, if We willed, We would have gouged out their eyes and blinded them to their error.

And We would have turned their sight from misguidance to guidance, so they would see their right course, be guided, and hasten to the path of the Hereafter. The meaning of ﴿Then how would they see?﴾ is: how would they see the path and handle its travel well, when they have no sight?

ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar read "fa-istabaqū" in the imperative form, meaning: it will be said to them, "Race!" In this there is a threat to them.

Then He repeated the threat to them, saying: ﴿And if We willed, We would have transformed them in their places﴾. Al-maskh is the alteration of the creation into a stone or something else of inanimate matter, or into a beast. Al-makāna means the place; that is, if We willed, We would have changed their form in the place where they are.

It is said: al-makāna is more specific than al-makān, like al-muqāma and al-muqām.

Al-Hasan said: that is, We would have made them sit still. ﴿So they would not be able to advance or return﴾: that is, they would not be able to go or come.

Al-Hasan said: they would not be able to move forward before them, nor turn back behind them, and likewise inanimate matter does not advance or retreat.

It is said: the meaning is, if We willed, We would have destroyed them in their dwellings. It is also said: We would have transformed them in the place where they committed the disobedience.

Yahya ibn Sallam said: all of this is on the Day of Resurrection.

The majority read ﴿ʿalā makānatihim﴾ in the singular. Al-Hasan, al-Sulamī, Zirr ibn Ḥubaysh and Abū Bakr (on the authority of ʿĀṣim) read "makānātihim" in the plural.

The majority read "muḍiyyan" with a ḍammah on the mīm. Abū Ḥaywah read "maḍiyyan" with a fatḥah on it, and it is narrated from him that he read it with a kasrah; this reading is also reported from al-Kisa'i.

It is said: the meaning is, they would not be able to return, so the verb was placed in the position of the verbal noun for the sake of the rhyming verse-ending (fāṣila). It is said: maḍā yamḍī muḍiyyan, when he went along the earth; and rajaʿa yarjiʿu rujūʿan, when he came back from where he had come.

﴿And whomever We grant long life, We reverse him in creation﴾. The majority read "nankusuhu" with a fatḥah on the first nūn, sukūn on the second, and a ḍammah on the kāf, lightened. ʿĀṣim and Ḥamzah read it with a ḍammah on the first nūn, a fatḥah on the second, and a kasrah on the kāf, doubled.

The meaning is: whoever We prolong his life, We change his creation, and make him the opposite of what he was at first in strength and freshness.

Al-Zajjāj said: the meaning is, whoever We prolong his life, We reverse his disposition, so that weakness replaces strength, and senility replaces youth. A similar verse is His words, glory be to Him: ﴿And among you is one who is returned to the most abject age, so that after knowledge he knows nothing﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 5], and His words: ﴿Then We returned him to the lowest of the low﴾ [al-Tīn: 5]. The meaning of ﴿Will you not then use your reason?﴾ is: will you not know by your intellects that whoever is capable of that is capable of the resurrection and the rising up?

The majority read "yaʿqilūn" with the third-person (yā’ taḥtiyya). Nāfiʿ and Ibn Dhakwān read it with the second-person (tā’ fawqiyya), as an address.

When the disbelievers of Makkah said that the Qur'an is poetry, and that Muhammad is a poet, God refuted them with His words: ﴿And We did not teach him poetry﴾. The meaning is the negation that the Qur'an is poetry. Then He negated that the Prophet is a poet, saying: ﴿nor is it befitting for him﴾, that is, poetry is not valid for him, does not come to him, and would not be easy for him even if he sought it or wished to say it. Rather, when the Prophet (ﷺ) wished to recite a line that a poet had composed, quoting it as an example, he would break its metre. When he recited the well-known line of Ṭarafah ibn al-ʿAbd, which is his saying:

"Days will reveal to you what you did not know, and there will come to you with news one whom you have not supplied."

He said: "and there will come to you with news one whom you have not supplied." And on another occasion he recited the saying of al-ʿAbbās ibn Mirdās al-Sulamī:

"Will you make my plunder and the plunder of ʿUbayd / between ʿUyaynah and al-Aqraʿ?"

He said: "between al-Aqraʿ and ʿUyaynah." And he also recited:

"Islam and grey hair are enough for a man as a restraint."

Abū Bakr said: "O Messenger of God, the poet only said: 'Grey hair and Islam are enough for a man as a restraint.'" He said: "I bear witness that you are the Messenger of God. God, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And We did not teach him poetry, nor is it befitting for him﴾."

Such things have occurred from him (ﷺ) many times.

Al-Khalil said: poetry was more beloved to the Messenger of God than much of speech, but it did not come easily to him. End of quote.

The wisdom of his not being taught poetry and his not being able to do it is to complete the proof and to refute the doubt, just as God made him unlettered, unable to read or write. As for what is narrated from him (ﷺ) of his saying:

"Are you anything but a finger that bled, and in the way of God what you have suffered?"

And his saying:

"I am the Prophet, there is no lie; I am the son of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib."

and the like, these are accidental coincidences that occurred without intent, as happens in some verses of the Qur'an. They are not poetry, nor is poetry intended by them. Rather it happened by chance, as occurs in much of people's speech, for people may speak in a way that, if one considered it, would fall into the metre of poetry, yet they do not count it as poetry. Such is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿You will not attain righteousness until you spend of what you love﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 92], and His saying: ﴿And basins like cisterns, and fixed cooking pots﴾ [Saba': 13]. Moreover, al-Akhfash said that the saying "I am the Prophet, there is no lie" is not poetry.

Al-Khalil said in Kitāb al-ʿAyn: what comes as rhymed prose (sajʿ) in two halves is not poetry.

Ibn al-ʿArabī said: the more apparent state of his (ﷺ) speech is that he said "lā kadhibu" with the ḍammah on the bāʾ of kadhib, and with the kasrah on the bāʾ of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib.

Al-Naḥḥās said: some said that the transmission is according to the inflection (iʿrāb), and if it is according to the inflection, it is not poetry, because if he opens the bāʾ of the first, or makes it dammed, or gives it tanwīn, and kasrahs the bāʾ of the second, it goes out of the metre of poetry.

It is said: the pronoun in "lahu" (for him) refers to the Qur'an, that is: it is not befitting for the Qur'an to be poetry. ﴿It is only a reminder﴾, that is, the Qur'an is only a reminder among reminders and an admonition among admonitions. ﴿And a clear Qur'an﴾, that is, a book among the heavenly books of God, comprising the legal rulings of the Sharia.

﴿That it may warn whoever is living﴾, that is, that the Qur'an may warn whoever is living, that is, whose heart is sound, accepting the truth and refusing falsehood; or that the Messenger may warn whoever is living.

The majority read with the yāʾ taḥtiyya. Nāfiʿ and Ibn ʿĀmir read with the tāʾ fawqiyya. On the first reading the intended one is the Qur'an, and on the second the intended one is the Prophet (ﷺ). ﴿And the word may be fulfilled against the disbelievers﴾, that is, the word of punishment is due against those who persist in disbelief and refuse to believe in God and His messengers.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Abi al-Dunya, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Ḥātim and Ibn Mardawayh have reported through various chains from Ibn ʿAbbās concerning His words ﴿Busy in joy, they are delighted﴾, that he said: "In the deflowering of virgins."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Abi al-Dunya, ʿAbd Allah ibn Aḥmad in Zawāʾid al-Zuhd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn Masʿud concerning the verse that he said: "The deflowering of virgins occupied them."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd reported from ʿIkrimah and Qatādah the same.

ʿAbd Allah ibn Aḥmad in Zawāʾid al-Zuhd reported from Ibn ʿUmar that he said: "Whenever the believer wishes for a wife, he finds her a virgin."

Something similar has been narrated as a hadith traced to the Prophet from Abū Saʿīd, traced to the Prophet, in al-Ṭabarānī's al-Ṣaghīr and Abū al-Shaykh's al-ʿAẓamah.

Something similar was also narrated from Abū Hurayrah traced to the Prophet, in al-Diyāʾ al-Maqdisī's Ṣifat al-Jannah.

Ibn Abi Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās concerning His words ﴿Busy in joy, they are delighted﴾, that he said: "Striking the lutes."

Abū Ḥātim said: "This is perhaps an error on the part of the listener; what it actually is, is the deflowering of virgins."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Ḥātim reported from him that he said: "Fākihūn means joyful."

Ibn Mājah, Ibn Abi al-Dunya in Ṣifat al-Jannah, al-Bazzār, Ibn Abi Ḥātim, al-Ājurrī in al-Ruʾyah, and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Jābir that he said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "While the people of Paradise are in their bliss, a light shines upon them, so they raise their heads, and behold, the Lord has looked down upon them from above them, and says: 'Peace be upon you, O people of Paradise.' This is the saying of God: ﴿Peace, a word from a Lord, Most Merciful﴾. He said: So He looks at them and they look at Him, and they do not turn to anything of the bliss as long as they are looking at Him, until He veils Himself from them, and His light and His blessing remain upon them in their dwellings." Ibn Kathir said: "In its chain there is something to be considered."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās concerning the verse that he said: "Indeed God Himself greets them with peace."

Aḥmad, Muslim, al-Nasāʾī, al-Bazzār, Ibn Abi al-Dunya in al-Tawbah (and the wording is his), Ibn Abi Ḥātim, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqī in al-Asmāʾ wa al-Ṣifāt reported from Anas concerning His words ﴿Today We will seal upon their mouths﴾, that he said: "We were with the Prophet (ﷺ), and he laughed until his molar teeth showed. He said: 'Do you know what I laughed at?' We said: 'No, O Messenger of God.' He said: 'At the servant's address to his Lord, saying: O Lord, did You not protect me from injustice? He says: Yes. He says: Indeed I do not accept against myself except a witness from myself. He says: Sufficient is your own self today as a witness against you, and the noble recording angels as witnesses. Then his mouth is sealed, and it is said to his limbs: Speak! So they speak of his deeds. Then he is left between himself and speech, and he says: Away with you, and ruin, it was on your account that I was contending.'"

Muslim, al-Tirmidhī, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqī reported from Abū Saʿīd and Abū Hurayrah, both of whom said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The servant meets his Lord, and God says: Say, did I not honour you, and make you a leader, and marry you, and subject to you horses and camels, and leave you to lead and pasture? He says: Yes, O Lord. He says: Did you think that you would meet Me? He says: No. He says: Then I forget you as you forgot Me. Then he meets the second and says the same, then he meets the third and says the same to him. He says: I believed in You, and in Your Book, and in Your Messenger, and I prayed, fasted, and gave charity, and he praises himself with good as far as he can. He says: Shall We not send our witness against you? He thinks to himself: Who is it that will testify against me? So his mouth is sealed, and it is said to his thigh: Speak! So his thigh speaks, and his mouth, and his bones, of his deeds, whatever they were. That is so that he has no excuse for himself, and that is the hypocrite, and that is the one with whom God is angry."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Ḥātim reported a similar hadith from Abū Mūsā.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 36, verses 55–70 (part 3 of 3):

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying: ﴿And if We willed, We would have obliterated their eyes﴾ he said: "We would have blinded them and led them astray from guidance." ﴿Then how would they see?﴾ meaning: how would they be guided?

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him regarding His saying: ﴿And if We willed, We would have transformed them﴾ he said: "We would have destroyed them." ﴿In their places﴾ he said: "In their dwellings."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related, saying: "It reached me that it was said to ʿAisha: 'Did the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ever recite any poetry?' She said: 'It was the most hateful speech to him, except that he would recite a verse of the brother of Banu Qays, and he would place its last part first, saying: "And there comes to you one who has not provided you with news."' Abu Bakr said: 'It is not like this.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Indeed, by Allah, I am not a poet, nor is it fitting for me.'" This refutes what we related earlier from al-Khalil, that poetry was more beloved to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) than much of speech.

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ahmad related from her, she said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was slow to receive news, he would recite the verse of Tarafah:
"And there comes to you with news one who has not provided."

Ibn Abi Shaybah related "from Ibn ʿAbbas, he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would recite from the poems:
"And there comes to you with news one who has not provided."

al-Bayhaqi related in his Sunan "from ʿAisha, she said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) never composed a line of poetry except one verse:
"Be optimistic with what you desire, and it will be; for rarely is it said of anything that it has happened but that it came true."
ʿAisha said: "He did not say 'tahaqquqan' (realization), lest he inflect it and it become poetry." Its chain is thus: He said: Abu ʿUbayd Allah al-Hafiz informed us, meaning al-Hakim; Abu Hafs ibn Ahmad ibn Nuʿaym narrated to us; Abu Muhammad ʿAbd Allah ibn Hilal al-Nahwi al-Darir narrated to us; ʿAli ibn ʿAmr al-Ansari narrated to us; Sufyan ibn ʿUyaynah narrated to us from al-Zuhri, from ʿUrwah, from ʿAisha, and he mentioned it."

Al-Mizzi was asked about this hadith and said: "It is munkar (rejected). He did not know the teacher of al-Hakim, nor the blind man (al-Darir)."

When God, glory be to Him, mentioned the state of the disbelievers, He followed it with a description of the state of His righteous servants. He placed this among what will be said to the disbelievers on that Day, as an increase in their regret, a completion of their distress, and a completion of the affliction that has befallen them and the misery they have witnessed. When they see what God has prepared for them of various kinds of punishment, and what He has prepared for His friends of various kinds of bliss, this reaches their hearts to a great degree, and it increases the tightness of their chests by an increase that cannot be measured.

The meaning is: the people of the Garden on that Day are occupied with the pleasures they are in, which are such that "no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and it has not occurred to the heart of any human" (cf. Hadith), so they are diverted from concern for the disbelievers and their destination to the Fire, even if they were their relatives.

It is preferable not to restrict the occupation (shughl) to any specific thing.

Qatadah and Mujahid said: their occupation that Day is the deflowering of virgins. Waki' said: their occupation is listening (to music).

Ibn Kaysan said: it is visiting one another. It was also said: their occupation is that they are, that Day, as guests of God.

The Kufans and Ibn 'Amir recited *shughulin* with two dammahs. The rest recited it with a dammah on the shin and a sukun on the ghayn. Both are dialects, as al-Farra' said. Mujahid and Abu al-Simak recited it with two fathahs.

Yazid al-Nahwi and Ibn Hubayrah recited it with a fathah on the shin and a sukun on the ghayn.

The recitation of the majority is *fakihun* with a raf' (nominative), as the predicate of *inna*, with *fi shughulin* (in occupation) related to it, or in a place of nasb as a circumstantial (ḥāl). It is permissible that *fi shughulin* be in a place of raf' as the predicate of *inna*, with *fakihun* as a second predicate.

Al-A'mash and Talhah ibn Musarrif recited *fakihina* with a nasb, as a circumstantial (ḥāl), and *fi shughulin* is the predicate.

Al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far, Abu Haywah, Abu Raja', Shaybah, Qatadah and Mujahid recited *fakuhun*. Al-Farra' said: they are two dialects, like *al-fari-hu* and *al-farihu*, and *al-hadhiru* and *al-hadharu*.

Al-Kisa'i and Abu 'Ubaydah said: *al-fakih* means one who possesses fruit, like *tamir* and *labin*, while *al-fakih* means one who enjoys himself and lives in comfort. Qatadah said: *al-fakihun* means those who are amazed (or pleased with themselves).

Abu Zayd said: it is said, "a man is *fakih*" when he is good-natured and cheerful.

Mujahid and al-Dahhak said as Qatadah said.

Al-Suddi said as al-Kisa'i said.

﴿They and their spouses are in shade, reclining on couches﴾. This sentence is a new (independent) sentence, brought to explain the manner of their occupation and their enjoyment, and to complete it with what increases their joy and delight, namely that their spouses are with them in this same state of reclining on couches. The pronoun *hum* is a subject (mubtada'), *azwajuhum* is conjoined to it, and the predicate is *muttaki'un* (reclining). It is permissible that *hum* be an emphatic pronoun for the pronoun in *fakihun*, with *azwajuhum* conjoined to that pronoun, and the raf' of *muttaki'un* as the predicate of an omitted subject. *Fi zilalin* is related to it or is a circumstantial, and likewise *'ala al-ara'iki*. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that *fi zilalin* be the predicate and *'ala al-ara'iki* be a new sentence.

The majority recited *fi zilalin* with a kasrah on the ẓa' and an alif, which is the plural of *zill* (shade). Ibn Mas'ud, 'Abd ibn 'Umayr, al-A'mash, Yahya ibn Wathhab, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf recited *fi ẓulalin* with a dammah on the ẓa' and without an alif, the plural of *ẓullah* (canopy). On both recitations, what is meant is the furnishings and curtains that shade them like tents and canopied beds. *Al-ara'ik* is the plural of *arikah*, like *safa'in* is the plural of *safinah*, and what is meant by it is the couches that are inside the canopied beds.

Ahmad ibn Yahya Tha'lab said: *al-arikah* is only a couch within a dome.

Muqatil said: what is meant by the shades is the shelters of palaces.

The clause ﴿For them therein is fruit﴾ explains what they enjoy in the Garden of food, drink and the like.

What is meant is abundant fruit of every kind of fruit. ﴿And for them is whatever they ask for﴾. *Ma* here is either the relative pronoun with an omitted returning pronoun, or a qualifying (descriptive) *ma*, or a verbal *ma*. *Yaddda'una* is the present tense of *idda'a*.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: *yaddda'una* means "they wish for" (yatamannawn). The Arabs say, "ask of me whatever you wish," meaning "wish." And "so-and-so is in the best of what he wishes for," meaning "what he desires."

Al-Zajjaj said: it is from *du'a'* (calling), meaning what the people of the Garden call for, and it comes to them, from "I called my servant," so the *iftial* form is in the sense of the simple verb, like *al-ihtimal* in the sense of *al-haml* (carrying) and *al-irtihal* in the sense of *al-rahl* (departing).

It was said: *if'ala* is in the sense of *tafa'ala*, meaning they call one another to it, like their saying *irtamaw* and *taramaw* (they threw at one another).

It was said: the meaning is that whoever among them claims something, it is his, because God has (p-1229) imprinted upon them that none of them claims anything except what is fitting and becoming for him to claim. *Ma* is the subject, its predicate is *lahum* (for them), and the clause is conjoined to what precedes it.

*Yad'una*, with lightening (takhfif), was also recited, and its meaning is clear.

Ibn al-Anbari said: stopping at *yaddda'una* is a good pause.

Then a new start: *salamun* (peace), in the sense of: for them is peace. It was said: *salamun* is the predicate of *ma*, meaning: what is granted is pure, or possessing safety.

Al-Zajjaj said: *salamun* is in the nominative as a substitute (badal) for *ma*, meaning: and for them is that God sends peace upon them, and this is the wish of the people of the Garden. The preferable view is that His saying ﴿and for them is whatever they ask for﴾ be understood in its generality, and this peace enters under it as a primary inclusion, and there is no basis for restricting it to a particular type, even if it is the noblest of its types, in order to realize the sense of generality and to respect what the Qur'anic composition requires.

It was also said: *salamun* is raised as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "peace" is said to them as speech. It was also said: *salamun* is the subject, and its predicate is the verbal noun that governs *qawlan* (speech), meaning: "peace" is said to them as speech. It was also said: its predicate is ﴿from a Lord, Most Merciful﴾. It was also said: the estimation is: "Peace be upon you." This is according to the recitation of the majority.

Ubayy, Ibn Mas'ud and 'Isa recited *salaman* with a nasb, either as a verbal noun (masdar) or as a circumstantial in the sense of "pure." *Al-salam* is either from greeting (tahiyyah) or from safety (salamah).

Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi recited *salmun*, as if he said: "peace" (salm) is theirs, without dispute over it. *Qawlan* is in the accusative as a verbal noun, with an omitted verb, in the sense of: God said that to them as speech, or He says it to them as speech, or it is said to them as speech. ﴿From a Lord, Most Merciful﴾ means: from His side. It was said: God sends a cloud to them with the peace.

Muqatil said: the angels enter upon the people of the Garden from every gate, saying: "Peace be upon you, O people of the Garden, from a Lord, Most Merciful."

﴿And separate yourselves today, O guilty ones﴾. This is by the omission of a verb of speech, corresponding to what was said to the believers. That is: it is said to the guilty: "Separate yourselves," meaning: withdraw, from *maza hu ghayrahu*. It is said: "I separated the thing from the thing" when you isolate it from it and remove it.

Muqatil said: its meaning is: withdraw today, meaning in the Hereafter, from the righteous. Al-Suddi said: be apart. Al-Zajjaj said: stand apart from the believers. Qatadah said: they are removed from every good. Al-Dahhak said: the guilty are separated from one another, so the Jews form one group, the Christians a group, the Magians a group, the Sabians a group, and the idol-worshippers a group. Dawud ibn al-Jarrah said: the Muslims are separated from the guilty, except the people of desires (ahl al-ahwa'), for they will be with the guilty.

Then God rebuked and reproached them with His saying: ﴿Did I not charge you, O children of Adam, that you should not worship Satan﴾. This is among what is said to them.

*Al-'ahd* means charge (wasiyyah), meaning: Did I not command you and inform you, through the tongues of My messengers, that you should not worship Satan, meaning: that you should not obey him.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: Did I not send forth to you, through the tongue of the messengers, O children of Adam? Muqatil said: he means those who were commanded to withdraw. Al-Kisa'i said: *la* is for prohibition. It was also said: what is meant by the covenant here is the pledge taken from them when they were brought forth from the loins of Adam. It was also said: it is what God set up for them of rational proofs in His heavens and His earth.

﴿Indeed he is to you a clear enemy﴾ is a justification for what precedes it, namely the prohibition against obeying Satan and accepting his whispering. ﴿And that worship Me﴾ is conjoined to *an la ta'budu* (that you should not worship). *An* in both places is either explanatory of the covenant, which contains the sense of speech, or it may be verbal in both places, meaning: I did not charge you that you should not worship and that you should worship Me, or: Did I not charge you regarding abandoning the worship of Satan and regarding worshipping Me? ﴿This is a straight path﴾, meaning: the worship of God and His monotheism, or the reference is to the religion of Islam.

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned Satan's enmity toward the children of Adam, saying: ﴿And he has certainly led astray from among you a great multitude﴾. The *lam* is the one that prepares for an oath, and the sentence is a new sentence for rebuke and reproach, meaning: "By God, he has certainly led astray," etc.

Nafi' and 'Asim recited *jibillan* with a kasrah on the jim and the ba', and a shaddah on the lam. Ibn Abi Ishaq, al-Zuhri and Ibn Hurmuz recited it with two dammahs and a shaddah on the lam. Likewise al-Hasan, 'Isa ibn 'Umar and al-Nadr ibn Anas recited it.

Abu Yahya, Hammad ibn Salamah and al-Ashhab al-'Uqayli recited it with a kasrah on the jim, a sukun on the ba', and a lightening of the lam. Al-Nahhas said: the first recitation is the clearest.

The proof of this is that they all recited: ﴿and the earlier generations (al-jibillata al-awwalin)﴾ with a kasrah on the jim and the ba' and a shaddah on the lam.

So *jibillan* is the plural of *jibillah*, and all of them derive from *jabala Allahu al-khalq*, meaning God created them. The meaning of the verse is that Satan has led astray a great many creatures, as Mujahid said.

Qatadah said: large multitudes. Al-Kalbi said: many nations.

Tha'labi said: all the recitations have the same meaning, creation. It was recited *jilan* with a jim and a yā' with two dots below (ya' tahtiyyah).

Al-Dahhak said: a single *jil* is ten thousand, and the many is what no one counts except God, Mighty and Majestic. This recitation was also narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib.

The interrogative particle in His saying ﴿Did you not then use your reason?﴾ is for rebuke and reproach, and the *fa'* is for conjunction with an implied element demanded by the context, as was mentioned in its parallels: meaning, do you witness the traces of punishments? Did you not then use your reason? Or: Did you not use your reason regarding Satan's enmity toward you? Or: Did you not use your reason at all? The majority recited *a-fa-lam takununa ta'qilun* with the second-person address. Talhah and 'Isa recited it in the third person.

﴿This is Gehenna, which you were promised﴾, meaning: it will be said to them when they approach the Fire: "This is Gehenna, which you were promised in the world through the tongues of the messengers." The one who says it to them is the angels.

Then they will say to them: ﴿Burn therein today for what you used to disbelieve﴾, meaning: taste its heat today, enter it, and taste therein various kinds of punishment for what you used to disbelieve, meaning because of your disbelief in God in the world, your obedience to Satan, and your worship of idols. This command is one of humiliation and degradation, like His saying: ﴿Taste, indeed you are the mighty, the noble﴾ [al-Dukhan: 49].

﴿Today We will seal over their mouths﴾. *Al-yawm* is an adverbial complement for what follows it. It was recited *yukhtamu* in the passive voice, and the agent is the prepositional phrase after it.

The commentators said: they deny polytheism and the denial of the messengers, as in their saying: ﴿By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ [al-An'am: 23]. So God will seal their mouths with a seal such that they will not be able to speak. In this there is a shift (iltifat) from address to the third person, to signal that their vile deeds call for turning away from addressing them. Then He said: ﴿And their hands will speak to Us, and their feet will bear witness to what they used to earn﴾, meaning: their hands will speak of what they used to do, and their feet will bear witness against them to what they used to commit.

Al-Jumhur recited *tukallimuna* and *tashhadu*. Talhah ibn Musarrif recited *wa-li-tukallimana* and *wa-li-tashhada* with the *lam* of purpose (lam kay).

The Prophet's (ﷺ) speech in the hadiths and the poetry are translated as they stand.

Some say the purpose of the sealing upon their mouths is that the people of the place of standing (al-mawqif) may recognise them. Others say their mouths were sealed so that the confession would come from their limbs, since the testimony of one who does not speak is more forceful as proof than the testimony of one who does, because it comes in the manner of a miracle. Others say: so that they would know that their limbs, which had been helpers to them in disobeying God, became witnesses against them. What the hands speak is treated as speech and confession, because they were the direct agents of most sins, and the speech of the feet is treated as testimony, because they are present at every act of disobedience. The speech of the doer is a confession, and the speech of one present is testimony. This is a reasoning based on what is most common, for otherwise the feet may also be direct agents of disobedience, just as the hands may be.

﴿And if We willed, We would have obliterated their eyes﴾, meaning: We would have removed their eyes and made them such that no slit and no eyelid would appear on them.

Al-Kisa'i said: "ṭamasa, yaṭmusu, and yaṭmisu; the maṭmūs and the ṭamīs, according to the lexicographers, is the one who has no slit in his eyes," as in His words: ﴿And if God had willed, He would have taken away their hearing and their sight﴾ [al-Baqarah: 20]. The object of the willing is omitted: that is, if We willed to obliterate their eyes, We would have obliterated them.

Al-Suddi and al-Hasan said: the meaning is that We would have left them blind, wandering, unable to see the path of guidance. Ibn Jarir chose this view. ﴿So they would race toward the path﴾ is coordinated with "We would have obliterated" — that is, they would hasten to the path to cross it and proceed along it. The word "al-ṣirāṭ" (the path) is in the accusative by the removal of the preposition, meaning: they would race toward it. ʿAṭāʾ, Muqātil and Qatādah said: the meaning is, if We willed, We would have gouged out their eyes and blinded them to their error.

And We would have turned their sight from misguidance to guidance, so they would see their right course, be guided, and hasten to the path of the Hereafter. The meaning of ﴿Then how would they see?﴾ is: how would they see the path and handle its travel well, when they have no sight?

ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar read "fa-istabaqū" in the imperative form, meaning: it will be said to them, "Race!" In this there is a threat to them.

Then He repeated the threat to them, saying: ﴿And if We willed, We would have transformed them in their places﴾. Al-maskh is the alteration of the creation into a stone or something else of inanimate matter, or into a beast. Al-makāna means the place; that is, if We willed, We would have changed their form in the place where they are.

It is said: al-makāna is more specific than al-makān, like al-muqāma and al-muqām.

Al-Hasan said: that is, We would have made them sit still. ﴿So they would not be able to advance or return﴾: that is, they would not be able to go or come.

Al-Hasan said: they would not be able to move forward before them, nor turn back behind them, and likewise inanimate matter does not advance or retreat.

It is said: the meaning is, if We willed, We would have destroyed them in their dwellings. It is also said: We would have transformed them in the place where they committed the disobedience.

Yahya ibn Sallam said: all of this is on the Day of Resurrection.

The majority read ﴿ʿalā makānatihim﴾ in the singular. Al-Hasan, al-Sulamī, Zirr ibn Ḥubaysh and Abū Bakr (on the authority of ʿĀṣim) read "makānātihim" in the plural.

The majority read "muḍiyyan" with a ḍammah on the mīm. Abū Ḥaywah read "maḍiyyan" with a fatḥah on it, and it is narrated from him that he read it with a kasrah; this reading is also reported from al-Kisa'i.

It is said: the meaning is, they would not be able to return, so the verb was placed in the position of the verbal noun for the sake of the rhyming verse-ending (fāṣila). It is said: maḍā yamḍī muḍiyyan, when he went along the earth; and rajaʿa yarjiʿu rujūʿan, when he came back from where he had come.

﴿And whomever We grant long life, We reverse him in creation﴾. The majority read "nankusuhu" with a fatḥah on the first nūn, sukūn on the second, and a ḍammah on the kāf, lightened. ʿĀṣim and Ḥamzah read it with a ḍammah on the first nūn, a fatḥah on the second, and a kasrah on the kāf, doubled.

The meaning is: whoever We prolong his life, We change his creation, and make him the opposite of what he was at first in strength and freshness.

Al-Zajjāj said: the meaning is, whoever We prolong his life, We reverse his disposition, so that weakness replaces strength, and senility replaces youth. A similar verse is His words, glory be to Him: ﴿And among you is one who is returned to the most abject age, so that after knowledge he knows nothing﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 5], and His words: ﴿Then We returned him to the lowest of the low﴾ [al-Tīn: 5]. The meaning of ﴿Will you not then use your reason?﴾ is: will you not know by your intellects that whoever is capable of that is capable of the resurrection and the rising up?

The majority read "yaʿqilūn" with the third-person (yā’ taḥtiyya). Nāfiʿ and Ibn Dhakwān read it with the second-person (tā’ fawqiyya), as an address.

When the disbelievers of Makkah said that the Qur'an is poetry, and that Muhammad is a poet, God refuted them with His words: ﴿And We did not teach him poetry﴾. The meaning is the negation that the Qur'an is poetry. Then He negated that the Prophet is a poet, saying: ﴿nor is it befitting for him﴾, that is, poetry is not valid for him, does not come to him, and would not be easy for him even if he sought it or wished to say it. Rather, when the Prophet (ﷺ) wished to recite a line that a poet had composed, quoting it as an example, he would break its metre. When he recited the well-known line of Ṭarafah ibn al-ʿAbd, which is his saying:

"Days will reveal to you what you did not know, and there will come to you with news one whom you have not supplied."

He said: "and there will come to you with news one whom you have not supplied." And on another occasion he recited the saying of al-ʿAbbās ibn Mirdās al-Sulamī:

"Will you make my plunder and the plunder of ʿUbayd / between ʿUyaynah and al-Aqraʿ?"

He said: "between al-Aqraʿ and ʿUyaynah." And he also recited:

"Islam and grey hair are enough for a man as a restraint."

Abū Bakr said: "O Messenger of God, the poet only said: 'Grey hair and Islam are enough for a man as a restraint.'" He said: "I bear witness that you are the Messenger of God. God, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And We did not teach him poetry, nor is it befitting for him﴾."

Such things have occurred from him (ﷺ) many times.

Al-Khalil said: poetry was more beloved to the Messenger of God than much of speech, but it did not come easily to him. End of quote.

The wisdom of his not being taught poetry and his not being able to do it is to complete the proof and to refute the doubt, just as God made him unlettered, unable to read or write. As for what is narrated from him (ﷺ) of his saying:

"Are you anything but a finger that bled, and in the way of God what you have suffered?"

And his saying:

"I am the Prophet, there is no lie; I am the son of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib."

and the like, these are accidental coincidences that occurred without intent, as happens in some verses of the Qur'an. They are not poetry, nor is poetry intended by them. Rather it happened by chance, as occurs in much of people's speech, for people may speak in a way that, if one considered it, would fall into the metre of poetry, yet they do not count it as poetry. Such is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿You will not attain righteousness until you spend of what you love﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 92], and His saying: ﴿And basins like cisterns, and fixed cooking pots﴾ [Saba': 13]. Moreover, al-Akhfash said that the saying "I am the Prophet, there is no lie" is not poetry.

Al-Khalil said in Kitāb al-ʿAyn: what comes as rhymed prose (sajʿ) in two halves is not poetry.

Ibn al-ʿArabī said: the more apparent state of his (ﷺ) speech is that he said "lā kadhibu" with the ḍammah on the bāʾ of kadhib, and with the kasrah on the bāʾ of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib.

Al-Naḥḥās said: some said that the transmission is according to the inflection (iʿrāb), and if it is according to the inflection, it is not poetry, because if he opens the bāʾ of the first, or makes it dammed, or gives it tanwīn, and kasrahs the bāʾ of the second, it goes out of the metre of poetry.

It is said: the pronoun in "lahu" (for him) refers to the Qur'an, that is: it is not befitting for the Qur'an to be poetry. ﴿It is only a reminder﴾, that is, the Qur'an is only a reminder among reminders and an admonition among admonitions. ﴿And a clear Qur'an﴾, that is, a book among the heavenly books of God, comprising the legal rulings of the Sharia.

﴿That it may warn whoever is living﴾, that is, that the Qur'an may warn whoever is living, that is, whose heart is sound, accepting the truth and refusing falsehood; or that the Messenger may warn whoever is living.

The majority read with the yāʾ taḥtiyya. Nāfiʿ and Ibn ʿĀmir read with the tāʾ fawqiyya. On the first reading the intended one is the Qur'an, and on the second the intended one is the Prophet (ﷺ). ﴿And the word may be fulfilled against the disbelievers﴾, that is, the word of punishment is due against those who persist in disbelief and refuse to believe in God and His messengers.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Abi al-Dunya, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Ḥātim and Ibn Mardawayh have reported through various chains from Ibn ʿAbbās concerning His words ﴿Busy in joy, they are delighted﴾, that he said: "In the deflowering of virgins."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Abi al-Dunya, ʿAbd Allah ibn Aḥmad in Zawāʾid al-Zuhd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn Masʿud concerning the verse that he said: "The deflowering of virgins occupied them."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd reported from ʿIkrimah and Qatādah the same.

ʿAbd Allah ibn Aḥmad in Zawāʾid al-Zuhd reported from Ibn ʿUmar that he said: "Whenever the believer wishes for a wife, he finds her a virgin."

Something similar has been narrated as a hadith traced to the Prophet from Abū Saʿīd, traced to the Prophet, in al-Ṭabarānī's al-Ṣaghīr and Abū al-Shaykh's al-ʿAẓamah.

Something similar was also narrated from Abū Hurayrah traced to the Prophet, in al-Diyāʾ al-Maqdisī's Ṣifat al-Jannah.

Ibn Abi Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās concerning His words ﴿Busy in joy, they are delighted﴾, that he said: "Striking the lutes."

Abū Ḥātim said: "This is perhaps an error on the part of the listener; what it actually is, is the deflowering of virgins."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Ḥātim reported from him that he said: "Fākihūn means joyful."

Ibn Mājah, Ibn Abi al-Dunya in Ṣifat al-Jannah, al-Bazzār, Ibn Abi Ḥātim, al-Ājurrī in al-Ruʾyah, and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Jābir that he said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "While the people of Paradise are in their bliss, a light shines upon them, so they raise their heads, and behold, the Lord has looked down upon them from above them, and says: 'Peace be upon you, O people of Paradise.' This is the saying of God: ﴿Peace, a word from a Lord, Most Merciful﴾. He said: So He looks at them and they look at Him, and they do not turn to anything of the bliss as long as they are looking at Him, until He veils Himself from them, and His light and His blessing remain upon them in their dwellings." Ibn Kathir said: "In its chain there is something to be considered."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās concerning the verse that he said: "Indeed God Himself greets them with peace."

Aḥmad, Muslim, al-Nasāʾī, al-Bazzār, Ibn Abi al-Dunya in al-Tawbah (and the wording is his), Ibn Abi Ḥātim, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqī in al-Asmāʾ wa al-Ṣifāt reported from Anas concerning His words ﴿Today We will seal upon their mouths﴾, that he said: "We were with the Prophet (ﷺ), and he laughed until his molar teeth showed. He said: 'Do you know what I laughed at?' We said: 'No, O Messenger of God.' He said: 'At the servant's address to his Lord, saying: O Lord, did You not protect me from injustice? He says: Yes. He says: Indeed I do not accept against myself except a witness from myself. He says: Sufficient is your own self today as a witness against you, and the noble recording angels as witnesses. Then his mouth is sealed, and it is said to his limbs: Speak! So they speak of his deeds. Then he is left between himself and speech, and he says: Away with you, and ruin, it was on your account that I was contending.'"

Muslim, al-Tirmidhī, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqī reported from Abū Saʿīd and Abū Hurayrah, both of whom said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The servant meets his Lord, and God says: Say, did I not honour you, and make you a leader, and marry you, and subject to you horses and camels, and leave you to lead and pasture? He says: Yes, O Lord. He says: Did you think that you would meet Me? He says: No. He says: Then I forget you as you forgot Me. Then he meets the second and says the same, then he meets the third and says the same to him. He says: I believed in You, and in Your Book, and in Your Messenger, and I prayed, fasted, and gave charity, and he praises himself with good as far as he can. He says: Shall We not send our witness against you? He thinks to himself: Who is it that will testify against me? So his mouth is sealed, and it is said to his thigh: Speak! So his thigh speaks, and his mouth, and his bones, of his deeds, whatever they were. That is so that he has no excuse for himself, and that is the hypocrite, and that is the one with whom God is angry."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Ḥātim reported a similar hadith from Abū Mūsā.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 36, verses 55–70 (part 3 of 3):

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying: ﴿And if We willed, We would have obliterated their eyes﴾ he said: "We would have blinded them and led them astray from guidance." ﴿Then how would they see?﴾ meaning: how would they be guided?

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him regarding His saying: ﴿And if We willed, We would have transformed them﴾ he said: "We would have destroyed them." ﴿In their places﴾ he said: "In their dwellings."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related, saying: "It reached me that it was said to ʿAisha: 'Did the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ever recite any poetry?' She said: 'It was the most hateful speech to him, except that he would recite a verse of the brother of Banu Qays, and he would place its last part first, saying: "And there comes to you one who has not provided you with news."' Abu Bakr said: 'It is not like this.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Indeed, by Allah, I am not a poet, nor is it fitting for me.'" This refutes what we related earlier from al-Khalil, that poetry was more beloved to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) than much of speech.

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ahmad related from her, she said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was slow to receive news, he would recite the verse of Tarafah:
"And there comes to you with news one who has not provided."

Ibn Abi Shaybah related "from Ibn ʿAbbas, he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would recite from the poems:
"And there comes to you with news one who has not provided."

al-Bayhaqi related in his Sunan "from ʿAisha, she said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) never composed a line of poetry except one verse:
"Be optimistic with what you desire, and it will be; for rarely is it said of anything that it has happened but that it came true."
ʿAisha said: "He did not say 'tahaqquqan' (realization), lest he inflect it and it become poetry." Its chain is thus: He said: Abu ʿUbayd Allah al-Hafiz informed us, meaning al-Hakim; Abu Hafs ibn Ahmad ibn Nuʿaym narrated to us; Abu Muhammad ʿAbd Allah ibn Hilal al-Nahwi al-Darir narrated to us; ʿAli ibn ʿAmr al-Ansari narrated to us; Sufyan ibn ʿUyaynah narrated to us from al-Zuhri, from ʿUrwah, from ʿAisha, and he mentioned it."

Al-Mizzi was asked about this hadith and said: "It is munkar (rejected). He did not know the teacher of al-Hakim, nor the blind man (al-Darir)."

When God, glory be to Him, mentioned the state of the disbelievers, He followed it with a description of the state of His righteous servants. He placed this among what will be said to the disbelievers on that Day, as an increase in their regret, a completion of their distress, and a completion of the affliction that has befallen them and the misery they have witnessed. When they see what God has prepared for them of various kinds of punishment, and what He has prepared for His friends of various kinds of bliss, this reaches their hearts to a great degree, and it increases the tightness of their chests by an increase that cannot be measured.

The meaning is: the people of the Garden on that Day are occupied with the pleasures they are in, which are such that "no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and it has not occurred to the heart of any human" (cf. Hadith), so they are diverted from concern for the disbelievers and their destination to the Fire, even if they were their relatives.

It is preferable not to restrict the occupation (shughl) to any specific thing.

Qatadah and Mujahid said: their occupation that Day is the deflowering of virgins. Waki' said: their occupation is listening (to music).

Ibn Kaysan said: it is visiting one another. It was also said: their occupation is that they are, that Day, as guests of God.

The Kufans and Ibn 'Amir recited *shughulin* with two dammahs. The rest recited it with a dammah on the shin and a sukun on the ghayn. Both are dialects, as al-Farra' said. Mujahid and Abu al-Simak recited it with two fathahs.

Yazid al-Nahwi and Ibn Hubayrah recited it with a fathah on the shin and a sukun on the ghayn.

The recitation of the majority is *fakihun* with a raf' (nominative), as the predicate of *inna*, with *fi shughulin* (in occupation) related to it, or in a place of nasb as a circumstantial (ḥāl). It is permissible that *fi shughulin* be in a place of raf' as the predicate of *inna*, with *fakihun* as a second predicate.

Al-A'mash and Talhah ibn Musarrif recited *fakihina* with a nasb, as a circumstantial (ḥāl), and *fi shughulin* is the predicate.

Al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far, Abu Haywah, Abu Raja', Shaybah, Qatadah and Mujahid recited *fakuhun*. Al-Farra' said: they are two dialects, like *al-fari-hu* and *al-farihu*, and *al-hadhiru* and *al-hadharu*.

Al-Kisa'i and Abu 'Ubaydah said: *al-fakih* means one who possesses fruit, like *tamir* and *labin*, while *al-fakih* means one who enjoys himself and lives in comfort. Qatadah said: *al-fakihun* means those who are amazed (or pleased with themselves).

Abu Zayd said: it is said, "a man is *fakih*" when he is good-natured and cheerful.

Mujahid and al-Dahhak said as Qatadah said.

Al-Suddi said as al-Kisa'i said.

﴿They and their spouses are in shade, reclining on couches﴾. This sentence is a new (independent) sentence, brought to explain the manner of their occupation and their enjoyment, and to complete it with what increases their joy and delight, namely that their spouses are with them in this same state of reclining on couches. The pronoun *hum* is a subject (mubtada'), *azwajuhum* is conjoined to it, and the predicate is *muttaki'un* (reclining). It is permissible that *hum* be an emphatic pronoun for the pronoun in *fakihun*, with *azwajuhum* conjoined to that pronoun, and the raf' of *muttaki'un* as the predicate of an omitted subject. *Fi zilalin* is related to it or is a circumstantial, and likewise *'ala al-ara'iki*. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that *fi zilalin* be the predicate and *'ala al-ara'iki* be a new sentence.

The majority recited *fi zilalin* with a kasrah on the ẓa' and an alif, which is the plural of *zill* (shade). Ibn Mas'ud, 'Abd ibn 'Umayr, al-A'mash, Yahya ibn Wathhab, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf recited *fi ẓulalin* with a dammah on the ẓa' and without an alif, the plural of *ẓullah* (canopy). On both recitations, what is meant is the furnishings and curtains that shade them like tents and canopied beds. *Al-ara'ik* is the plural of *arikah*, like *safa'in* is the plural of *safinah*, and what is meant by it is the couches that are inside the canopied beds.

Ahmad ibn Yahya Tha'lab said: *al-arikah* is only a couch within a dome.

Muqatil said: what is meant by the shades is the shelters of palaces.

The clause ﴿For them therein is fruit﴾ explains what they enjoy in the Garden of food, drink and the like.

What is meant is abundant fruit of every kind of fruit. ﴿And for them is whatever they ask for﴾. *Ma* here is either the relative pronoun with an omitted returning pronoun, or a qualifying (descriptive) *ma*, or a verbal *ma*. *Yaddda'una* is the present tense of *idda'a*.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: *yaddda'una* means "they wish for" (yatamannawn). The Arabs say, "ask of me whatever you wish," meaning "wish." And "so-and-so is in the best of what he wishes for," meaning "what he desires."

Al-Zajjaj said: it is from *du'a'* (calling), meaning what the people of the Garden call for, and it comes to them, from "I called my servant," so the *iftial* form is in the sense of the simple verb, like *al-ihtimal* in the sense of *al-haml* (carrying) and *al-irtihal* in the sense of *al-rahl* (departing).

It was said: *if'ala* is in the sense of *tafa'ala*, meaning they call one another to it, like their saying *irtamaw* and *taramaw* (they threw at one another).

It was said: the meaning is that whoever among them claims something, it is his, because God has (p-1229) imprinted upon them that none of them claims anything except what is fitting and becoming for him to claim. *Ma* is the subject, its predicate is *lahum* (for them), and the clause is conjoined to what precedes it.

*Yad'una*, with lightening (takhfif), was also recited, and its meaning is clear.

Ibn al-Anbari said: stopping at *yaddda'una* is a good pause.

Then a new start: *salamun* (peace), in the sense of: for them is peace. It was said: *salamun* is the predicate of *ma*, meaning: what is granted is pure, or possessing safety.

Al-Zajjaj said: *salamun* is in the nominative as a substitute (badal) for *ma*, meaning: and for them is that God sends peace upon them, and this is the wish of the people of the Garden. The preferable view is that His saying ﴿and for them is whatever they ask for﴾ be understood in its generality, and this peace enters under it as a primary inclusion, and there is no basis for restricting it to a particular type, even if it is the noblest of its types, in order to realize the sense of generality and to respect what the Qur'anic composition requires.

It was also said: *salamun* is raised as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "peace" is said to them as speech. It was also said: *salamun* is the subject, and its predicate is the verbal noun that governs *qawlan* (speech), meaning: "peace" is said to them as speech. It was also said: its predicate is ﴿from a Lord, Most Merciful﴾. It was also said: the estimation is: "Peace be upon you." This is according to the recitation of the majority.

Ubayy, Ibn Mas'ud and 'Isa recited *salaman* with a nasb, either as a verbal noun (masdar) or as a circumstantial in the sense of "pure." *Al-salam* is either from greeting (tahiyyah) or from safety (salamah).

Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi recited *salmun*, as if he said: "peace" (salm) is theirs, without dispute over it. *Qawlan* is in the accusative as a verbal noun, with an omitted verb, in the sense of: God said that to them as speech, or He says it to them as speech, or it is said to them as speech. ﴿From a Lord, Most Merciful﴾ means: from His side. It was said: God sends a cloud to them with the peace.

Muqatil said: the angels enter upon the people of the Garden from every gate, saying: "Peace be upon you, O people of the Garden, from a Lord, Most Merciful."

﴿And separate yourselves today, O guilty ones﴾. This is by the omission of a verb of speech, corresponding to what was said to the believers. That is: it is said to the guilty: "Separate yourselves," meaning: withdraw, from *maza hu ghayrahu*. It is said: "I separated the thing from the thing" when you isolate it from it and remove it.

Muqatil said: its meaning is: withdraw today, meaning in the Hereafter, from the righteous. Al-Suddi said: be apart. Al-Zajjaj said: stand apart from the believers. Qatadah said: they are removed from every good. Al-Dahhak said: the guilty are separated from one another, so the Jews form one group, the Christians a group, the Magians a group, the Sabians a group, and the idol-worshippers a group. Dawud ibn al-Jarrah said: the Muslims are separated from the guilty, except the people of desires (ahl al-ahwa'), for they will be with the guilty.

Then God rebuked and reproached them with His saying: ﴿Did I not charge you, O children of Adam, that you should not worship Satan﴾. This is among what is said to them.

*Al-'ahd* means charge (wasiyyah), meaning: Did I not command you and inform you, through the tongues of My messengers, that you should not worship Satan, meaning: that you should not obey him.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: Did I not send forth to you, through the tongue of the messengers, O children of Adam? Muqatil said: he means those who were commanded to withdraw. Al-Kisa'i said: *la* is for prohibition. It was also said: what is meant by the covenant here is the pledge taken from them when they were brought forth from the loins of Adam. It was also said: it is what God set up for them of rational proofs in His heavens and His earth.

﴿Indeed he is to you a clear enemy﴾ is a justification for what precedes it, namely the prohibition against obeying Satan and accepting his whispering. ﴿And that worship Me﴾ is conjoined to *an la ta'budu* (that you should not worship). *An* in both places is either explanatory of the covenant, which contains the sense of speech, or it may be verbal in both places, meaning: I did not charge you that you should not worship and that you should worship Me, or: Did I not charge you regarding abandoning the worship of Satan and regarding worshipping Me? ﴿This is a straight path﴾, meaning: the worship of God and His monotheism, or the reference is to the religion of Islam.

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned Satan's enmity toward the children of Adam, saying: ﴿And he has certainly led astray from among you a great multitude﴾. The *lam* is the one that prepares for an oath, and the sentence is a new sentence for rebuke and reproach, meaning: "By God, he has certainly led astray," etc.

Nafi' and 'Asim recited *jibillan* with a kasrah on the jim and the ba', and a shaddah on the lam. Ibn Abi Ishaq, al-Zuhri and Ibn Hurmuz recited it with two dammahs and a shaddah on the lam. Likewise al-Hasan, 'Isa ibn 'Umar and al-Nadr ibn Anas recited it.

Abu Yahya, Hammad ibn Salamah and al-Ashhab al-'Uqayli recited it with a kasrah on the jim, a sukun on the ba', and a lightening of the lam. Al-Nahhas said: the first recitation is the clearest.

The proof of this is that they all recited: ﴿and the earlier generations (al-jibillata al-awwalin)﴾ with a kasrah on the jim and the ba' and a shaddah on the lam.

So *jibillan* is the plural of *jibillah*, and all of them derive from *jabala Allahu al-khalq*, meaning God created them. The meaning of the verse is that Satan has led astray a great many creatures, as Mujahid said.

Qatadah said: large multitudes. Al-Kalbi said: many nations.

Tha'labi said: all the recitations have the same meaning, creation. It was recited *jilan* with a jim and a yā' with two dots below (ya' tahtiyyah).

Al-Dahhak said: a single *jil* is ten thousand, and the many is what no one counts except God, Mighty and Majestic. This recitation was also narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib.

The interrogative particle in His saying ﴿Did you not then use your reason?﴾ is for rebuke and reproach, and the *fa'* is for conjunction with an implied element demanded by the context, as was mentioned in its parallels: meaning, do you witness the traces of punishments? Did you not then use your reason? Or: Did you not use your reason regarding Satan's enmity toward you? Or: Did you not use your reason at all? The majority recited *a-fa-lam takununa ta'qilun* with the second-person address. Talhah and 'Isa recited it in the third person.

﴿This is Gehenna, which you were promised﴾, meaning: it will be said to them when they approach the Fire: "This is Gehenna, which you were promised in the world through the tongues of the messengers." The one who says it to them is the angels.

Then they will say to them: ﴿Burn therein today for what you used to disbelieve﴾, meaning: taste its heat today, enter it, and taste therein various kinds of punishment for what you used to disbelieve, meaning because of your disbelief in God in the world, your obedience to Satan, and your worship of idols. This command is one of humiliation and degradation, like His saying: ﴿Taste, indeed you are the mighty, the noble﴾ [al-Dukhan: 49].

﴿Today We will seal over their mouths﴾. *Al-yawm* is an adverbial complement for what follows it. It was recited *yukhtamu* in the passive voice, and the agent is the prepositional phrase after it.

The commentators said: they deny polytheism and the denial of the messengers, as in their saying: ﴿By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ [al-An'am: 23]. So God will seal their mouths with a seal such that they will not be able to speak. In this there is a shift (iltifat) from address to the third person, to signal that their vile deeds call for turning away from addressing them. Then He said: ﴿And their hands will speak to Us, and their feet will bear witness to what they used to earn﴾, meaning: their hands will speak of what they used to do, and their feet will bear witness against them to what they used to commit.

Al-Jumhur recited *tukallimuna* and *tashhadu*. Talhah ibn Musarrif recited *wa-li-tukallimana* and *wa-li-tashhada* with the *lam* of purpose (lam kay).

The Prophet's (ﷺ) speech in the hadiths and the poetry are translated as they stand.

Some say the purpose of the sealing upon their mouths is that the people of the place of standing (al-mawqif) may recognise them. Others say their mouths were sealed so that the confession would come from their limbs, since the testimony of one who does not speak is more forceful as proof than the testimony of one who does, because it comes in the manner of a miracle. Others say: so that they would know that their limbs, which had been helpers to them in disobeying God, became witnesses against them. What the hands speak is treated as speech and confession, because they were the direct agents of most sins, and the speech of the feet is treated as testimony, because they are present at every act of disobedience. The speech of the doer is a confession, and the speech of one present is testimony. This is a reasoning based on what is most common, for otherwise the feet may also be direct agents of disobedience, just as the hands may be.

﴿And if We willed, We would have obliterated their eyes﴾, meaning: We would have removed their eyes and made them such that no slit and no eyelid would appear on them.

Al-Kisa'i said: "ṭamasa, yaṭmusu, and yaṭmisu; the maṭmūs and the ṭamīs, according to the lexicographers, is the one who has no slit in his eyes," as in His words: ﴿And if God had willed, He would have taken away their hearing and their sight﴾ [al-Baqarah: 20]. The object of the willing is omitted: that is, if We willed to obliterate their eyes, We would have obliterated them.

Al-Suddi and al-Hasan said: the meaning is that We would have left them blind, wandering, unable to see the path of guidance. Ibn Jarir chose this view. ﴿So they would race toward the path﴾ is coordinated with "We would have obliterated" — that is, they would hasten to the path to cross it and proceed along it. The word "al-ṣirāṭ" (the path) is in the accusative by the removal of the preposition, meaning: they would race toward it. ʿAṭāʾ, Muqātil and Qatādah said: the meaning is, if We willed, We would have gouged out their eyes and blinded them to their error.

And We would have turned their sight from misguidance to guidance, so they would see their right course, be guided, and hasten to the path of the Hereafter. The meaning of ﴿Then how would they see?﴾ is: how would they see the path and handle its travel well, when they have no sight?

ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar read "fa-istabaqū" in the imperative form, meaning: it will be said to them, "Race!" In this there is a threat to them.

Then He repeated the threat to them, saying: ﴿And if We willed, We would have transformed them in their places﴾. Al-maskh is the alteration of the creation into a stone or something else of inanimate matter, or into a beast. Al-makāna means the place; that is, if We willed, We would have changed their form in the place where they are.

It is said: al-makāna is more specific than al-makān, like al-muqāma and al-muqām.

Al-Hasan said: that is, We would have made them sit still. ﴿So they would not be able to advance or return﴾: that is, they would not be able to go or come.

Al-Hasan said: they would not be able to move forward before them, nor turn back behind them, and likewise inanimate matter does not advance or retreat.

It is said: the meaning is, if We willed, We would have destroyed them in their dwellings. It is also said: We would have transformed them in the place where they committed the disobedience.

Yahya ibn Sallam said: all of this is on the Day of Resurrection.

The majority read ﴿ʿalā makānatihim﴾ in the singular. Al-Hasan, al-Sulamī, Zirr ibn Ḥubaysh and Abū Bakr (on the authority of ʿĀṣim) read "makānātihim" in the plural.

The majority read "muḍiyyan" with a ḍammah on the mīm. Abū Ḥaywah read "maḍiyyan" with a fatḥah on it, and it is narrated from him that he read it with a kasrah; this reading is also reported from al-Kisa'i.

It is said: the meaning is, they would not be able to return, so the verb was placed in the position of the verbal noun for the sake of the rhyming verse-ending (fāṣila). It is said: maḍā yamḍī muḍiyyan, when he went along the earth; and rajaʿa yarjiʿu rujūʿan, when he came back from where he had come.

﴿And whomever We grant long life, We reverse him in creation﴾. The majority read "nankusuhu" with a fatḥah on the first nūn, sukūn on the second, and a ḍammah on the kāf, lightened. ʿĀṣim and Ḥamzah read it with a ḍammah on the first nūn, a fatḥah on the second, and a kasrah on the kāf, doubled.

The meaning is: whoever We prolong his life, We change his creation, and make him the opposite of what he was at first in strength and freshness.

Al-Zajjāj said: the meaning is, whoever We prolong his life, We reverse his disposition, so that weakness replaces strength, and senility replaces youth. A similar verse is His words, glory be to Him: ﴿And among you is one who is returned to the most abject age, so that after knowledge he knows nothing﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 5], and His words: ﴿Then We returned him to the lowest of the low﴾ [al-Tīn: 5]. The meaning of ﴿Will you not then use your reason?﴾ is: will you not know by your intellects that whoever is capable of that is capable of the resurrection and the rising up?

The majority read "yaʿqilūn" with the third-person (yā’ taḥtiyya). Nāfiʿ and Ibn Dhakwān read it with the second-person (tā’ fawqiyya), as an address.

When the disbelievers of Makkah said that the Qur'an is poetry, and that Muhammad is a poet, God refuted them with His words: ﴿And We did not teach him poetry﴾. The meaning is the negation that the Qur'an is poetry. Then He negated that the Prophet is a poet, saying: ﴿nor is it befitting for him﴾, that is, poetry is not valid for him, does not come to him, and would not be easy for him even if he sought it or wished to say it. Rather, when the Prophet (ﷺ) wished to recite a line that a poet had composed, quoting it as an example, he would break its metre. When he recited the well-known line of Ṭarafah ibn al-ʿAbd, which is his saying:

"Days will reveal to you what you did not know, and there will come to you with news one whom you have not supplied."

He said: "and there will come to you with news one whom you have not supplied." And on another occasion he recited the saying of al-ʿAbbās ibn Mirdās al-Sulamī:

"Will you make my plunder and the plunder of ʿUbayd / between ʿUyaynah and al-Aqraʿ?"

He said: "between al-Aqraʿ and ʿUyaynah." And he also recited:

"Islam and grey hair are enough for a man as a restraint."

Abū Bakr said: "O Messenger of God, the poet only said: 'Grey hair and Islam are enough for a man as a restraint.'" He said: "I bear witness that you are the Messenger of God. God, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And We did not teach him poetry, nor is it befitting for him﴾."

Such things have occurred from him (ﷺ) many times.

Al-Khalil said: poetry was more beloved to the Messenger of God than much of speech, but it did not come easily to him. End of quote.

The wisdom of his not being taught poetry and his not being able to do it is to complete the proof and to refute the doubt, just as God made him unlettered, unable to read or write. As for what is narrated from him (ﷺ) of his saying:

"Are you anything but a finger that bled, and in the way of God what you have suffered?"

And his saying:

"I am the Prophet, there is no lie; I am the son of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib."

and the like, these are accidental coincidences that occurred without intent, as happens in some verses of the Qur'an. They are not poetry, nor is poetry intended by them. Rather it happened by chance, as occurs in much of people's speech, for people may speak in a way that, if one considered it, would fall into the metre of poetry, yet they do not count it as poetry. Such is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿You will not attain righteousness until you spend of what you love﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 92], and His saying: ﴿And basins like cisterns, and fixed cooking pots﴾ [Saba': 13]. Moreover, al-Akhfash said that the saying "I am the Prophet, there is no lie" is not poetry.

Al-Khalil said in Kitāb al-ʿAyn: what comes as rhymed prose (sajʿ) in two halves is not poetry.

Ibn al-ʿArabī said: the more apparent state of his (ﷺ) speech is that he said "lā kadhibu" with the ḍammah on the bāʾ of kadhib, and with the kasrah on the bāʾ of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib.

Al-Naḥḥās said: some said that the transmission is according to the inflection (iʿrāb), and if it is according to the inflection, it is not poetry, because if he opens the bāʾ of the first, or makes it dammed, or gives it tanwīn, and kasrahs the bāʾ of the second, it goes out of the metre of poetry.
